div.head: POULTRY PEN.
div.p: POULTRY PEN.
HINTS AND INTERESTING FACTS AND CHATS FOR AMATEURS.

FRESH AIR IN THE POULTRY HOUSE. It is absolutely necessary, if fowls are to be kept healthy and in good condition, that there zhall be kept an adequate supply of fresh air in the sleeping quarters. Ventilation without a draught is the ideal to aim for in the con- struction of a poultry house. Suitable Ventilation Essential.

All kinds of houses are to be met with. There are those to meet the requirements of the back- yarder, and of the man who adopts the semi- intensive system. Then 'there is the farmer's colony poultry house and buildings suitable for the exhibitor. All these different forms may be purchased very cheaply, or constructed by the owner himself at .a reasonable cost. In so many of these various kinds of houses, excellent as moSt,of them are in every other direction, insufficient provision is made for proper ventilation. A popular kind of house is one made with a raised floor, the object being to provide shelter underneath. This, of course, so far as the shelter is concerned, is very good, but often the floor is raised, much higher than is necessary, which takes from the air space of the house, and adds to the difficulty of securing ventilation without a draught. Avoid a Draught.

Open-fronted houses are becoming very popu- lar, and, if properly constructed; a great deal is to be said in their favour. It is frequently contended that such houses are draughty. This, however, does not naturally follow, since there is no through current of air in which the birds perch, and in this lies the greatest danger. Whatever form of the house is used, whether large,. small or medium, whether portable or permanently fixed, endeavour should always be made to obtain a sufficiently powerful current of air to pass through the house that will carry away all impure air, and supply the oxygen required to keep the house sweet, and, con- sequently, the inmates healthy. The ventila- tion holes, or louvre boards, should be at the highest parts of the ends of the house. It is important in this connection that the perches be placed near the ground-18in. high—and so arranged that the birds escape draught from their entrance trap-door. Fresh air is an im- portant factor in the successful 'rearing of poultry, and neglect in this direction will probably bring trouble in the way of disease. The origin of many of the diseaies from which fowls suffer may be traced to breathing impure air.—Middlesex, in "Farm and Home."

div.head: DEMAND FOR POULTRY.
div.p: DEMAND FOR POULTRY.

The alarming shortage of cattle for consump- tion must, I think, directly affect the poultry- man, because it will increase the demand or poultry produce. Those who have good stocks of early chickens should be able to dispose of the cockerels somewhat readily this year, and prices should be of a paying standard. I am afraid there will not be the supplies in the country to meet requirements, because the cost of foodstuffs has undoubtedly influenced breeders, and those who have fowls to dispose of now that have any pretentions to table pro- perties will experience a quick sale whenever they are ready to market them. The condi- tions, too, and immediate prospects emphasise it that poultry-keepers should early dispose of all unprofitable specimens for consumption. The chickens in question of feeding will be making their presence felt more and more daily, and a reduction of the number of superfluous heads whilst prices are good will permit of better attention and stronger rations for the youngsters. If business must be made in any degree profitable now, strict details of economy must be put into practice, and it is the small matters that are most important.—" The Feathered World."

div.head: BACKYARDER.
div.p: THE BACKYARDER.

The prices of poultry foods are still on the rise. But, as eggs and all meats are also gradually on the rise too, it will pay' the back- yarder to raise a few chicks so that they will come in for table purposes later. Such a lot have sold out of their stock, and others are not raising any, that it will make it better for those who are chancing it. • Maize seems to be the main food, and other corns are hard to get. I have noticed several backyard pens empty, but I expect that after a good crop of vegetables they will fill up again after the war, and be benefited by the rest, for some backyards have had fowls running in them for years, and with no change. It is wise to take the old soil out yearly and put some fresh in its place, and I also like to supply plenty of grit and lime and give fresh litter pretty regularly,: and even if you have to pay top price for good straw it pays in the long run.

No doubt those who have some early chicks are eyeing them very 'cutely now, picking out the wasters'and turning them over to the pot or oven department. It won't pay to feed on wasters. Stock will sell at toy price later. and the poultry-keeper must be prepared to be in with others for prices are sure to be very high, and real good stuff will be in great demand. I would advise the‘backyarder to obtain every bit of vegetable which is being wasted, chop it up and boil and dry off with bran and middlings. It is surprising what a great saving vegetables are.—" The Feathered World." ,

div.p: ROUSING CALL TO THE 'IOtPIG IViEpt,
Oratory And Music Induce Many To Take Up Arms And Play Their Part.

div.head: SUCCESSFUL WEEK-END RECRUITING CAMPAIGN.
div.p: SUCCESSFUL WEEK-END RECRUITING CAMPAIGN.

The monster recruiting campaign organised in Warrington and district by Lord Derby and his co-workers, lasted over the week-end, and closed on Tuesday, after a series of meet- ings and demonstrations which will long remain in the memories of those who took part in, or witnessed, them. The appeal for more men to swell the ranks of the local Territorial battalions, or to join the Regular Arrily was cairied into every part of the town—into the streets, into the parks, into the works, into the theatres and into the picture palaces—and we are glad to learn that it was not without encouraging response on the part, of those to whom it was addressed, recruits coming for- ward as a result of each of the meetings held, inspired to do so by the stirring music of the three bands engaged—Lord Derby's, the South Lancs. and the Liverpool Scottish Pipers—and the earnest eloquence of the many speakers, military and civilian, whose services were requisitioned.

military age, or otherwise unfitted for service themselves, to do all they could to stimulate and encourage their fellows to join the glorious Army •or the equally glorious Navy, which in these terrible days were doing so much for the nation. First and foremost, perhaps, they wanted 400 more men for the Warrington Bat- talion—the 4th (Territorial) Battalion of the South Lancashire Regiment, .of whose record and achievements all in that town were so justly proud—(cheers)—and in whom they were so in- tensely interested. Had they read of the casual- ties the brave body of Warrington lads at the Front had already sustained? No doubt they had, and be Wanted each of them within reach of his voice to do what they could to send more, and still more, of the lads of the town to avenge the deaths of the brave sons of Warrington who had gone under in the country's glorious cause. " One of His Own Boys!' in Belgium.

Might he also make an appeal on behalf of the Liverpool Scottish, because, one of his boys was in Belgium fighting with . that fine regi- ment? (Cheers.) He-wanted Other lads to come from Warrington to help him and his comrades. Even after they had done their best in War- , rington for the Territorials and the Liverpool Scottish, there would still be plenty of young men who might, nay, ought to go to help some of the other regiments. "Those "—.-said his Worship in ringing tones that evoked a. tornado of cheers—" who can go and won't go are lnly cowards of the worst . degree. I cannot-help feeling pained and grieved when I walk along the streets, particularly at nights, and notice all the young fellows who spend their tilne strolling about, when they really augnt t; go and take a hand in this business." Fe tried to find 4,1, excuse for them—that they were iork- ing on 'mpinticns of war; but at Jte v 2, 1 of it all he was teund to come to the conclusion that there were very few of them who could not be spared for the sterner work at the Front. (Hear, hear.) Let them all do what they could—men and women, old and young alike—for the coun- try of which they were so proud; let those among them who were young enough and fit not hesi- tate, but offer themselves forthwith as recruits for Great Britain's glorious army, and. by so doing not only help their country, but also assist in upholding the tradition i of which War- rington was so proud, and justly proud. (Cheers.) " TERRIERS " AS SPIRITED AND AS • BRAVE AS THE REGULARS.

Colonel Moggridge, who was greeted with cheers on rising to speak, said that it was not so long ago since the Regulars and the Terri- torials were very distinct, one .from the other; but that time had gone. (Hear, hear.) The Territorials were now fighting alongside the Regulars in the trenches—fighting with exactly the same spirit and exactly the same bravery; indeed, one did not and must not look upon 'them as being in any degree different from the Regular troops. (Cheers.) In these -days every able.-bodied man should either be fighting or working—the,fighter was necessary and so was the worker. An army was no good unless it had rifles and guns and the other necessary munitions, just as rifles and guns and muni- tions were no use unless there were men to use them; and it was the duty of the people at home to supply both men and munitions. Every time they went into the streets they saw able- bodied young men—mostly bachelors—who Were neither working nor fighting, and it was a shame. (Hear, hear.) -When " the Boys" Come Home!

To such young men he would like to say: "Think of the future! What are you going to say when the boys come home? They are going to ask you some awkward questions; they are going to say 'What have you done?' " It would be awkward if they had no satisfactory; answer! Every eligible than should enlist whilst there was a chance. There was a chance now; there might not be tn the near future. "Don't," concluded the Colonel, "let other men fight your battles for you; come and help to fight them for yourselves—and for your country." (Cheers.) EVERY YOUNG MAN SHOULD BE FIGHT- ING, OR

Major Monks, the next speaker, said that 400 men were wanted for the "Third-Fourth " and wanted as soon as possible! Did all the young unmarried men between the ages of 20 and 30, who had not yet given in their names, consider that they had done, or were doing, their duty? Were they making munitions, or were they merely working for their owm com- fort, as usual? Nowadays, young men should either be fighting or working on munitions of war! (Hear, hear.) If they did not do one or the other of those two things, then the country could not survive
THE TWO ALTERNATIVES, And the One the Country Will Chocse.

Mr. Tyson Wilson, M.P., said that in his opinion the time ha 4 gone past for debating whether the country should be at war or not. and there were now only two courses open—and, one was to see the war through to an early and successful conclusion and the other to back out. There was only one of the alternatives that the country could possibly adopt—the former. (Hear hear.) The " Tommies "at the Front were continually writing home and asking what their peace-time comrades were doing to help them. What were they doing, or what were they prepared to do to help? He hoped that every eligible young man in Warrington, provided his services were not required for the manufacturing of armaments would come for- ward that night. (Hear, hear;) The only eligible son he had was serving in a regiment whose headquarters used to be in Warrington. (Applause.) He was in the King's Liverpools— (renewed applause)—and he was out at the Front. A certain section of the Press—as, also, certain individuals—were accusing the working men, generally, of being slack6rs, but he absolutely denied the truth of that allegation. (Hear, hear.) The average worker was ready and willing to do his utmost to produce munitions of war, and if there had been a shortage in the past it was no fault of the work- ing man. (Hear, hear.) It was due to bad organisation on the part of the employers. (Hear, hear.)
A Reflection Upon Christianity.

At the same time there were, perhaps, a large number of men who did not realise the serious position in which the country was placed. Was it not time that those men made a serious effort at waking up? It was up to the eligible men of this country to see to it that the spirit of German militarism, which was a standing menace to the peace of the world—a reflection upon civilisation and Christianity-:--was crushed. (Applause.) Aye, it was up to every young man to see the Present terrible business through, and to see it through successfully. Did the young men need a 'rouser '? Then let them think of the cold-blooded, deliberate murders that had recently taken place on the high seas! The sinking of peaceable vessels was abominable—(hear, hear)—and it ought to be stopped. The mere fact that it had taken Place ought to have brought to the side of the Allies every civilised nation in the world. (Cheers.) He was hoping that .America would now realise that it was her duty to step in and use all the influence she co-uld to put an end to the abominable sea-outrages that, of late, had become painfully frequent. A Task For Every Fit Man.

The duty to fight devolved upon every fit man of: military age, and there was the duty devolving upon every other ale man of seeing to it that the lads at the Front were not short of the munitions of war. (Hear, hear.) It rather disguested him when he heard some, of his political friends quarrelling about sixpence or a shilling a week, and going about demand- ing increases in wages because living and coal and rent had gone up, and forgetting the greatest cost of all—the cost in human lives which the war was exacting as toll. He was a man of peace and believed in peace, but there could be no peace, and would be none, until they had completely smashed the Germans, and they could not do that until they had sufficient men and ammunition. (Hear, hear.) It had been often debated, he knew, but he believed that it was absolutely impossible for this country to

have kept out of the war—especially after what took place in Belgium. (Hear, hear.) The Mayor then called upon Captain Gordon Roberts for a few words, remarking that he had been' to the Front and had bled for them, and was now recruiting his health by trying to recruit more men.

div.head: WARRINGTON 'TERRIERS" PROUD BOAST.
div.p: WARRINGTON 'TERRIERS" PROUD BOAST.
Among First To Offer For Boer War And Among The First Now.

Captain Gordon Roberts, who is home from the Front, wounded, presided at a recruiting meeting held at Bridge Foot on Saturday after- noon. The principal speakers were Mr. J. Parker, M.P., and Mr. Tom Smith.
UPHOLDING A GOOD REPUTATION. Who Will Off6l. To Fill Up a Gap?

Captain Roberts, in the course of a short opening speech, said they were there that after- noon to' try and get recruits for the Territorial Battalion which belonged to Warrington. They were also prepared to take men for the Line. The 1/4th Battalion, which was the original Territorial unit, belonging to this town, was now out in Flanders, and had been there sine the third day of February. The battalion, in the old days, alwajs had a good reputation, and it had kept that reputation to this very moment. It was one of the first Volunteer battalions to offer its services in the South African War, just as it was also one of the first Territorial battalions to offer its services last August. It was also one of the first battalions to be accepted for foreign service. "We are," said the gallant Captain, "losing men—we can- not help losing them—and we want these recruits for the 3rd/ 4th battalions. so that they can be trained, and sent out when they are needed to fill up the gaps. There are two or three reasons why I appeal to Warrington to send more men—we want another fdur hundred. Sights That Would—and Should—Fire the Blood. ,

If you had seen Belgium as I have seen cottages, houses, churohes, schools; in fact every building composed of bricks and mortar; simply razed to the ground—there would be no need to be holding these meetings to get the young men to join the colours. When we were not in the trenches we Used to see Belgian women and children fleeing from their homes —trying to find another temporary -residence, until we could push back the German devils— they are nothing else! (Hear, hear.) When r was in hospital„ a Scottish officer told me of an incident which he saw with his own eyes. A fellow-officer of his was wounded in the head. Blood was streaming down his face, and for the time being it blinded him. Captain Roberts Describes a Cowardly Murder.

Two German officers—so called—came out of their trench and getting hold of him, led him back to their trench. A German " TOmmy " then came behind with his bayonet fixed, and bayoneted the officer in the back and killed him. (Murmurs of horror.) That is murder, not war, and if you men have got any grit in you, you will be prepared to avenge these crimes. We do not want any men who are engaged in Government work, for they are doing their duty just as well as the men in the trenches, for we must have guns and ammunition. (Applause.)

div.head: WHAT IS IT KEEPS THE SINGLE MEN
div.p: WHAT IS IT KEEPS THE SINGLE MEN
BACK?

Mr. Tom Smith began by saying that they were there that afternoon for one purpose. About a month ago Lord Derby instituted a recruiting campaign throughout West Lanca- shire, and the result was that they had got five or six thousand recruits for the West Lanca- shire Territorials alone. Although that seemed a large figure it was not nearly enough, for Lord Kitchener had said that if the Terri- torials who were now out in Flanders were to be kept up to fighting strength, it was essential that they should raise many more men. He was delighted ,to see so many men in khaki in Warrington and, When he saw them, he was set thinking as to what it was ,that was holding the young men back. They were not asking for the married men yet,.6B per cent. of Kitchener's Army were married men. As to the men who were engaged in the making of munitions of war, they did not ask for them, for they were helping to win the war by sticking to their work—helping as much as the men in the trenches. They had to realise that it was necessary to fight the Germans in. France, or they would have to fight them here in England, maybe even; in Warrington itself. Germany meant business. She was perfectly organised, and would never rest content until she came here with her army. He believed, and the Government believed, that the Germans would not only make an attempt to land in this country. but that they would succeed in land- ing. Whether they would get back or not was different matter, but they would come, as sure as the sun would set that evening.

div.head: For Mother, For Sister—and For Country!
div.p: For Mother, For Sister—and For Country!

"Think of it," said the speaker. "Our women. sisters and mothers, may be subjected to the unspeakable crimes perpetrated upon the 'Belgians. Our houses andfc'hureles Imv also be razed to the ground. I think more of my sister than of the whole German Empire put together. What do you think of yours, young man?" (Applause.)
A WORD TO THE " COME-WHEN-WE-ARE- FETCHED " MtN.

Mr. J. Parker, M.P., said it was of the utmost importance that the war should be brought to a successful conclusion, Although the working- class had .responded very well, there were still some who said "We will come when we are fetched." He did not want to see compulsory service instituted. What was it that was keep- ing the young man back? He was sure it was not lack of courage—cowardice. No, it was thoughtlessness. There was not a better insti- tution to which the young man could belong than the British Army. (Cheers.) The band played several selections before, the meeting.

div.head: ROUSING MILITARY
div.p: ROUSING MILITARY
TATTOO.
Hit' Crowd Listens To Stirring
Xppeals And Stirring Music.

The biggest meeting of the loeal campaign was undoubtedly that held on Saturday even- ing .on the beautiful Stretch of lawn fronting the Town Hall. The crowd numbered thousands, and was intensely enthusiastic, cheering loudly the patriotic appeals made by the different speakers, and applauding with gusto the strik- ing military tattoo in which the various bands engaged during the week-end figured, and which proved a striking finale to an altogether rousing meeting. "THOSE WHO CAN GO, BUT WON'T."
" Cowards of the Worst Degree," Says the Mayor.

The Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) was in the chair, and he began by emphasising the fact that the purpose of that gathering/wat; business, not pleasure—the business of getting more men for the service of their King ad country. They wanted all who were fit and could go, and ought to go, to go, and they wanted all and sundry, who were above the

div.head: CAPTAIN GORDON ROBERTS'S CAla.
div.p: CAPTAIN GORDON ROBERTS'S CAla.

Captain Roberts, who received a splendid ovation, said he appealed first of all for men for his own battalion, which, ever since the days of the old Volunteers, had always enjoyed a good record. Since February it had been out in Flanders, taking duty alongside the Regulars in the trenches and like 7 them, of course, it had suffered casualties, and, through him, the men of that battalion were now appealing to their workmates and friends in Warrington to rally round and complete the new 3rd/4th battalion in order that when they wanted assistance out at the Front, the men, trained and eager to help, would be at hand. (Applause.) . Had they seen what he had seen in Flanders there would be no need to hold recruiting meetings; the men would not wait to be coaxed or goaded—they would simply flock into the ranks. "Now then, men—if you are men," said the Captain in conclusion, "you know what has been going on in Belgium; you know how the inhabitants of that once happy country had been treated and you know how the Huns have treated our own kith and kin! Doesn't that sort •of thing want finishing? (Shouts of assent.) Very well then, it's up to you to come and help us to finish it. (Cheers.) Every man who is not engaged in making munitions or in some other necessary work for the Army or Navy, and who is of the requisite age, should be standing shoulder to shoulder with his mates in his country's service, and there is no excuse for any man hanging back! (Cheers.)

div.head: "SMASH THE KAISER AND HIS BARBARIANS."
div.p: "SMASH THE KAISER AND HIS BARBARIANS."
Captain Townroe added a few words of appeal to the young men of Warrington, not already enrolled, to "come forward and help to smash the Kaiser and his German bar- barians:',

This concluded the speeches, and then, came the military tattoo, in which the three bands engaged in the recruiting campaign and a firing party took part, the audience also being called in to aid by assisting in the singing of the hymii "Abide with me," with which the tattoo ended,

After listening to the national anthems of the Allies and singing their own with great heartiness, the crowd dispersed. Later in the evening there was a lantern dis- play from the van furnished by Mr. J. S. Ark- wright, the former Unionist M.P. for Hereford. The pictures shown included war scenes and 'portraits of national leaders, and they were described by Mr. A. J. Harman and Ex-Corporal Weir, who fought in the South African cam- paign.
BIG CROWD AT BRIDGE FOOT.
More Men and More Time Required to Beat
the Germans.

The last meeting of the campaign that was held in Warrington itself was that at Bridge Foot at noon on Monday, when, despite the some- what awkward' hour,, a large crowd gathered to listen .to the appeal for men, as voiced by Mr. Tom Smith, Mr. IL Ternent, and others. Second-Lieutenant Townroe was the chairman, and Mr. Smith told his enthusiastic -auditors that he never for a moment refused to believe but what Britain and' her gallant Allies would beat the Germans to "a frazzle," but empha- sised the fact that more 'men and more time were required.

- --- In the course of his rousing Speech,. 36.. Ter- nent said, . amid cheers, that the Territorials had proved ,their worth over and Over again, and nobody could now sneer at them and call them Saturday night soldiers. If the Germans came to Warrington they would not be content with wrecking • suburban villas; they would go to the thickly-populated Parts and attempt to murder the working classes.

div.head: IN THE RURAL DISTRICTS. Series Of Successful Village Meetings.
div.p: IN THE RURAL DISTRICTS. Series Of Successful Village Meetings.

The remainder of Monday was devoted to a tour of the rural districts more., or less adjacent to Warrington. Lord Derl4l3 Band toured the area between Warrington and Kenyon, via Manchester-road, and took part in meetings held at the Glue Works, Martinscroft Green; at Woolston, at Hollins Green, at Culcheth, at Croft and at Lang End, just beyond Kenyon— each meeting beink,addresed by an officer and by one or more well-known local gentlemen.

div.head: CALL SOUNDED- AT PEN KETH.
div.p: THE CALL SOUNDED- AT PEN KETH.

In the evening the band went to Penketh, where an enthusiastic meeting was held in the Recreation Ground, under the chairmanship of Dr. Murray who,. in the course of a rousing call to the young men, said that he was afraid that before the war was over everybody would be called upon to do something for their country—either to fight, to make munitions, to tend the wounded, or to perform some other national service.

Captain Townroe said that if the Germans once got a foothold in this country it would be a ease of "God help any women or children who got into their clutches. The best way to prevent the enemy coming into our fair land and ravaging it, as they had ravaged Belgium, was to go over to France "and fight him." In conclusion th%Captain said that he understood that there were in Penketh about sixty men who were not engaged on war work, and who could be spared to join the colours, and he hoped to see them come forward.. Mr. Ternent also spoke.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY LISTENS TO THE APPEAL.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY LISTENS TO THE APPEAL.

Whilst the Penketh meeting,was in progress the band left for Great Sankey, where another open-air meeting of considerable proportions was being held, under the chairmanship of the Vicar (the Rev. J. R. Jones), who said that the present war was not a battle between aristo- crats, or between we-alth and wealth, or even between the armies of the respective kingdoms; but it was a battle for righteousness, justice and truth, against .slavery, murder and lust. (Hear, hear.) At the close of the Vicar's speech three working men—one of them married—stepped forward, the grime of the honest toil which they had just left still upon them, and an- nounced- their intention of enlisting; where- upon they were whirled away to the Drill Hall in Warrington. Captain Townroe referred to the, scheme before Parliament for making provision .for the future of men disabled in the war, and said that he believed that under that scheme the disabled soldier would receive a pension of something like 15s. a week and would be helped in the matter of obtaining suitable em- ployment.
Mr. Tom Smith also addressed the meeting.
SPEECHES AT SANKEY BRIDGES.
The closing meeting of the evening was held at Sankey Bridgos—near the tramway terminus in Liverpool-road.

Mr. W. Furness, who presided, said in the course of his brief remarks, that every effort was being made to avoid ,conscription, and if this country could do her part in winning the war on voluntary lines it would certainly be a great feather in her cap, and would be some- thing that she could look back upon with intense pride and satisfaction. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Ternent addressed the meeting.

div.head: TWO BANDS .I'f STOCKTON lIKITH
div.p: TWO BANDS .I'f STOCKTON lIKITH
The same evening the band of the 2/4th South I4aneashire Regiment and the Scottish Pipers visited -Stockton Heath, when a large assembly was addressed by Mr. E. Wynne Jones and others.
The meetings in the various outlying villages were reached by motor vehicles. Placed at the disposal of the speakers and bandsmen by various local owners and by the Warrington Corporation.

div.head: FIFTEEN-YEAR-OLD HERO.
div.p: FIFTEEN-YEAR-OLD HERO.
AVounded Whilst Signalling For The
" Lion's " Gunners.

A fifteen-year-old sailor boy—he really looked younger than his years—formed an interesting figure at many of the big recruiting meetings, especially when it became known that young as he is he has actually been wounded in the service oi his country and is at present on sick- leave. div.head: STUDY LANGUAGES!
div.p: STUDY LANGUAGES!
Commercial Tra‘ellers And Openings
After The War.

Mr. W. P. Ashton (chairman) presided at the quarterly general meeting of the Warrington and District Branch of the United Kingdom Commercial Travellers' Association, held at the Lion Hotel last Saturday. The attendance also included Mr. H. Walsh (vice-chairman) and Mr. T. Percival (hon. secretary). Before the business began a vote of con- dolence was passed with Mr. Fulton-Smith (a vice-president of the branch) by the members standing. • The Chairman and Mr. W. G. Hayes, in pre senting a very interesting report of the annual

conference of the Association, which was held in Manchester in Whit-week, spoke of • the stress which had been laid on the necessity for the study of foreign languages. It had been men- tioned speciallf by Sir Richard Cooper, the retiring president, and also by Sir Wm. Mather, the new president. This refers not to commercial travellers alone, but to men in all classes of trade for, as was pointed out, after the war is over there will certainly be many good openings for men to go abroad. A hearty vote of thanks was passed to the delegates, on the motion of Mr. P. O'Brien.

It was unanimously agreed that a letter of congratulation be sent to Sir Arthur 11. Cros- field, Bart., on the honour recently conferred upon him. Sir Arthur is one of the oldest vice- presidents of the branch, and has always taken a great interest in the work.

ROUSING CALL TO THE YOUNG MEN.-

cheeks and a mischievous sparkle in his eyes— is Stanley Robert's, and he'beloUgs to Liverpool and is borne on the hooks of H.M.S. Lion, being rated as a "boy." The story of how .Stanley came to be wounded was told to a mass meeting at Bridge. Foot by Mr. Tom Smith. Putting his hand on Stanley's shoulder, whilst the boy smiled proudly,- Mr. Smith said: "I wonder if the man who is al-. ways wanting to know why he should fight and who is always pointing out that he has no property or possessions worth fighting for would like to .put his question to this little chap—Boy Stanley .Roberts, of His Britannic Majesty's Man-o'-War. Lion.' What had this lad to fight for?

div.head: Lesson to Other Boys and Young Men.
div.p: A Lesson to Other Boys and Young Men.

"Do you women who are standing around here know that you have been protected by this little boy? Do you men knew it, who are not working on war munitions, °but who are smoking cigarettes and strolling about the, streets or attending places of amusement, with an air of nonchalance more suitable for time: of peace? DO you know this little boy has been defending Your hearth and home? He is 15 years Of age, and he was on H.M.S. Lion u_s a signaller in the North Sea fight, when that. ship, with others, sank the Blucher. (Cheers) This little, boy was wounded in the arm while he was blowing, the signal for the gunners to Make their shots. He has been invalided home -La wounded sailor 15 years of age. And Yet young men walk about the ,streets and say

'What have I to fight for?' Surely f you have got a mother, a sister, or a wife, or a sweet- heart. Are they not worth defending? If you do not think they are, •surely your own pre- cious skin is worth defending." (Laughter.) As he left the " platform " Stanley was given yet another rousing cheer and a few in the crowd yelled for a speech, hut the lad smil- ingly shook his head in denial.

Captain Townroe's Comment And Thanks.

Captain 'rownroe, the lion. acting secretary for Lord Derby's campaign, has sent the fol- lowing letter to Liententint C. L. Williamson, with the request that it should be published in the local Press:—

. "*On behalf of Lord Derby, chairman of the West Lancashire Territorial Association, I beg to thank all the Warrington' gentlemen who generously placed cars at the disposal Of the recruiting campaign in your area. Without the cars it would have been impossible to have covered so large a tract of country in so short a time, and the 4th South Lancashire Regiment owe a debt of gratitude to the car owners for their hearty response to your appeal. Although so many men in 'Warrington are engaged on war service, that recruits are not eaily ob- tained, nevertheless we met, as you know, many eligible unmarried men in the shops and in the country districts, and there is little doubt that persistent effort should bring the 3/ 4th up to strength. We have written to the Mayor asking. him to thank the Town Council for placing at our disposal the Town Hall, Park, and the Parr Hall last Saturday, but we also have to . thank the Corporation for allowing us the use of an omnibus ,'on. which to transport the band during this week. FARM AN D CARDEN,
SOLDIERS FOR THE HAY HARVEST.

The Board of Agriculture and Fisheries have been informed by the Army Council that in view of the possible shortage of agricultural labour for the hay harvest, furlough will be given, at the discretion of the military authorities, to a limited number of soldiers of the new Armies and of the Territorial force for work in the hay harvest as circumstances may permit. The furlough granted to each soldier will last • only for such number of days, not ex- ceeding fourteen, as4he is actually required for haymaking. The employment of soldiers in the hay harvest Will be subject to the following conditions:- 1. That suitable labour cannot be obtained in the locality. 2. That the farmer will undertake to pay each soldier sent at his request:

(a) 4s. kday if the soldier provides his own - board and lodgings; (b) 2s. Gd. a day if board and lodgings is provided by .the .farmer. • 3. That the. farmer Will" provide conveyance from and to the nearet railway station. No charge will be made to the farmer for railway travelling expenses. Every endeavour will he made to ensure that the men released have been accustomed to farm ,work, but no guarantee to this . effect can,.be given. The above arrangements will not apply to the 'corn harvest, in respect of which fresh regulations be issued. . .

Applications from farmers who desire to employ soldiers in the hay harvest must be made as soon as possible to the Board of Trade Labour Exchanges, when the application will be transmitted to the military authorities. Forms for the purpose are obtainable from the local Labour Exchange, the address of which can be obtained from the nearest post office.

div.head: CROP PROSPECTS.
div.p: CROP PROSPECTS.

The Crop Reporters of the Board, in com- menting on agricultural condition ‘l in England and Wales on June Ist, •state that wheat is ,generally .in a healthy and vigorous condition. and has improved during the month, though on some of the heavy lands it is rather discoloured. Barley and oats are somewhat backward, the cold nights and dry weather having retarded their growth. Early potatoes have been affected by the frosts in some districts, but are mostly healthy. The planting of the main crop is nearly com- pleted, but very little is yet showing above ground. The area planted is estimated to be ahouti the same as in last year. Nearly all the mangels have been got in, but germination is slow. Where it is up, the plant is looking healthy.

div.head: .1 CHESHIRE FARMER AND HIS
div.p: .1 CHESHIRE FARMER AND HIS
MILK.
Case Disnlissed.

At the Manchester City Police Court on Wed- nesday, George - Massey, of Blackden, Holmes Chapel, was summoned for consigning to the Failsworth Industrial Society, Ltd., milk from which fat had been abstracted to the extent of 121 per cent. Mr. Pickford, of the Prosecuting Solicitors' Office, prosecuted, and Mr; T. S. Steel, of Warrington, defended. Inspector HoUliston stated that on the 11th of May he took samnles at the Mayfield Station. Manchester. of milk consigned by the defendant to the Failsworth Society. One sample on analysis proved to contain 2.8 per cent. of fat, and as 'compared with milk taken from the cows at the defendant's farm the following morning which attained 3.2 per cent, of fat, it was deficient in fat to the extent of 12.1 per cent. In answer to Mr. Steel. the Inspector stated that when compared with the staPdard laid down by the Board of Agriculture, the milk was only 6 per cent. deficient in fat. He took samples from three tankards, and two out of the three were above the standard. Mr. Steel, in defence, said that the 'defendant had a child seriously ill, and in conseonenee. on the morning in onestion. was not able to super- vise the milking of the .eows. One of his emnloyes was an old mnn, and a poor milker. and as the Insnector had admitted, on his visit to the farm. be had occasion to null the old man up with regard to his milking. The deficiency in this one tankard conld easily he caused imnroper milking, and that was the only explanation the,defendant could give. Tie had been sending .milk Jo Manchester for several NWT'S. and this was the first complaint he had had. -Mr. Steel suggested that under the circumstances it was not a case for conviction, and that 'justice , would be met by the payment of the costs. • •
Eventually' the case was dismissed on the pay- inent of costs.

div.head: HOME OF HEALING.
div.p: A HOME OF HEALING.
Where Peace And Beauty HeIP To Mend Wounded Warriors.

Nothing .heals the mind .seared by the sanitY" straining experiences of the modern battlefield like the peace and the beauty of Nature at her loveliest. The war-worn heroes who return t° the hospitals at home need something besides mere physical healing, important though that . is. The mind re:quires .mending as well as the body, and, not only so, but the mending of the. body may be greatly accelerated by the mending of the mind, a fact that is universally reeog" nised in the world of medicine and surgerY• Thus, the importance of paying attention to the surroundings in which our wounded soldieri' are brought baok to a condition rendering theto once again ready for the firing line cannot he overestimated. - The first consideration of the average person, in the matter of 'the treatment of the returned soldier, is, of course, not .40 much the preparation. of the man to take his niece at the earliest possible moment in the trench or behind the gun. Rather do they thinof what he has been through. and what, by that token, be is entitled to.. It is humanity "0 think of before utility in doing what we earl to ensure the comfort and happiness of ou,. gallant lighters struck down in their country battles. This is as it should be.,

CALM AFTER STORM. Debts of honour must be paid, not the least those owed to "Tommy Atkins." When 1 - comes home battered from the wars he shouhl have the best of everything we can give bin). In at least one quiet backwater in the old country convalescent soldiers are receiving treatment that may well be considered idea The place we refer to is not many miles out of Warrington. - It is a beautiful. private -resi- dence, with glorious, grounds, that has bee° converted into a temporary auxiliary. hospital" Here the tennis racquet is substituted for the sword, the bowl for the hand-grenade, the billiard cue for the rifle, the croquet mallet f°l; the ramrod of the big gun. Here the song 01 birds does (lewd* for the scream of murderous ~ shells; and God-given perfumes for the aeria , smell of powder and the devilish poisons of mis-used science. Here sacred life is saved all° .., guarded, not destroyed by ingenious machinet that belch out death till the metal it is ulguer of boils the water that surrounds it and prevents it melting.' -Here the sights til'a Q,Teet the warriors' eve are soothing, y.-bere: before they harrowed. E"ere the rule elf artificial ..•hate recedes into .the background, ft incredulity, and kindness and mercy, t'''.•• droppeth as the gentle rain from ileacci'‘ is supreme. A SPLENDIDLY MANAGED HOSPITAL. The splendidly managed hospital at Thelival! Hsc eys is the outcome of a heme inangurate( some little Iv/bile age by Mrs. F. A. Frost, °I Grappenhall: Tn making her arrangementg; Mrs. Frost was loyally supported by a hand 01 enthusiastic helpers. The hospital, which can accommodate.twentY six patients, is excellently staffed. The fund!' far, its upkeep are principally raised hr tb Working Men's Committee, which was forine°, • seine six or seven weeks avo. The members 0' this committee have worked nobly for a noble cause. Their suce-ssfal efforts nt raising nmone.st their workmates constitutes'one of 00 . highest features of the undertaking. A SURGICAL TRIUMPH.

At the Present time there are twenty-three patients in the hospital, five of whom are on tile point of leaving, four for a week's furlough prior to departure for the Front, and one t° be discharged from the Army. There is case with which the surgical and nursing stli are particularly preaspd, and that is the case of a soldier who came into the hospital four wounds. Skin-grafting operations hal"' been performed on him with marked success' The present complement of patients includeS Belgian who was wounded in fourteen places: , Re has been three times to the Front, and ~15 keenly desirous of getting back there again. authorities are very much indebted to 6' Latchford barber who visits the hospital twiefii a week and shaves and shears the men in ne,e of such operations. Drs. Langdale and Rel"s son constitute a very efficient surgical medical staff. The nursing staff includes following ladies:' Mrs. Erie Fairclough, Misses N. and J: Fairclough, Mrs. Parker, Graham Hutchings, Mrs. Densham, Tranton, Miss Wright, Miss Blood, Kirconncll. Mrs. Kerfoot, Miss Layton, Elgood, Miss Sloan 111 rs. Craigy and Siste Walker.

Ran Up a Lodging Bill and Disappeared.

Subsequently, however, she said that she had left the laundry and had gone to work at Messrs. Crosfield's. That statement was be- lieved, and, on the strength of it, she was given board and lodgings between April 29th and May 13th. She then disappeared and the next seen of her was when she was arrested by the Liver- pool police. In answer to the first charge she told D'etective Turner that she did work for a time in Warrington, but not during the last two weeks she was 'with Mrs. Ward. When she was brought back Mr. Siddle complained to the poliw that money had been stolen from his house, and that he suspected that prisoner had t4ken it, as she had visited his house from time to time. Altogether he had missed a sum of about £5, but she was only charged with steal- ing £2 ss.—an amount she admitted taking. In reply to this charge she said, "Yes, I did take , it." Almost every time she went to the house she purloined something. The Salvation Army man and his wife did all they possibly could for the woman, and, in return, she " did " them. Prisoner was a married woman, and was living apart from her husband, who made her an allowance of ss. a week.
Asked whether she hadanythingtosayprisoner said, amid sobs and tears, "It's all true." An Accomplished Woman.

Mr. Hudson, the police court missionary at Newton-le-Willows, said that he first met the woman two and a half years ago, when she ap- peared in the local Police Court on a charge of larceny. She -told him that she committed the theft. for food and she was bound over, and he took an interest in her. She then entered an inebriates' home in Upper Parliament-street, Liverpool, where she remained for two years, giving more than satisfaction in the home. In many ways she was really an accomplished woman and formerly she was a school teacher at Culeheth. After leaving the home she went to the Y.W.C.A., and was placed out in service, and she appeared to do very well until two or three months ago, when she absconded. Prior to making her appearance in the court at New- ton, there- was evidence that she had been in- temperate, and, for that, -her husband would appear to be somewhat to. blame. Her life was not a good life then, but it was better in the home, and better since she left it, until this hap- pened.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
PAID UP AND IS ACQUITTED.
"A BOLD IRISHMAN."

Sequel To Shop Window Smashing Finds Himself Disillusioned When It Episode. Comes To Paying The Fine. The man Austin Macdonald, who was recently "I am a bold Irishman and there's not a before the Borough, magistrates on a charge of man in the town who can take- any inoney out wilfully damaging a plate-glass window belong- of me!" This statement was attributed by a ing to Messrs. Pendlebury, Winwick-street,, police-constable at Monday's Police Court to should have made another appearance in con- Martin Rogers, a stranger to the town, who nection with the same matter at Monday's was charged with having been drunk and dis- Police Court,. but there was •no need for him orderly in Barbauld-street. to •do so, explained the • Chief Constable, for he The evidence further showed that at 9.30 at had not only deposited .t. 5 17s. 7d. to pay the night, prisoner, who was drunk, was creating cost of the damage done, but had also called a disturbance and made use of most filthy and left 10s. to cover the Court costs. Under language. He refused to go away when spoken the circumstances he (the Chief Constable) to. thought the Bench 'might mark , the charge- The Chief Constable said that the man had sheet "Discharged." When the case Was heard £1 2s. 7d. on him when arrested, am! .suggested it was not considered that, the damage was that the Bench should demonstrate to him the altogether wilful and that there was a great fallaciousness of his boast that there was no deal of the accidental about it. man who ould take anything off him. The magistrates decided to act on the Chief . The •Bench - decided to " take" 9s. Constable's suggestion.

div.head: BELLICOSE FEMALES.
div.p: BELLICOSE FEMALES.
Two Women Bound Over For Street
Fi9hting.

Before the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), Aldermen Bolton and Pierpoint, Councillor Wilkinson, and Messrs. W. Furness, G. Piling, S. Wright and T. Locker, garriet Wright and Harriet .Chesters, two married women, of Turner-street, . were charged with having com- mitted a breach of the peace in Turner-street, by fighting, on Saturday. The Chief Constable told the Court that the case arose out of a complaint made to the police by the husband of Abe woman Chesters.`lje came down to the Police Station in .the early hours of Sunday morning and complained that he had been stabbed in the eye with a knife. He had evidently been struck with some wea- pon, for he had a nasty cut just over the eye. Inquiries were made and it was ascertained that the two prisoners had been fighting and they were locked up. The bother, it would appear from inquiries, started at 9.30 p.m. and was kept up until past eleven. o'clock. Wright had been before the Court nine times, the last occasion leing in September, 1907. Chesters had not been there previously. Turner-street, on Saturday nights, was a perfect. "bear garden." .
• . The 'women were ordered to\find sureties for their good behaviour for six ntonths,- or other- wise to. go to gaol for 14 days. They were also each oidered to pay Gs. costs.

div.head: THREW THE " CROCKS " ABOUT.
div.p: THREW THE " CROCKS " ABOUT.
%VlHut Damage At Lodging-Houses
Leads To Month In Gaol.

A crockery-smashing scene in the kitchen of a common lodging-house in Ship-yard, was described to the Borough Magistrates on Mon- day morning, when David Mainwaring, a labourer, of no settled abode, was charged with doing wilful damage, to 'the extent of 2s. 2d., to six plates, three basins, a dish and a pint mug, the property of Mary Rogerson. Sarah Ann ,Leatherbarrow, who lives with her husband at 14, Ship-yard, said that •about 7.30 on Saturday night, she was sitting outside 12, Ship-yard, when she heard a crash inside the house. She went inside and there saw the prisoner pick up a pint mug and throw it across the floor. The tables and forms in the room had all been overturned, and several other articles of crockery lay broken on the floor. Asked why he had committed the damage, he said lam having my 2s. 4d. Worth !" The reference was to some money which he had. had to pay for some damage he had committed earlier in the day—the smashing of a chair and a jug. His wife had paid the 2s. 4d. and he had resented it.

div.head: " Due to a Desire to Level Up Accounts."
div.p: " Due to a Desire to Level Up Accounts."

Prisoner said the chair broken earlier in the day was broken more by accident than anything else. The landlady of the house, working ,on his wife's fears, had extracted from her 2s. 4d. for a chair that was not worth elevenpence. "My second visit," he said, "was due to a desire to level up accounts:" (Laughter.) Mrs. Rogerson told the Court that she saw the prisoner purposely break the chair, a couple of plated being also smashed.- Witness asked him why he did the damage. He had a portion of the broken chair in his hand ana was about to strike a blind lodger with it, when witness intervened. • She turned prisoner out of the house and actually returned him a shilling which he had paid for his lodgings. His wife, however, pleaded with her to allow him to return and, upon the wife paying for the chair, he was allowed to do so. • The Chief Constable said the man admitted that he had been locked up in Wrexham, and he was now sent to prison for a month, with hard labour.

div.head: PARK PESTS.
div.p: PARK PESTS.
Two Drunken And Noisy Men Fined For Obnoxious Conduct.

Before the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) and other magistrates, at the Borough Police Court on Monday morning, Joseph McMullin, a man of the labouring class' was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Bank Park on Saturday. He denied that he was drunk; saying that he only had two pints all day. The evidence was that at 6.25 in the evening the man was drunk and was shouting.. The atten- tion of the pollee was drawn to him by an alderman and his daughter who were 'passing through the Park and heard him using filthy language. lie had been five times previously before the Court for a similar offence, the last time being as recently as the 11th of last month. ,
Prisoner was fined 19s. Gd., with the alterna- tive of fourteen days' imprisonment, with hard labour.
Thomas . Williams, charged with a similar offence committed in the same place the same day, pleaded that he had only had "a drop of but owing to the hot weather that had "got him under."
He was said to have been shouting and yell- ing.

There were twelve previous convictions, and this was his tenth appearance for drunkenness He was last before th:, Court in April, 1914, when he was sent to prison for fourteen days for baying been drunk and disorderly.
A fine of 135., with the-;iiernative of 14 days' imprisonment, was imposed.
FRIGHTENING THE CHILDREN.

At Tuesday's Court George Smith, a labourer, of no settled abode, was charged with commit- ting a breach of the peace by behaving in a disorderly manner in Victoria Park the pre- vious day. Re pleaded not guilty. George Corbett, the park keeper, deposed that at about 4.40 on Monday afternoon a little girl came up to himin the park and complained of prisoner frightening the children and misbehav- ing himself in another part of the Park. Wit- ness and his foreman gardener went after the man, and .when the prisoner saw them he made for the bridge. The gardener gave chase and brought him back.

Child • Fainted From Fright. There . were Several little girls in the park, and two of them, aged about eleven, were crying, whilst one child had jut fainted .owing to pris- oner having frightened her. He was lying in the long grass and was trying to decoy the girls. A lady spoke to ILim of his conduct and'he used filthy language ,to her. lie was under the influ- ence of drink.
George Sanders, the head gardener, gave cor- roboiative evidence.

Prisoner said he had only just got: into the park when the bother happened, and he did nothing to frighten the children; they were frightened by a dog which accompanied another man. He, said nothing to no one.

div.head: Prisoner's Record.
div.p: Prisoner's Record.

The Chief Constable said the man had been twenty times before the Court. It was palpable, when he with brought to the lock-up, that he had been drinking. It was a shameful thing that men of his stamp should go about the parks frightening innocent children, as he was undoubtedly doing.
In default of finding a. surety in £5 for his iood behaviour for a period of six months, he was ordered a mouth's hard labour.

div.head: PENALTY OF PEACEMAKING.
div.p: PENALTY OF PEACEMAKING.
Woman Who Intervened Received Blow Meant For Another.
William O'Hara, a labourer, of no settled abode, was charged at Monday's Borough Police Court with having been drunk and disorderly, and also with committing an assault on a woman.

A police-officer said that at 10.25 on Saturday night he was called to the lodging-house, 5, Stanley-street. He was told that the female deputy of the house had been struck in the face by the prisoner, and he, aecordingly, ejected him_ from the premises, and, as he was drunk, subsequently, with assistance, took him to the Police. Station.

Elizabeth Wynne, the deputy of the lodging- house in quegtion, stated that she was in the kitchen of the house at 10.10 on Saturday night, when prisoner Came in drunk. She asked him to go to bed, but he refused and wanted to argue with another man, rrli wife of the man intervened and did her best to persuade the prisoner to go to bed. Instead of taking the woman's advice prisoner struck at her, and witness, in endeavouring to shield the woman, received the blow in the. face. A policeman was then called in.
• The Chief Constable said the prisoner was before the Court on Saturday. He was fined 19s. 6d., or 14 days' hard labour.

div.head: FATHER OF FOUR SOLDIER-SONS.
div.p: FATHER OF FOUR SOLDIER-SONS.
Charged With Being Drunk And Disorderly.

That he was not guilty and that he was the father of four soldier sons—three of whom are at the Front—was it plea put forward at the Borough Police Court on Monday by Thomas Mullin, a bundler, of 2, Cyril-street, when he was charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly in Market-street on Saturday night. A constable said that he was in the Market- place at about nine o'clock on Saturday night, when he saw a large crowd gathered in the street outside. He proceeded to investigate the reason, and found the prisoner standing in the middle of the crowd. The man was drunk and he was shouting. When Witness asked him to be quiet he said, "I repeat what I have been saying—that any person going into a shop like that of the who owns that one (pointing to a butcher's shop near by) ought to be off the earth." It was stated by another witness that when the man was brought into the charge office at the Police Station he was very noisy, and he continued to be so when put into the cells, kicking the door, so that the witness "had to go in and suppress him."

_ The Chief Constable said that nothing prior to this was known against the man, who, him- self, told the Court that he had just before the .trouble happened, come from the recruiting meeting in the Park. In Market-street he met a soldier with a ribbon in his cap, who pointed to a-certain shop and said. " What AO you think of people going in there?" He (prisoner) re- plied, "Well, if they don't go in the people will have to close up." Then a police officer came up and put his hand on his (prisoner's) shoulder.
The Bench imposed a fine of 65., with the alternative of seven days' imprisonment.

div.head: HAD ENLISTED TWELVE TIMES. – Motor Cycle Thief's Statement To The Police.
div.p: HAD ENLISTED TWELVE TIMES. - Motor Cycle Thief's Statement To The Police.

Victor Edward Claremont, a decently- dressed young man, said to have no occupation and to be of no settled abode, was charged, on remand; at the Borough Police Court on Tues- day morning,. with having stolen a "Levis" motor cycle, valued at £26. the property of the London and North-Western „Railway Co., and, further, with being a deserter from the Army Service Corps since November 27th. To the first charge he pleaded guilty and elected to be dealt with summarily, and the second charge was withdrawn. How Suspicion Was Aroused.

Mr. Arthur Browne prosecuted on behalf of the London and North-Western Raihkay Co. He said that on the afternoon of June 7th prisoner called at the shop of a Mr. Dendy, in Knutsford-road, and asked "if he could have a start with his motor cycle," adding that he had only had it a fortnight and that that was but his third time out. Not being satisfied with the explanation given by prisoner as to his ignorance of the mechanism of his machine, Mr. Dendy filled the carburetter with petrol and then turned the tap on so that , prisoner would not be able to, travel more than about a hundred yards. He then watched to see how the man got on, and eventually cycled after him and said .that he had received a telephone message from the Police Station instructing him to ask prisoner for his licence. Prisoner said that he had left it at home, whereupon Mr. Dendy said that he would have to go back to the shop... On the way back they met P.C. Bennett, and to the con- stable he said that he had left his licence in the pocket of another suit of clothes that had been 'sent on to Crewe. , He also said that the cycle was his own, but subsequently admitted that he took it off the railway station at Crewe that morning. He added that he had enlisted in the Black, Watch, and that he.went to sleep in the waiting-room at Crewe and missed his train for Scotland. He then saw the motor cycle standing against a pillar and told the guard that it was his and' had it' put in one of the luggage vans. When he got to War- rington he had it taken out. At the ticket barrier at Bank Quay he showed a pass to Perth. When he saw the bicycle at Crewe Station it had a ticket on it, which he tore off and put into his pocket. That ticket proved to be a Great Western Railway label and, it showed Owl the cycle was consigned from:Swindon (Wilts.) to Edinburgh—to a Mr. J. E. Alkins. As he was passing the ticket- barrier, he was asked for his ticket for the bicycle,, and he replied: "I have not got one; lam on Government service." When told that that made no difference and he would have to have a ticket for he said he had not sufficient money to pay, forr one .and he handed his Army papers over, showing that he had joined the Black Watch. His Army travelling warrant was made out from Haver- fordwest to Perth. He explained that no was going to Perth as a dispatch-,ider. Prisoner, asked what he had to say, said: "I am guilty of this and wish to be punished for it here; or will you send rue back to the Army, please?"

div.head: Why He Kept On 'Listing.
div.p: Why He Kept On 'Listing.

The Chief Constable said that it was pretty obvious that the prisoner was as little desir- ous of serving in the Army as he was of working, for, according to his own statement,. he had enlisted on no less than twelve oeca, sions, for the sake; presumably, of the travel- ling and maintenance Money that was given his idea in joining ,a regiment that involved so long a journey _as- that from Haverfordwest to Perth ' was that he would get a little more money. In October,- 1910, he was .sent to Borstal for twelve months for stealing money, other offences, committed at Accrington and Oldham, being taken into con- sideration. He enlisted in the A.S.C. in Nov- ember and deserted, and in January re- enlisted in the Royal Fusiliers. He was next heard of at Newcastle-on-Tyne, where he was looking afta ieg. 11e tlica jcized a 'Egli-

div.head: Sorry Could Not Give Him Two Years.
div.p: Sorry Could Not Give Him Two Years.

The Chairman (Councillor Roberts), in sen- tencing the prisoner to six months' imprison- ment, with hard labour, said that he, person- ally, was very sorry that the Bench Could not give him two years. He had Oxploited the British Army for his own selfish indulgence, and he deserved all the punishment he could get.

div.head: ILLEGAL KIN 1 ESS.
div.p: ILLEGAL KIN 1 ESS.
Warrington Alarket Dealer Fined For Exchanging Soldiers' Boots.

Bernard Abrahamson, of 44, St. Ducie-street, Manchester, and Stall 57, Block C., Warrington Market, Private Leese, of the sth King's Own Yorkshire Light Infantry, and Lance-Corpotal Ford, of the King's Royal Rifles (the two latter inmates of the Whitecross Hospital) were sum- moned at the Warrington Police Ccmrt en Saturday for an offence against a law which forbids the sale or exchange by soldiers f eny portion of their clothing outfit. Mr. A. Browne appeared fOr.the defendants.

The Chief Constable said that the pros3er.; tion was taken under the Act whiCh said tat any person who buys, exchanges, takes in pawn or receives from a soldier or any person :icting on his behalf or any pretext whatever, inles he prove that he acted in ignorance, shall; be liable, on summary conviction for a first offence, to a fine of £2O. On Wednesday, 26th May, Private Leese went to Mr. Abrahamson's stall in the Warrington Market Place and ex- changed his regimental boots for a lighter sort. He went in uniform, and Mr. Abrahamson clearly knew him for a soldier. When taxed with the offenee, Mr. Abrahamson Pointed. out that he was doing a charitable thing in ex- changing the boots. Mr. Nicholls said he did not propose to offer any evidence as to the second offence till after- wards.

div.head: An Act of Kindness:
div.p: An Act of Kindness:

Mr. Browne said he admitted all the facts. The Act of Parliament ~was passed to prevent the sale or exchange of :articles of a:soldier's outfit in the Ordinary time of peace. The pre- sent was not peace-time, .unfortunately. Mr. Abrahamson did not exchange with a soldier on duty as a soldier. What he did was an act of kindness. A wounded soldier came to him and said "I can't stand these heavy boots," and his client, -out of pure kindness, without any profit whatver, showed him a number of pairs of lighter boots, and eventually a pair fitted him. Mr. Browne concluded by asking- the Bench to reserve their deeision till after the evidence as to the second offence had been given.

div.head: Only Had To Ask At The Hospital.
div.p: Only Had To Ask At The Hospital.

The Chief Constable .stated that on Wednes- day, June 2nd, Private Leese told Lance- Cornoral Ford. who also found the regulation boots too heavy, where he could exchange the " regulations " for a lighter pair of boots. They went to the Market and another exchange took place. He (Mr. Nicholls) was not suggest- ing that Mr. Abrahamson made anything out of the transaction. The boots he gave in ex- change for the " regulations " were excellent. The soldiers acted in ignorance, but they ought to have it pointed out to them that they had not acted pronerly. One of them ,had plenty of money in his nos;ession o buy a pair of light hoots. They could both have got a pair_ at the hospital by .asking for them. The kind of boots they had obtained in exchange were good boots for ordinary wear. but they were no' use for active service, and they would have to go bar* sortie time.
Caned into the witrass brnv. one of the s.ldiers gaid tha4- be was Territorial, and had paid for his first pair of boots. '
Nothing Surreptiticus.

Mr. Browne said that there was nothing surreptitious about the proceedings. Mr. Abrahamson helped the soldiers on with Weir boots and laced them up in the open Market Place. with many people about. He acted as he did out of pure kindness. He had been carrying on business in the Market ,Place for eleven years. and had had no complaints. Mr. Browne concluded by appealing to the Bench not to penalise a men for acting kindly. lie had committed an offence, but only a technical one.'
The Bench, after retiring, imposed a fine of 25.
The Chief Constable saki he brought the sum- mons under the instructions of the military authorities.

div.head: SCHOOL TEACHER'S DOWNFALL. Drink, Theft, False 'Pretences-Ind
div.p: SCHOOL TEACHER'S DOWNFALL. Drink, Theft, False 'Pretences-Ind
Prison.

The story of a woman teacher's downfall through drink was told at the Borough Police Court on Tuesday morning, when Martha Adam- son, whose last address was in Liverpool, was charged on remand with obtaining from Mrs. Ada Clara Ward, of 9, Hamilton-street, food and lodgings to the value of £l. A further charge was preferred against her of stealing from the dwelling-house, 70, Battersby-lane, £2 55., the property of John Siddle.

Posed as Assistant Matron of Inebriates' Home. The Chief Constable said the woman was before the Court last week on the false pre- tences charge and had been remanded for fur- ther inquiries. It appeared that she came to Warrington, with a recommendation from some- body at Chester, and went to the house of a member of the Salvation Army—Mr. Siddle. He obtained apartments for her, she stating that she was the Assistant matron of an inebriates' home at Chester, and • that she had come to fetch some woman from Grafton-street. How- ever, she added, the home was not ready to receive her yet, and so she had, for a short time, to 'keep .the patient undgr observation in War- rington. She remained t the lodgings for some little the, and then went to the house of Mrs. Ward, whom she told that she was working at

div.head: Sorry, and Ashamed of Herself.
div.p: Sorry, and Ashamed of Herself.

Prisoner, still in tears, said she was very sorry for, and ashamed of, what she had done. The Chief Constable said the woman was con- victed at Leigh in 1902 on a charge of false pre- tences—obtaining food, etc. She was bound over .for two years. Her last conviction was on January 30th, 1913, at Newton-le-Willows, when she was again bound over and placed under pro- bation, as the result of a charge of stealing clothing.

The tench sentenced prisoner to a month's imprisonment on each charge, the sentences to run concurrently, and the Chairman (Councillor Roberts) expressed the hope that that would be the woman's last appearance in the dock.

div.head: COSTLY TRIP TO EARLESTOIX N.
div.p: COSTLY TRIP TO EARLESTOIX N.
Man Who "Lost A Turn" Ordered To
Pay £lO Damages.
GOVERNMENT WORK DELAYED.

At Tuesday's Borough Police Court, a well known local firm claimed the sum, of £lO from Ernest Noton, of 111, Bostock-street, as damages sustained by them owing to his having absented himself from his work on June 7th.— r. S. Steel (acting- on the instructions of Messrs. Henry Greenall and Co., solicitors), appeared for the plaintiffs, whilst Mr. Arthur Browne was for the defendant.

Threw Nearly Twenty Men Out of Work. Mr.. Steel, in opening the ease, said that defendant was employed by the firm Hi ques tion as a -bolter-down at their Bin. mill. lie should have started work at 6 o'clock on the evening of Monday, June 7th, but he did not turn in to his work, with the result that the Sin. mill could not be run, and there was an actual loss to the firm of £l5, although they were only claiming £lO. In addition to the loss to the firm, twenty men were affected by the absence of the defendant, and they lost wages totalling in the aggregate to £8 19s. sd.

div.head: Went to Earlestown.
div.p: Went to Earlestown.

It appeared that the man left -honie shortly after 2 o'clock on the afternoon of Monday, June 7th, taking with him a labourer employed in another department of the same establishment. They set out for Earles• town, and arrived there at 8 o'clock in the even- ing in a very drunken condition. They remained in Earlestown until Tuesday morn- ing. Defendant should have been working on a job which led up to the Government work, and the stoppage of his mill considerably reduced the output of the firm. The firm in question looked on • this as a very serious case, and the man had , threatened that if he ivere mulcted in damages that morning he would put the firm in a hole and would not tend his machine again. ,
The manager of the works gave evidence bear- ing out Mr. Steel's opening statement, and added that defendant could earn from lis. to 18s. per shift.

div.head: Not a Single " Stand-by" in the Works.
div.p: Not a Single " Stand-by" in the Works.

In answer to Mr. Browne, the witness said that he knew that on previous -occasions when defendant had been absent a substitute had been found to take his place, but at•present the con- ditions were rather different, for the firm had allowed so many of its men to go to the Front that at the moment- they had not a single " stand-by " in the works. He knew that the man had tried to enlist, and the firm did not try to prtvent him. Went to Try and Enlist.

Do you know that he went to enlist at Earlestown on this occasion?—He told me on the Wednesday that he went to enlist at Earles- town on the Monday. And that the military authorities would not take him on account of his chest measurement ? —No; he told me it was because he was work- ing on Government work. The witness added, in answer to a: further question, :that the de- fendant was a good workman when he was at it. The foreman over the Bin. mill said that when defendant was asked whether he would turn up after the case was over, he said that if he was fined he would not go to work at all. If he carried out that threat the. works would be placed in a difficulty. - Mr. Browne: He has only to give a week's notice and Tou cannot stop him leaving. As a matter of fact he worked yesterday. The labourer who went to Earlestown with the defendant said `.` We'm both had a tidy drop of beer and we went to Earlestown to 'list. We were told to come again next day. Fourteen Years With the Firm.

Mr. Browne said defendant 'had been in the employment' of the firm for fourteen years, and the manager had admitted he was an excellent workman. The Monday in question was a very hot day, and defendant, with the other 'man, took some drink and did not go to work. Deft,Admit was under the impression that one of for-men, who had taken his place on pre- vious Occasions; would do se that night, and therefore .felt he was not doing • anything wrong. • He regretted his conduct -exceedingly, although be denied making use of the threat referred to, but Simply said that lie. would give notice to leave, which he was entitled to do. •

div.head: Firm's Sporting Offer.
div.p: Firm's Sporting Offer.

Defendant was ordered to pay the amount claimed, the Chairman (Councillor Roberts) remarking that no doubt if the man went back to work the firm would make arrangements for the money to be paid by defendant as. easily as possible, provided he behaved himself and stuck to his job. Mr. Steel said that was so, and mentioned that the defendant in the last case of a similar charac- ter brought by the firm had paid his damages, and, that the lesson had had a good effect, was proved by the fact that he had not lost a single hour since. The Chairman ond "the Slackers."

The Chairman: My firm opinion is that a very‘,- very large percentage—perhaps •95 ~per cent., or possibly 971 per cent.—of the. working men in this country are doing splendidly. There are an oild man or two here and'there not doing their duty, and as far as I, as a magis- trate' can make them conceive what their proper duty is, I am going to help them to do so. I have, no compunction\ in using the law to its fullest possible extent in this time of crisis and national danger to insist that if a man does not recognise what his duty to the country is, we will try and make him do so.

div.head: I Wonder if All Mothers Are Ill!
div.p: I Wonder if All Mothers Are Ill!
