"LAST IN THE ' PUB: "
Story Of A Pair Of Boots That Disappeared.
DRUNK AND ASLEEP.

Patrick Flynn, labourer, of 10, Town-hill, was charged at the Borough Police Court on Thursday with stealing a pair of men's boots, the property of John Hayes, of 13, Dial-street, in a bar of the Lower Angel, Buttermarket- street, on June 16th. The prosecutor said that he went into the Lower Angel on the day .in question for re- freshment. After he left the house he remem- bered that he had forgotten a parcel cunt•lin- ing a pair of boots that he had just Lad stretched. lie went back and asked to see the licensee, with whim he proceeded to search the bars and failed to find the parcel. Scene: The Lower Angel. Time: 11 O'clock. The licensee of the Lower Angel gave evi- dence as to seeing prisoner unwrap a parcel containing a pair of boots. He thought no more of it at the time, but at eleven o'clodc the prosecutor came to his house and asked about the parcel. Then he recalled seeing the prisoner with the parcel, but they could not find it.
Magistrates' Appeal To Publicans For Co-operation.

At the Warrington Police Court on Thurs- day, John Wells, licensee of the Lion Hotel, Bridge-street, was summoned for selling beer to a drunken person on Saturday, June sth. Mr. Steel represented the defendant. "On a Seat and Apparently Asleep."

The Chief Constable said that on the even:- ing of the sth June, Sergeant Reddington and P.C. Anderson entered the vaults of the Lion Hotel. They went into the centre of a com- partment and observed a man named Wheldon sitting on a seat, apparently asleep._ Samuel Worthington, the manager of the bar, roused the man, who was drunk. His \beer, about three-quarters of a pint, was taken from him and he was turned out. When Ile got outside he started swearing at the manager. He was taken into custody, charged with being drunk, and wag fined at the next Court The mana- ger, Worthington, was seen by P.S. Reddington and said: "I must have served him myself, as I am in charge of the bar. I didn't notice his condition, as he came in with the rush' from the Hippodrome."

div.head: "Seven Months and a Good Feed."
div.p: "Seven Months and a Good Feed."

P.C. Foast said that he went to the house of the prisoner on the night in question and found him in bed. Witness asked him if he knew anything about a pair of boots, and prisoner replied in the negative. Witness looked about and found the boots under the bed. When asked where he got the boots, prisoner said that he bought them from a man. On the way •to the Police Station he said: "I brought them out of the 'pub.' No one else has had anything to do with it. I hope I get seven months, so that I can get a good feed." Witness searched the corner of Buttermarket-street and found the box in which the boots had originally been packed. , The prisoner, asked if ...he had anything to say, replied: "He's telling a pack of lies. I was the last one to leave the 'pub.' " The Chief Constable asked for a seven days' adjournment, to enable the police to find out something as to prisoner's antecedents. Wholesome If Not Luxurious.
The Chairman (Mr. Rymer Young): Seven days and a good feed?
The Chief Constable: Yes. -It will -be good and wholesome if not exactly what he might desire.
The prisoner was remanded for seven days

div.head: NEGLECTING WIII-WORK.
div.p: NEGLECTING WIII-WORK.
Warehouseman Repents Off Lightly.

Horace Peers, of 9, Allcard-street, Warring- ton, a warehouseman employed by a well- known local company, was on. Thursday, at the Warrington Police Court, summoned by his firm for neglecting his work so as to involve them in a loss of £lO.

div.head: Neglected His Work Owing to Drink.
div.p: Neglected His Work Owing to Drink.

Mr. Steel, for the prosecutors, said that- de- fendant was engaged on very important (lov- ernment work, and owing to drink he had neg- lected it on three successive days, viz., the 7th, Bth and 9th of June.. On the first day he came to work at 9.30, instead of 7.30, and was in and put of the works all the morning in a fuddled State. The following morning he went to work later than he should haue done, and went away at 10.30. That, of course, was rather an import- ant time. (Laughter.) Their Worships would be aware of what happened in these days at 10.30. Defendant returned in a drunken condi- tion. Next day he did not turn up to time again. It was most necessary that he should understand that whilst his firm were engaged on war werk. he must attend to his work regu- larly. He had been in the employ of the firm some time. He had an aged father dependent on him.

Had Expressed His Very Great Regret. lie had seen the manager of the works and expressed his very great regret at his behaviour. Realising how important it was for him to attend regularly and punctually at his work, he had now promised to do so. The firm did not wish to press the matter. In 'those circum- stances, he (Mr.- Steel) asked for an adjourn- ment for a month. to see if defendant carried out his promise. Ile was a good workman and was needed.
The Chairman's Admonition.

The ,Chairman (Mr. J. 'Rymer Young). ad- dressing the defendant : The magistrates think the prosecution is treating you very leniently. Your case will be adjourned for a month, on the understanding that you do not do this sort of thing again. You ought to help the authori- ties at such a time'.
The Clerk: Do you promise not to do it again?
Defendant: Yes.

div.head: And Is Let
div.p: And Is Let
The Case for the Defence.

Mr. Steel said that the Chief Constable had given a fair presentment of the facts, but he wanted to put before the Bench the position before the police entered the house. The man Wheldon came into the vaults with another man and walked quite straight. He took his beer from the counter and walked again quite straight, over to a table. About five minutes later the police came in. P.S. Reddington went across to" the man and shook him and told him to go away. Wheldon then got up aml walked, quite straight, to the door. There was no disturbance. The other people in the house did not know anything had happened. The manager exercised reasonable care in the matter. Messrs. Walker had a reputation for the conduct of their houses. They thought more of the character of their houses than of selling drink.

div.head: Too Much To Lose To Take Risks.
div.p: Too Much To Lose To Take Risks.

They had too much to lose to take risks. The instructions in force in their houses included injunctions that several characters well known in the town were not even to be admitted into the house. The houses were periodically visited by representatives of the firm, and if it was found that instructions were not being carried out it was a serious matter for the offenders. Worthington had been in the em-. ploy of the firm for fourteen years, and had spent six years in the Lion vaults. With regard to Mr. Wells, the licensee of the Lion, he was a man of the highest character and was well known to the Bench. He felt the sum- mons very keenly, coming as it did after forty years in the Trade. He relied entirely upon the trusted services of Mr. Worthington.
Local " Celebrities " Not Served—Drunk or Sober!

The Chief Constable said he could not and did not wish to dispute anything Mr. Steel had said. lie (Mr. Nieholls) was bound to take those proceedings, though he did so with some reluctance. Messrs. Walker were excep- tionally careful in the conduct of their houses. There were many local "celebrities" whom they would not serve, drunk or sober. The manager was a man of excellent character, and the house rendered the police great assist- ance. Ile was hound to say that, in fairness to the defendant.

div.head: "A Good Deal of Drunkenness Going On."
div.p: "A Good Deal of Drunkenness Going On."

The Bench (over whom Councillor Henry Roberts presided), decided unanimously to dis- miss the case on the 'payment of the costs. "We're satisfied," Mr. Roberts said, "that reasonable care was taken, but at the same time I would like to say a word to the licen- sees in general. There is a feeling amongst the magistrates that there is a good deal of drunkenness going on, and we want the licensed victuallers to be extremely careful—l am not referring to this particular house, now —not to serve anyone who appears to be, in any way, the worse for liquor.‘ I hope this warning will be accepted in the' spirit it is given. We want them loyally to co-operate with the authorities in suppri,ssing drunken- ness, and we feel sure they will. So far as you are concerned, Mr. Wells (turning to the licensee); you may leave the Court feeling that there's no reflection on you, at all."

div.head: WAR LOAN BILL.
div.p: WAR LOAN BILL.

The War Loan Bill to be introduced in the House of Commons on Monday will, it is under- stood, be similar in form to the measure passed last August, and will in general terms authorise the Treasury to raise by loan any part of the sums voted by Parliament. for the financial year.

div.head: THAT MOTOR AMBULANCE!
div.p: THAT MOTOR AMBULANCE!

Are we all doing our fair share in supporting the various war funds ? There are signs that the local lists are not being supported quite so well as they should be. Many are giving according to their ability, and so doing their bare duty, but it is clear that many are not. Some people are as much afraid of making an inroad upon their wealth as of' risking their limbs. We see many inglorious examples in this direction.

There are many wealthy men in our midst who have done nothing, or next to nothing, to help those who are fighting for them, and without whose protection their wealth would rapidly go the way of that of the late resi- dents of Antwerp and Louvain. Let us take, the case of the motor ambulance, as an ex- ample. Many weeks have passed since the MAYORESS first appealed for a few paltry pounds to enable the ambulance: men at the Front to get the. shattered pieces of humanity that come into their hands to the hospital with reasonable speed. It is a matter of life and death that depends upon the chances of a few Minutes Or a suitable nieans of convey- But, so far as Warrington is con- cerned, the MAYORESS is still appealing, and the men are hobbling and dragging 'themselves to permanent crippledom or to deatl2.
ance.
The MAYOR has sent us a letter' he has received from PRIVATE A. J. E. HOYLE, late secretary of the Junior Liberal Association, now a motor ambulance driver "somewhere

in France," who says : Dear Mr. Mayor,—l see through "The Examiner" that your good lady is appealing for subscriptions for an ambulan-ce car for the British Red Cross Society. I hope that she will succeed in her good work. If the people of Warrington only knew or ,could see the valu- able work that is done by these motor ambu- lances they would not be long in .finding the money. If they could only see the wounded "Townies" walking or limping along, perhaps Seven miles to a hospital, because pur cars are full of more serious cases, they would soon see that we had more cars. It is a noble work, and I hope she will 'soon su&eed in her efforts. I should be proud to be driver of the car from the good old town, but I am afraid that is not possible. If they could only see! We ought to be able to realise, if we cannot actually see. Perhaps, if the wealthy people who have not given according to their means still refuse to do so, the poorer people will help the band of well-to-do people who have done their duty nobly so far to a furtber effort. In any case, the ambulance must be provided. It is long overdue, both for the needs in the field and the r6putation of Warrington.

div.head: CONGRATULATIONS.
div.p: CONGRATULATIONS.

Sin ARTHUR and LADY CaosriLD have been much gratified by the many warm messages of congratulation they have received from Warrington and other friends. As, the list which we publish to-day shows, those friends belong to all ranks and to all parties, and we are sure the messages eManating from the opposite camp will be highly-treasured by the recipients. The old workmen at Messrs. CROSFIELD'S works, the Friendly Societies, the Cemetery Hotel Bowling Club, and the great firms engaged in the soap and kindred indtis- trieg, who feel the honour , reflected upon themselves through SIR ARTHUR and the'social and political friends, local, national and inter- national, who figure in the list, combine to show how general is the goodwill that is entertained towards one who has been selected for this signal honour at the hands of his SOVEREIGN-.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 19, 1915.

div.head: HONOURING THE SOAP TRADE.
div.p: HONOURING THE SOAP TRADE.

As will be seen by the list, numerous firms in the soap industry sent congratulations. All looked upon the honour from a trade as well as a personal point of view. The resolution sent by the Board of Directors of Lever Bros., Limited, stated:

"On the granting by His Majesty the King to Mr. Arthur H. Crosfield of a Baronetcy of the United Kingdom, the Directors ,of Lever Brothers, Lanited, desire to 'extend to Sir . Arthur • IL Crosfield, Baronet, their sincerest congratulations on the dignity thereby conferred upon him, and feel that in thus honouring him His Majesty has also honoured the soap trade; of the United Kingdom; and the Directors further wish Sir Arthur and Lady Crosfield long life and. happiness to. enjoy the honour and dignity of their new estate."
At a Board Meeting of John Barrington and Sons, Ltd., it was resolved:— ,

"The Chairman and Directors of John Barrington and Sons, Ltd., have much pleasure in congratulating Sir Arthur Crosl field, Bart. upon the honour Tecently con- ferred on him and through him to the soap trade generally."

div.head: SERVICES TO THE TRADE,
div.p: SERVICES TO THE TRADE,
The resolution passed by the Board of Messrs. Edward Cook and Co., Ltd:, on Monday June 7.th, was as follows:

"That the heartiest vote of congratulation of the Board of Edward Cook and Co., Ltd., be forwarded to Sir Arthur H. Crosfield, Bart., on the great honour done him by His Majesty, and that the directors heartily wish Sir Arthur and Lady Crosfield health, long life and happiness, and the fullest enjoyment of the honours so justly conferred on them by His Majesty. The directors always re- member the very great services rendered by Sir Arthur to the Soap Trade, with which he wag closely identified for many years, and that he always worked unselfishly for the whole good of the trade and for the common interest of all concerned."

The Board ,of ,Directors of Messrs. Christo- pher Thomas and Bros., Bristol, passed the fol- lowing resolution : "It was proposed by Mr. Walls and sec- onded by Mr, Worsfold, that the hearty con- gratulations of .Christopher Thomas and Bras. Ltd., be sent to Sir Arthur Crosfield, Bart., on the high honour recently conferred upon him by 11.111.. the King."

div.head: WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE.
div.p: WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE.
The resolution of the Working len's Infirm- ary Committee runs:—

"It was unanimously passed by the Work- ing Men's Infirmary Committee last night that the hon. secretary write to congratulate Sir Arthur 11. Crosfield upon having received the honour of a baronetcy at the hands of the King, Sir Arthur having-given very valuable assistance to the committee, and having kindly promised to continue to 'help forward its efforts!'

FROM "SOMEWHERE IN FRANCE." To the Editor of " The Examiner." Sir,—As an old worker of the party in War- rington, will you allow me to say, through the medium of your paper, how pleased I am to hear of the honour that the King has bestowed on our (esteemed friend, Mr. A. H. Crosfield? Although I am not in the same part of the country •as the Lancashire " Terriers " from Warrington, I feel sure that they will be delighted at the news, and b;= }Yith me in wish- ing our late member long life and; health ,to enjoy the distinction so veil earned. I remain, j , Yours sincerely, , A. J. E. HOYLE, No. 4 rield Ambulance, B.E.F.

div.head: Rival Shorthand Systems.
div.p: Rival Shorthand Systems.

At 'a well-attended nieeting of the Warring- ton Shorthand Writers' Association, a lecture and demonstration on the Gregg system of Shorthand was given by the Secretary (Mr. T. Lowe). The lecturer said that he believed that -the Gregg system of shorthand would be the system of the 'future, and he, hoped that all shorthand writers 'would look into this rival system, which was making, such a stand for complete supremacy. The system was fully explained. Mr. J. Metcalfe said that several of the outlines suggested by the lecturer did not, in his opinion, stand out as clearly and con- cisely as the Pitman outlines, but at the same time he had made up his mind that he 'would look deeper into this' rival system before taking up the position of a critic. The discussion was continued by the President (Mr. • -2. W. Durant), li. B. Bell and ,Mr. A. Nurse. The lecturer said he' was pleased that the. members had shown such a broadminded spirit, and he hoped that all present would follow in the foot- steps of Mr. Metcalfe, and study the Gregg system of shorthand. , _

div.head: LADY HOUSE SURGEONS.
div.p: LADY HOUSE SURGEONS.
A Prejudice War Conditions
Will Break Down.
Mr. George Walker presided over a meeting of ,the Working Men's Infirmary Committee, held at the Druids' Hall on Wednesday even- ing, Alderman Burton, though reported to be being unable to attend.

div.head: WHITE HEATHER DAY GALA.
div.p: WHITE HEATHER DAY GALA.

It was reported that the Caledonian Associa- tion intended to hold a White Heather Day gata on the Warrington cricket Club ground on Saturday, August 21st, the proceeds of which would be divided among the Nursing Association, the Poor Children's Camp, and the Infirmary. The following were appointed the committee representatives on a joint committee for making the arrancrements:—Messrs. George Shaw, R. Cook, and A. E. Wickham.

div.head: UNITED CHURCH CHOIR FESTIVAL.
div.p: UNITED CHURCH CHOIR FESTIVAL.

The Hon. Secretary (Mr. J. H. J. HamPson) stated that thP committee engaged in consider- ing the advisability of holding the customary open-air musical festival in the Park, qn Sunday, August 22nd, which had hitherto been given by the Free Church choirs, invited repre- sentatives from the Church of England and Roman Catholic choirs to attend their last meeting. There was a large attendance, and the result was that the festival would now be given by all ,the representative places of wor- ship in the town and district. Mr. George Walker said that committee seemed especially fortunate in bringing people together. When there were two male voice choirs in the town the committee were instru- mental in getting them together on one plat- form. Now they had been instrumental.' in getting the choirs of all denominations to join forces. He thought that was a feather in their cap as a committee, which was always seeking to promote goodwill. Mr. Payton would con- duct and Mr. Darby would accompany the choirs.

The following were appointed a committee to make the arrangements for the festival and also the annual concert' in October :—Messrs. Walker; Woodcock, Daintith, Reddish, Wads- worth, ,Bradley, Weston, Knowles, Binks, iladkiss, Egerton, W. Rigby and the Hon. Secretary.

div.head: SIR ARTHUR CROSFIELD.
div.p: SIR ARTHUR CROSFIELD.

Mr. George Walker mentioned that Mr. A. H. Crosfield, who had given much valuable assist- ance to the committee and would continue to help them in the future, had been made a baronet by the King; and it was decided to send Sir Arthur hearty congratulations.
SHORTAGE OF DOCTORS AND NURSES.

Mr. T. Wadsworth reported a shortage of nurses and doctors. The Board of Manage- ment were having ,to offer larger salaries to nurses and lady doctors would have to be ap- pointed house surgeons as the doctors continued to go to the Front, and it was now impossible to obtain successors.

Mr. Daintith said the Board of Management .had decided to advertise for a lady senior house surgeon at £lBO and a lady junior house sur- geon .at £l2O. The ladies would have the usual diplomas, and he did not see why they would not fill the positions as .well as men. Mr. Wadsworth explained that all the doctors in town had volunteered their services at the Lord Derby Military Hospital, Winwick. Those who were on tha honorary staff at the Infir- mary had suggested a curtailment of their duties at the Infirmary. One idea was .that patients, after the first attendance at the Infirmary,' should be passed on to their panel doctor, but the representatives of the Working Men's Committee had objected to this and carried their point. , Mr. Walker said that was a principle for which they had successfully fought for over thirty years—that the Infirmary should com- plete the cases they undertook. We were living in difficult 'times and would have to make allowances. For instance, it was desired that such cases as operations for adenoids sent 'fron the school clinic should be taken not at a specified time, but at the convenience of the doctors, within a reasonable time, . The Educa- tion Committee made no contribution to the funds of the institution; for the number of cases they sent they should contribute liber- ally. Mr. George Shaw was pleased to hear of the coming appointment of lady house surgeons. It would be the opportunity for breaking down the local professional prejudice against lady doctors, who ought to be as capable, and worth as in,uch money, as men.

div.head: FLAG DAY!
div.p: FLAG DAY!
To-day's Effort For The Allies' Wounded.

To-day is "Flag Day." That, is from early this morning till late to-night a large band of ladies will spread themselves all over the town and district offering flags for sale at any price the purchaser may care to give, beginning at the minimum of one penny. The proceeds will be devdted to the funds for our own wounded, soldiers in the Warrington hospitals, and the fUnds being raised to give succour to the wounded soldiers of Russia, France, Belgium and Servia. 1

The helpers will work in couples, one having a special box containing the flags and the other a box in which it is hoped an unlimited num- ber of the coins of the realm will be dropped. Some of these helpers have arranged to be in the streets as early as half-past five in order to meet the men leaving the works after having worked the night shift and the men who are about to begin work for the day. The manage- ments of the various places of -entertainment have kindly consented to allow the helpers to collect from their respective patrons. In order to cover, the outlying districts, the committee will be glad to receive the assistance of owners of motor cars to, convey the collectors to their appointed stations. , A largely-attended and enthusiastic meeting of the helpers was held at Parr Hall on TUPS- dav night, when the Mayor and Mr. j. Smethurst. explained the plan of campaign.
To-clay, the Town Hall Will be head4ua-rters.

div.head: SCALDING SENSATION.
div.p: SCALDING SENSATION.
Workhouse Fatality The Result Of Misplaced Rath keys.

At Wednesday's meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, the Medical Officer's report, included in the minutes of the House Committee, contained the following reference to the ease in which a mental patient was fatally scalded, whilst bathing, by another, mental patient "This accident would not have occurred had the bath keys been in their proper place—i.e., locked in the cupboard instead of on the top of it. I should like to take, this opportunity of suggesting that. a fully-trained medical and mental attendant be appointed to act as superintendent, in the mental ward. He would, of course, take the same hours of duty as the present staff, but he would be senior, and would supervise the conduct of the block. I consider some arrangement of this kind most essential. SYMPATHY WITH RELATIVES.

The Clerk was instructed by the committee to express their sympathy with the relatives of the deceased man, and to place on record their .regret at the unfortunate occurrence. It was further decided that the Chairman and Vice-Chairman of the committee and the Chair- man of the Board, together with the Clerk, be appointed a sub-committee to investigate fully the circumstances leading tb the death, of the man, and report to the committee.

SUPERINTENDENT TO BE APPOINTED. The recimmendatiou of the medical officer with regard to the appointment of a trained medical and mental superintendent to super- vise the work of the attendants was approved, and the Clerk was instructed to issue advertisements inviting applications for the position at a galary of £l5 per annum, to- gether with emoluments; '• The Master was instructed to confer with the superintendent nurse, and report at the next meeting on the staffing and control of the female imbecile wards.

div.head: I LOCAL INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: I LOCAL INTELLIGENCE.
The Time Tables.

The existing railway time tables will, for the most part, remain in force till July 12th, when important alterations for the season will take. place. The Warrington A.B.C. Guide for July wal- be published a few days before the 12th of next month.
Co-operative Employes' Outing. On Thursday the employes of the Warrington-, Equitable Co-operative Society had their annual outing, and spent an enjoyable day in Liverpool and New Brighton.

Rich Musieal Treat in Store. On Sunday evening, June 27, Crosfield's band will provide a special programme of music in Bank Park. The fee allowed the band for , their attendance will be devoted to the Crosfield Band Fund for Wounded Soldiers, and a col- lection will be taken at the entrances to the Park. for the same object.
Citizens' Temperance League. An open-air meeting, arranged by the local Rechabites in connection with the above.
League, will he held in Bewsey=street at 7.39 on Friday evening next, when the special speaker will be the Rev. W. Harris, of Ashton-'Makerfield.

div.head: Thursday Cricket.
div.p: Thursday Cricket.

A team representing 'the Warrington (Thurs- day) Cricket Club -journeyed to Chester on Thursday afternoon and there met the Colle: gians. The Warrington men made a score .of 85 and Chester responded with 57. for four wickets, the game therefore ending in a draw.

The Hon. Treasurer of the Infirmary ,grate- fully acknowledges the receipt from his Wor- ship the Mayor of cheque value five guineas. being one-half of the amount granted to the Mayor by the Order of Druids FriendiY Society, for • distribution amongst charitable institutions in Warrington.

The recently established military convales- Cent home at Thelwall Heys will be open rtkr the public, on Thursday next, when gifts of pocket-handkerchiefs, tobacco, stationery, fresh eggs, groceries, ,&c., will be welcome. Visitors. are respectfully requested not to take children .- with them When making their call.

div.head: Fatal Fall Downstairs.
div.p: Fatal Fall Downstairs.

At the Warrington Coroner's Court yesterda2i an inquest was held on the body of Mary Cup- ninghani, aged 77, a widow, who lived at 283,- r 'Winwick-road. It appeared from the evidence that she fell down downstairs whilst going tO. bed on Tuesday night and was found by her son lying in a fool of blood at the foot of the staircase the following morning. The jury 1C? - turned a verdict of "Accidental death."

LEGH HOLDEN.
Shot In Head Whilst Looking Over Trench-Parapet.

Great sympathy is felt with Mr. H. Holden, and Mr's. Holden, of The Cottage, ,Thelwall, in the loss they have sustained by the death of their second son, Lieutenant Legh who has gallantly given his life for country. Lieutenant Holden joined the Territorials on the outbreak of war, feeling, as he himself often expressed it, that it was up '0 every fit young man to render what service ,te could to his country. He received his corn- 'lission at the end of August After com- Veting his war training he proceeded to the ront some four months ago. The news of his death reached his home last week-end, being 1911veYed in two letters, the one from Colonel _ rereton Fairclough, who is in command of the I).attalion, and the other from the deceased 11,e9tenant's company officer, Captain Egerton airclough.

PTE. J. W. LIVINGSTONE.
Stockton Heath Hero Who Will Re Sadly Missed.

The news • that came to hand this week of the death of Private J. W. Livingstone, of 2, Gibson-street, Stockton Heath, caused con- siderable regret in the township. Private Livingstone, who is the son of Mr. and Mrs. John Livingstone, was actively identi- fied with the Sunday School and Band of HQpe work of St: Thomas' Church.

Twenty years of ages.Private,Livingstone, who was employed, prior to the outbreak of war, at Me4.srs. Greenall's Brewery at Wilderspool, was one of the earliest to enlist. He joined the 4th South Lancs. (Territorial) Regiment, and devoted himself keenly to his training. He departed for, the Front in the best spirits. Firing at a dummy which the enemy raised over the edge of their trenches, Private Livingstone was shot in the head. This detail as to the manner in which the young soldier cam by his end, was supplied by Lance-Corporal Isherwood, writing to his mother, who resides at 22, Bedford-street, Stockton Heath. The late Private Livingstone is spoken of highly by 5n officer in a letter to Mr. and Mrs. Living- stone.

Thei Livingstone family grave in the Church- yard was covered on Sunday with a 'Union Jack, surmounted by a wreath with tbe inscription: "From the workers of St. Thomas' Band of Hope as an expression of sympathy with the
PRIVATE J. W. LIVINGSTONE.
Killed.

• loved ones of their late fellow-worker, Jack Livingstone, who gave his life for his King and his county, June 9th, 1915. Who will come and take h(S)place?" As a boy, Private Livingstone attended St. Thomas' School. Prior to entering the service of Messrs. ,Greenall, Whitley, Ltd., he was employed by 'Mr. Edward Wallington, builder. He was a member of Mr. John Hallows' Bible Class, of the Boys' Brigade, and (formerly) of the Wilderspool Brewery Cricket Club. He has a brother (James) in the Royal Engineers, wild is anticipating being sent to the Dardanelles.
• In his last letter home, Private Livingstone said he hoped to be back by August Banl: Holiaay.

div.p: PRIVATE SAMUEL THOMAS

div.head: And Ammunition.
div.p: And Ammunition.

The news that Private Samuel ,Thomas—of the 4th South Laneashires—had given his life for Kivg and countiy, first reached his wife at 39, Forshaw-street, on Saturday morning, when .shc .received a letter from her brother, Private Harold Bailey, of the same battalion. The letter was dated the 9th, and ran:—

i" I daresay by the time you receive this you will have heard about poor Sam. It came as a great shock to me, and I know it will be hard for you all to bear—especially for our Edith; but try and comfort her as much as possible. All I know is what Al- bert told me. He came to me yesterday about 7 p.m., and told me that he had been hit and (lied. soon after. I can hardly realise that it is true, for he was in good spirits when I was talking to him the night when we came up to the trenches. We received a parcel before we came up here; I don't know whe- ther he has written and told our Edith or not.
"Arthur Monk's rifle was struck with lightning, the same day, and he bad to be taken out; I suppose it would be the shock.
PRIVATE S. TIIOXIAS.
Killed.
Well, I can't say any more this time. - • - - -
good-night awl, God- bless you all."
The letter was also addressed to his parents, Mr. and Mrs. John W. Thomas, of 55,. Liver- pool-road.
From Arm to Arm.
At the fiam e time Mrs. S. Thomas receiVed from her cousin, Private Albert Porter, a short note. which ran :

have got bad news .for you. Break it gently. ~ Sam has been killed. He was hit thrhugh the chest; the bullet wet through from: arm to arm.. Harold is writing. I'll have to finish now to get it through quickly."

div.head: "A Dear Comrade."
div.p: "A Dear Comrade."
On Tuesday morning Sergeant R. Caslin wrote a letter dated June 9th :

"It is with • great regret that I have to in- form you of the death of your husband. I feel it is a very painful duty indeed. I was in command of his platoon when he got killed at 530 p.m. on the Bth of June. He was hit under tho left arm. It may be a Comfort to you to

his King and country. It is a noble thing to die for one's country, and I hope that if you have children you will ever teach them the noble thing that their father did for them. I only wish those at-home could realise what
~ an awful war this is—there would be no

trouble in getting recruits, if the young men would only feel, as these dear lads do here, the importance of giving their lives if need be for their country. May I commend you to God's gracious keeping, and may you have grace to bear up under the burden is the.sin- cere prayer of yours very sineerely, "W. BRACECAMP (Chaplain)." "Doing His Little Bit."

Private' John Brinielow, 22, Pickmere-street, a relative by martiage, writing home from the Front, says that Private Ratcliffe was killed on Thursday, June 10. "His platoon were in the trenches, and we were in the firing line. He was, I believe, filling sandbags at the time it occurred. He was given a full Christian burial tire same night. . . . Will you please give Louie my deepest sympathy? I know it will be a big blow to her, but perhaps it will be some consolation to her to know he was doing his little bit at the time. If I manage to get through myself I shall be able to give you full details."

I am pleased to say I am in the best of spirits, and am looking forward to seeing you and the children very shortly. So cheer up and don't worry. I am all right. Write as soon as you get this."

div.head: His Mate's Tribute.
div.p: His Mate's Tribute.

• Private J. Bentley, a mate of the dead Terri- torial, also writes : • "Dear. Mrs. Thomas,—Just a ,few lines to let you know the sad news that your husband, and my xtwte, was killed while we were •in the trenches. He was a good lad to me, and was always jolly when we were in the trenches to- gether. You must not let it upset you, for he died for his King and. country. All the boys send their deepest sympathy;we' all Miss him now, for he was well liked with our battalion .and boys. I think you will know the news before this letter reaches you. I would have written sooner, but I thought I would let ilarold break the news to you. I hope • you will keep your heart up; I knew it will be a bit hard for you—and it will for me, losing a good 'mate like Sam was to me. . , . lie was killed on the 9th day of June, and passed away quietly by My side. . . . Be told -me the same day as he got killed about his child .jUst starting going to school. . . With all my deepest sympathy, from his mate,. JACK."

div.head: Sergeant Also Killed In Wood.
div.p: Sergeant Also Killed In Wood.

On Wednesday morning, Private H. Bailey wrote to his sister—Mrs. Cunningham, also of 39, Forshaw-street : can hardly realise it yet. He has been buried With a sergeant who was killed in the Bathe wood. Jack Bentley was at his side at the time. I think he was hit by a sniper, and I have been told since that they have caught this sniper—with three hundred rounds of ammunition and four days' rations. I hope it is right. I wish I had hold of the one that hit him; you can bet that he would not hit any more. . . ."

div.head: MONKS, HALL EMPLOYE.
div.p: MONKS, HALL EMPLOYE.

Born at Manchester thirty years ago, Private Samuel Thomas came to live at Warrington at the age of about „eighteen, entering the rivet department of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.— where •he had remained ever inee.. In that department he acted as treasurer for the Gas Workers' Union.

At the end of August he joined the Terri- torials—having some years previously already had about five years' experience in the. Volu- nteers: Early in February he crossed to the Front, training in Scotland and the South of England having been completed. The Private was married at St. Peter's Church nearly six years ago, and leaves besides his widow a five-year-old son, as well as his, parents; two brothers and five sisters.

div.head: Foul' Others In Army.
div.p: Foul' Others In Army.

Three brothers-in-law of his are also in the Army—Private H. Bailey, in the same batta- lion; Bombardier Joseph Badl•y, of the R.F.A., now en route for foreign parts; and Private T. Cunningham, Of the 4th South Lancashires, now in hospital, recovering from wounds. Private Albert .Porter was his cousin.

div.head: PRIVATE F. RATCLIFFE.
div.p: PRIVATE F. RATCLIFFE.

Private Frank -Ratcliffe. 103, Wiftwick-road. a fitter's labourer at the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co.'s Works, has been killed. He was a Reathside schoolboy. On the eve of going to the war he was 'married at Tunbridge Wells, by the Rev. W. Bracecamp, whose sad duty it has now been' to send the sad news of his death to his young widow. He was 21 years of age. His. father, Mr. Thomas Ratcliffe, who is dead, formerly belonged to the Fire Brigade, and lived in the vicinity of the Fire Station. Private Ratcliffe's widowed mother lives. in Sharp-street.

div.head: Noble Death.
div.p: A Noble Death.
The Rev. W. Rraceeamp, writing last Satur- day, says:—
"The Headquarters, 149 Brigade, 50th Divi- sion, Expeditionary Force, France. _ _

_ '"Dear Mrs. liatcliffe,—l am • afraid I have some very sad news to tell you. I heard this afternoon that your husband was killed a few days ago. Try and ,cheer up under. the circnnititances. You have the satisfaction of knowing that your husband gave his life for
PRIVATE FRANK RATCLIFFE. Killed.

div.head: Would Do His Best.
div.p: Would Do His Best.
Private Ratelilf4p, writing on the sth inst. to his brother-in-Iw, Mr. D. Elwell, 84,. Forster- street, said

" We are fairly among it here, I can tell you. The pick of the British Army have been sent here, and we /are among them. I don't know how we will go on, but we will do our best, you bet. I have seen Stan. Furness since I have been out here, and we had a good time."

div.head: WOUNDED.
div.p: WOUNDED.
CAPTAIN CLILDE ROBERTSON.
Slightly Wounded In Shoulder By Shrapnel,

Captain Claude Robertson, of the 4th South Lancashires, is reported wounded. On Thurs- day evening news was received that he had been slightly wounded in the shoulder by shrapnel. The Captain himself also sent a telegram from Dover Pier'; at that time, how- ever, he was not able to say whither he was proceeding. No further news is yet to hand. Pearson and Knowles' Engineer.

Born in Gloucester, Captain Robertson is the son of the Rev. William Robertson (Vicar of St. Kathleen's; Gloucester) and Mrs. Robertson. With his wife and little daughter he lives at Brantwood, Moore; and is, in peace time, an cnameer with Mer\srs. Pearson and Knowles, of Warrington. On the outbreak of war he joined the Terri-. torials, and afiter seven months' training pro- ceeded abroad. He had 'only been promoted to his present 'tank so recently as May Ist.
Wounded.
mile journey. When we get three miles off the trenches we are surrounded with Germans.
Germans Shell AU the Transports.

"They shell all the transports. They can see us coming up, because we are on flat ground, and our only hope of escape from their atten- tions is to go up :when it is pitch dark. We ,have lost one horse and -have, had two Wounded, whilst two men have also been wounded. I can assure you I only wish this war was over. When the lads go to the trenches they relieve the,' 2nd Life Guards.' They have made that name for themselves, as they are put straight in the main line of trenches, instead of reserves, eo they are side by side with the 2nd South Lancashires from the Barracks. I must close my short letter to you, as duty calls me away. . . I only wish I could see you all, instead of having to be satisfied with a glance at the photo I have, and which I carry about with me."
CORPORAL W. WATSON.

div.head: CAPTAIN
div.p: CAPTAIN
Member Of Parr's Bank Staff Slightly
Wounded In The Head.

At Hilltop House, Latchford, arrived on Thursday evening a telegram despatched from Dover Pier by Captain Alfred Skinner, of the 4th South Lancashires, stating that he had been slightly wounded in the head. Further news is expected hourly. The eldest son of Mr. and Mrs. William Skinner, now of Latchford, Captain Skinner was born in Sale, Cheshire, and received his education at the Boteler Grammar School, as well as at a Scottish institution, and after- wards privately. He is single, and resides with his parents; holding in times of peace a position upon the staff of Parr's Bank, Limited.

The Territorial movement he joined no less than six years ago—since which time he has taken an active and enthusiastic part. Since the battalion proceeded in February to Flanders, he has been in the region of Ypres. The considerable number of officers previously wounded caused him practically to perform the manifcild duties of captain over two companies for some. time before being gazetted to his recently-attained rank.

div.head: CORPORAL AVILLIAM WATSON.
div.p: CORPORAL AVILLIAM WATSON.

Corporal William Watson, whose home is at 73, Oldham-street, Latchford, is said to be wounded, but the report is not confirmed. The last letter which Mrs. Watson received from her husband auived on Monday and bore the date June 10th. After acknowledging the receipt of a letter and a parcel containing eggs. butter, cocoa, and a big cake, which enabled him to have a most enjoyable meal, he says: "I am in the best of health. I wish I could only get my holidays. It's a hell-hole where we are•now. " Every place is in ruins, and when we go to the trenches ft is a matter of a ten-

div.head: Formerly a Lymm Volunteer.
div.p: Formerly a Lymm Volunteer.

Corporal Watson, who is 30 years of age. has two children—one six years of ago and the other only five months old. He was for two years a member of the Lymm Volunteer Regiment, which he left about ten years ago in order to join the Warrington Territorials. Shortly after the outbreak of war be volun- teered for war service, and was in training at Tunbridge Wells and in Scotland. He was at one time a• moulder at Messrs. Fletcher, Rus- sell and Co.'s works and latterly was employed as a van-driver in the sanitary works of the Corporation. He was• very fond a, and kind to, horses, and at his home there are to be seen two framed diplomas presented to him by the Warrington branch of ,the R.S.P.C.A. for keep- ing the animals under his care in excellent con- dition. He is spoken of in Latchford as a kind, genial and upright man. He has regularly attended tho services held at the Kent-street Mission.

div.head: PRIVATE J. DITCHFIELD.
div.p: PRIVATE J. DITCHFIELD.
Nlnsician Shot 'While Bearing Fallen
Comrade.

Private James Ditchfield, 55, Orford-lane, an employe of the St. Helens Cable Co., in the ebqnite department, has been wounded in the legs. From a letter received by a friend of the family in town it appears that he was engaged carrying a fallen comrade to the place of

div.head: Another Battalion Needed.
div.p: Another Battalion Needed.
In a previous letter to his father. Private Ditelifield saiti

"We are now in the trenches again for' a few days. We were shelled in our billets yesterday, and I am sorry to say we had a man killed and one wounded. One shell knocked the top of the house right off; and we were lucky there were no more. It was awful, though, to see the poor women and children having to ,fiee from their homes. If the people in England would only realise the sufferings of these people I don't think they would hesitate to come forward. I hear they are getting another battalion at War- rington, and I hope they will soon get them. The sooner we get them the sootier the War will be over." .

Writing to his mother-in-law, Mrs. Jr. Gregory, 105, Orford-lane, Private Ditehfield again refers to the families being driven out by the shells. When they return they find their homes all blown to atoms and everything they possessed gone.

div.head: Pies and Eggs for the Trenches.
div.p: Pies and Eggs for the Trenches.

Writing to his wife before he was wounded, Private Diteligeld, acknowledging the receipt of a pie, said he "enjoyed it all right, and you can send me another.. I am sorry to say the eggs were smashed, so don't bother about them —we can buy them at farms here for lid. each. I enjoyed the pine apple all right, too, and I can imagine Jack and Hilda buying those toffees for me; bless them. I wish I could only see. them!"

div.head: PRIX-ATE 11. LITTLEWOOD.
div.p: PRIX-ATE 11. LITTLEWOOD.
Going On Fine "_After Being Hit In
The Chest.

- News reached. Mrs. Littlewood at her tem- porary . residence in Dickenson-street this week, that her husband, Private Holbrook Littlewood, of the Warrington Territorials, had been wounded in action. He himself, broke the news to his wife, when writing under date June 10th, he said:—

A Tribute to the Nurses. "I am very sorry to say' that I received a very nasty wound in the chest oil the 9th instant. The bullet hit me in the middle of the chest, just catching the second • rib from the bottom on the' right-hand side. After it went in, it turned upwards, and lodged in my right shoulder, between ,the collar bone and the shoulder blade. So, you see, they Will have to take the bullet out Wore I am really fit to move. I am going on fine up to now. owing td the nurses in the hospital, whoLlook after us like sisters would look after "their brothers. Ido not think I have anything else to say, as I am tired, and can hardly!. hold 'up. I am hoping to see you soon." Had a,Miraculous Escape.

Private Littlewood again wrote on June 15th, sayifig:—" I am going on fine at present, .so you not need worry yourself about me at all. for I am in very good hands, and being well looked after. I am now down at the base hos- pital at -Rouen, and I am only waiting for the boat to take me to England, as I have already got my ticket for there. They have taken the bullet out of my hack, so you see it went clean into me—in fact almost through me. The .doctors -say I have had 'a miraculous escape, for how it missed my heart they do not know. If the bullet had gonle straight, instead of in a sloping direction, I- should not have been writing this now. It went in between the fourth and fifth ribs, and almost in the centre of my chest. . . ." Recovering at Winwick War Hospital.
Private Littlewood has since been removed to he Lord Derby War Hospital at Winwiek, and
with the Naval Division at Antwerp in October and came through unscathed. . The dead Marine formerly worked at Messrs. Peter Walker's Brewery.
PIiIVATE JAMES DITCHFIELD.
Wounded.

burial when he was shot. Pkivate Ditchfield, who was in the band of the battalion, being ,a well-known local musician, was serving as stretcher-bearer. He is married, has two chil- dren, and is the son of Mr. James Ditchfield, 20, Church-street who, when the war broke out worked at Coxon's Tanneries, Latchford. Having been in the Volunteers for 47 years, he has been on duty at the Drill Hall during the war. Private Ditchfield, who is now 28 years of ...age, has been in the Volunteers and Terri- torials .since he' was thirteen ,years of age. As a boy he attended Hamilton-street School.

div.head: Better Than One in the Head.
div.p: Better Than One in the Head.
Writing to his wife, Juno 14th, Private Ditehfield sass:—

"I have been wounded in the right leg, which, lam sorry to say, is broken. The bullet wka straight through and caught the bone just above thm ankle, but anyhow that is better than getting one through the head. am in a fine hospital and get every at- tention anybody could wish for, so that is a lot to be thankful for. I had a long jonrw

div.head: GRAPPENHALL. '
div.p: GRAPPENHALL. '

Frost presiding. It was unanimously. decided, after speeches by. Mr. Frost and Mr. 11. G. Langley (hon. secretary of the battalion), that a Grappenhall detach- ment be formed. The following committee was appointed, and empowered to add to their hum- ber at their discretion: Messrs. F. A. Frost; It. W. Wilde, G. Hutchings, Emson. O. Lofthouse, A. Lister-Kaye,. Darbyshire, • Moirey, 'l'. B. Handley, John Lee, Nicholls, Rylands, Hartley, Cawley, Wood, Eastmant, Darlington, Lomas an. 4 JolurooN

PRIVATE G. C. *SOLLORY.

div.head: WOUNDED.
div.p: WOUNDED.
THOUGHTFUL OLD FRIENDS.
Mersey Hotel Club Sends Out Appreciated Parcels.

Rifleman T. Mason, of the Rifle Brigade, is 'wounded, and is recuperating at the West of England Sanatorium, Weston-Super-Mare. Mr. Wm. Vose, 79, Ellesmere street, Howley, secretary of a club at the Mersey Hotel, Mersey-street, the members of which provide the funds necessary to send out parcels of tobacco, &c. to former members now serving their country, has received a postcard from Rifleman Mason, saying he can walk on the left leg a little, and is on crutchei. In a letter to his "dear friends" of the club he says— "l am pleased and proud to receive your thoughtful gift of forty-eight stamps through the good inedi\um of Bill Vose. I -am glad to know you have a tobacco fund, and having pre- viously received a splendid parcel from you whilst I was in France, I can vouch for the benefits we old users of the Mersey Hotel derive from your goodness. Anything better than the stamps I could not at present receive. As regards my photo in bath chair, it is quite true. It was taken near the Atlantic Hotel; a lady staying there, paid for me to be taken. lam in good health. lam sorry so good a man as Mike Burke is so seriously ill, anti I wish him an early recovery. Men like him we can ill afford to lose. lam sorry to hear of A. Leigh's death. May he rest in peace. "Yesterday my bath chair was -dispensed with, and I can now walk with crutches fairly well, though on the left leg only as yet. My right one will take longer than I at first thought. Sir Arthur.

"I was pleased to know the King made A. 11.. Crosfield a Sir, because if ever a man earned that title it is Sir Arthur. He is an English gentleman in the truest sense of the word. "On Monday, for the second time, I was taken for a drive in Sir Richard Ashman's carriage. His father was the first Lord Mayor of Bristol. This is a splendid place. It reminds me of Morecambe Bay. Trams are free to us wounded, picture palaces, and on Thurs- days we often get tickets for the matinee at the theatre on the promenade pier. Now I get about myself I shall take advantage of these fine opportunities. - 'A Shake of the Hand.

"I hope you will all prosper, and that the time will soon come when I along with others who are serving their country can meet you, my friends, in the old spot where you asre doing good work in ,helping those, who, like myself, cannot help themselves. How I should like to shake each of you by the hand! "I lave The Examiner' sent from home each week," adds the gallant Rifleman, to let his friends know he is conversant with all that going on in the town.

- Rifleman Mason is a married man, -13 years of age, and resided at 18, Napier-street. He was formerly emplbyed as a wiredrawer at the Whitecross Co.'s works. In September he vacated this position and joined the Rif* Brigade, and was drafted to the Front. He was educated at the National School. Church- street, under the, headmastership of Mr. John Dewhurst, and attended the Parish Church and Bank-street Mission. He was an old football ). nlaver, and nlaved for the Pa ish Church Rugby Football Club, when they won a cup in 1893. He also took much interest in. cricket.

div.head: RAILWAY CLERKS.
div.p: RAILWAY CLERKS.
The Many Questions That Call For
Consideration.

At the eighteenth annual conference •of the Railway Clerks' Association held in Dublin. Mr. A. E. Moorfield, 10, Grafton-street, attended as the representative of the Warrington Branch. The association has a metabership of 34,000.

The Lord Mayor of Dublin, who offered the Conference a hearty welcome to the city, told the clerks that their motto should be organise, educate, agitate and federate. A resolution expressing horror at the Lnsi- tania outrage and recognising that the present. struggle must be prosecuted until the debasing principle of Prussian militarism is completely overthrown, was passed. Attention was called to the fact that since the introduction of joint working aoeements against competition and the increase of fares and rates, the companies' pro4ts had risen from £45,000,000 in 1907 to .252,000,000, and a resolution was passed pointing out to the Rail- way Commission that the public understood that all revenue from increased charges should be expended on improving the condition of railway employes. The increased cost of living, unaccoinpanipd by any improvement in wages, was discussed, and the Government was urged, by resolution, to take possession of all the necessaries of life and to, regulate prices. Other resnititions asked the companies to make it possible for officials having twenty years' service and upwards to attain to a salary of £l5O a year; for the nationalisation of rail- ways, mines and, other means of production, distribution, and exchange; for a revision here- after of the administrative changes caused by the war; calling attention to the serious condi- tion of many of the railway superannuation funds, due in some eases to the failure ade- quately to surcharge late-age entrants and late- age advances of salary; condemning employ- ment of female clerks at rates of pay below those paid to males; expressing dissatisfaction at the long and irregular hours at which clerks in certain departments, are obliged to work; and expressing approval of the parliamentary Labour party in co-operating in the national recruiting campaign, the issues of the present , war being Of transcendent importance to the I democracies of all the countries concerned.

div.head: "30MEWIEF. AT SA.'
div.p: "30MEWIEF. AT SA.'
"Don't Look VERY Downhearted,
Do We?"

We have received the following letter with the photograph which we reproduce from two Warringtonians who have been too modest to attach their names, but doubtless, they will be recognised by their friends in town. Their address is H.M.S. Glory, G.P.O. London. It will be seen that the writers are proud of War- rington, that. they have the breezy confidence of the British men of the sea, and that they request the public to neglect them in favour of
the men in the trenches when the sending out of comforts is concerned. Proud of the Old Town. •

"My Dear Editor," runs the letter—" Just a link to sax how proud. I am of the part played by the old town in this.awful war. As you see, I am (or rather we are) doing our humble bit somewhere at sea. I must not say where or state our mission, or the Censor will be down on me. I am glad to say that we have got over our worst part for the present. . We have practically cleared the seas in this part of the world of Germans. Of course there is still their commerce to be held up. . . . "Send it to Tcro my." •

"Now that the winter is past I should like to say a word about the many comforts that. are. being distributed amongst our sailors and soldiers, especially tobacco. It almost seems like carrying coal tq Newcastle . sending tobacco and fags aboard a warship. We have tons. Send it to 'Tommy' in the trenches, where he is not able to get is so easily, is the -wish of thousands of sailors beside myself. Of course we like to think we are remembered by those at home, but ' Tommy ' needs it most.
TWO WARRINGTONIANS AFLOAT.

div.head: Fair Smack Wanted.
div.p: A Fair Smack Wanted.
"All we want is a fair smack in at the Germans, not • nibbles like we have had, and may it come soon is the ardent desire of TWO WARRINGTONIANS SERVING .
AFLOAT.
"Kindly accept accompunying photo, WA don't look very downhearted after ten months of it, do we?"

div.head: WOUNDED DRUMMER'S PLUCKY ACT.
div.p: WOUNDED DRUMMER'S PLUCKY ACT.
Saves Two Children By Supporting Falling Iron Gates.

Drummer Jack lialford, of the Warrington Territorials, who is staying on sick furlough at his home, 9, Walker-street, Warrington, per- formed a prompt and plucky act which un- doubtedly saved a couple of children from terrible injury, if not from death, shortly after mid-day on Wednesday. The gallant drummer, who is 21 years of age—and whose father, Mr. R. H. Half ord, is an engineer at the Warrington Wire Rope Works, Bewsey—was wounded in the back in France on April 28th, and arrived. home partially recovered a few days agd. It appears that on Wednesday he was walking down Bold-street when he noticed a couple of little boys—Joseph Redfern, aged 3 • (the son of the manager of the Warrington Club) and Clyde Crooks, aged 4, who lives with his parents

div.head: DRUMMER lIALFORD.
div.p: DRUMMER lIALFORD.

at 4, Bold-street—swinging on one of the big gates at the front of the Wesley.,an Church. Suddenly he perceived, to his horror, .tat the massive gate—which, in fact,. weighs upwards of 6cwt.—had swung off its hinges and was slowly toppling over on top of the hapless little boys. Without a Moment's hesitation he rushed up and braeing himself under the falling gate, managed to hold it up sufficiently long for the children lo make good their escape. He could not, however, support so great a weight for many seconds, and before anybody was able to come to his hid and assist him in lowering the heavy ironviork, he was forced to let it drop, at the Same time endeavouring to jump clear. Unfortunately he could not do that. the top of one of the bars of the gate catching him on the leg and inflicting nasty wounds in two or three places, whilst another bar injured him in the qhest and a third badly damaged his ankle. The brave drummer was assisted. home with all despatch and Dr. Ferguson was called in to see him and attended to his hurts. It will be seine time before he is able to leave his couch again. It should be added that the parents of the two little boys are deeply appreciative of the drummer's promptitude and pluck, and that they are doing their best to compensate him for thopai he has suffered on behalf of their children.

div.head: FIGHTERS' DEPENDENTS.
div.p: FIGHTERS' DEPENDENTS.
Important New Regulations Issued.

are requested to call attention to an im- portant new Army order relating to " depend- ence " claims upon unmarried soldiers in the New Army and Territorials. Under a new Army Order, issued recently, no application of a " dependence " allowance will be considered if it is received later than the 30th of this month, or in the case of soldiers enlisting after the Ist of June, within one month after enlistment.

Corporal Wrn. Watson.—Corporal William Watson. of the 4th South Lancashire Terri- torials—fufl particulars of whose death we give ,)n another page—was f?r two years a member, ,)f the Lymm Volunteer Regiment.

Postmaster's Presentation.—With their best wisheti on the .occasion of their marriage, the staff of the tymm Post Office on Saturday aiorning breseiited Mr. J. Arnell and his bride with a handsome set of carvers.

- - On the Bch.—On the Petty Sessional Bench Vtrednesday Morning there were: Vice- Chancellor D. Stewart Smith (in the chair). Messrs. J. Cokon,. R. H. Gotobed .and T. J. . Ridgway. . Mr. J. Ilarri; (clerk) was . also present.
Lance-Corporal Reg. Hiiiier.—Mr. and Mrs
W. E. Hillier, of The Village, received on Sat- ; , urday morning a further letter from their wounded hon, saying be was progressing very well at the Malta Hospital. .

' May queen and " Terriers."—"lf ;von have • . , had the same kind of weather ah we have," ~ tai . writes Private Ernest Haddon from the Front, " Lymm must be looking at its very best—as it usually is at Whitsuntide., . It's a great pity 4 , • the May Queen had to be-cancelled."

Late Mr. W. Cooper.—With- regret we record the death of Mr. William Cooper, aged 37— which took place at his home, Booth's Hill, ,arly on Sunday evening from appendicitis. Ile had been under the care of Dr. De Jong. Mr. i:ooper attended .the Parish Church—whetie his funeral took place on Wednesday afternoon, the Rector officiating. The deceased leaves two brothers and four sisters to mourn their loss. He was unmarried.

Dog Versus Constable.—The adjourned sum- mons against George Eccleston wag again con- Adered at Wednesday's Petty- Sessions. He was summoned for—on the morning of April 24th—failing to keep his dog under control.—A constable said that in Sandy-lane at 3 o'clock on the morning in question the dog 'held him up for two or three minutes. He told Eccles- ton, who said: " I am very sorry; it is the first time." Ile had been cautioned before.—ln announcing that the fine would be .half-a- crown, the Chairman (Vice-Chancellor D. S. smith) advised the defendant to keep his dog ;.ied up.

Two Out Of Sixty.—At Wednesday's Petty .iessions, Daniel Massey—farmer, of Hob's- High Legh—was summoned in respect of his son Peter, aged 12, who had not attended school regularly.—Mr. Mercer stated that from April Bth to June-11th the school had been open sixty times, and the boy had been twice. He had been working on the farm for his father, and two .warnings had been ignored. The boy's absence entailed loss of • grant at the rate of twopence per day.—Defendant said he could .not get labour, and had Ito.do something. His son was nearly thirteen, and a good scholar; he had attended regularly ‘before.—A fine of 10s. was imposed.

The Chairman's Request. —Emma Wadsworth of Sandy-lane, Lymm, appeared at Wednesday's Petty Sessions for having been drunk and in- capable op May 2nd.—Sergeant Davies said she was at The Cross very drunk, and quite unable to go home. He brought her to the Police Station, and at midnight she was bailed "at by her husband. Both the woman and her husband were in regular work, and had no Family.—Defendant had • nothing to say.—The Chairman (Vice-Chancellor D. S. Smith): Don't you think you can try and be sober%— Defendant : Yes, sir; T'm very sorry, sir.—The Chairman: It doesn't happen very often, I know; but it ought not to happen at all.— Defendant paid 7s.- 6d.

" Ladless " Warrinntonion.—At Wednesday's' Petty Sessions was dealt with the adjourned case of Fred Walker—partner in a firm of mineral water manufacturers, Froghall Bridge. Warringion—whose offence was that he drove a Tarry withont control and government of the horse drawing it.—Asked to plead, he said:* "I am guilty of having no one in charge of the horse, hut I was delivering stuff."—Sergeant Davies said that on April 27th the lurrv, bear- ing mineral water. was on the slope of Lymm Bridge. During ten minutes nobody came near it. He found Walker in the Fleece Hotel, and pointed out the danger and time. Walker an- swered: "I didn't know I had been SO long."— Defendant said they could not -get lads for the earts, and could not afford two, men to a single lorse.---,The Chairman (Vice-Chancellor iD. S. Smith): It is a very dangerous thing to do. you know! We fine you ten shillings.

div.head: " BEECH WOOD GAS."
div.p: " BEECH WOOD GAS."
Repudiation Of Councillor Cowper'.
Allegations.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

. Sir,—l read in your esteemed paper of Satur- day, sth inst., under the heading of "Beech.. wood Gas." some allegations made by Council- lor Cowper. at the meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council, stating that the Belgians living in " Beechwood" Home are addicted to drinking. "I travel a lot," Mr. Cowper said, and "I see it everywhere that they are drink- ing."

fam a Belgian living at "Beechwood." I know perfectly well all my countrymen here; know perfectly well What they are doing, and I am able to affirm that not one. of the Belgians in "Beechwood" drinks.
Such allegations ought to be proved; if not, they, are common, low, unworthy of a gentle- man.

I should ;mot lower myself in trying to dis- prove those allegations; as they are too pitiful, were it not in order to enlighten your readers. who too often- are misled by foolish talk of certain persons, which an only tend to mis,- understanding between people of two countries bound by a strong friendship, and to slacken the debt of gratitude contracted by the Bel- gians for England and every good-minded Englishman. _
f hope, dear sir, that you will publish this letter in your next edition, and remain, yours truly, M. lIENDRItaX.

div.head: LIEUTENANT A. E. Al ATKIN.
div.p: LIEUTENANT A. E. Al ATKIN.
Progressing Favourably At Boulogne
Hospital:

We are glad to 'state that Lieutenant Alfred Edward Wiitkin, of the 3rd Royal Welsh •Fusi- liers—who, as was fully reported in our last issue, has been seriously wounded whilst on ser-- vice with his regiment in France—is favourably progressing, though still suffering a great deal. His parents, Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Watkin, of Danebank, Lymm—of whom the former was to leave Boulogne on Thursday—have received from the doctors at the hospital very encourag- ing reports; and the wounded Lieutenant is hoping at an early date to cross over to England and enter the hospital at Netley. He is natur- ally very anxious to reach the homeland. In the meantime he receives every attention at the Boulogne hospital; and has been inoculated against lockjaw.
Mrs. A: E. -Watkin has decided at present to remain :4 t Boulogne with her husband.
LIEt TENANT JULIEN GROVES.
Slightly "Gassed" On Return To The
Front.

Lieutenant Julien Groves,. of .the Chesbires— the son of Mr. and Mrs. John E. G. Groves—has this week arrived home at Dean's Green, Lyiram. It will be remembered that he was wounded by shrapnel in the shoulder at Mons whilst serving with his regiment. '
A few weeks ago he returned to the 'Front, but had only been there for threo days when be-was-N:, unfortunate as to he slip,thtly "gassed." Happily he is recovered very well. _

part of the trench at the time, I ain•told by the officer si(ho was with him that he was killed instantly. '" It is a very great blow to me to have to paTt with two such excellent men as ,your son and Private J. Guest within a day or two of one another. I have known your ,son al- most as long as any of my men, for I Came across him soon after we went, to live in Lymm. And, having always been in close touch with him through the Territorials and •'Lads' Club more particularly, I can confi- dently say that you have lost a good arid Ndutiful son, and the country a good soldier. • In conclusion I want to express my very deepest sympathy with you in your very sad loss, and one which the whole company will feel very much." The Rector of Oughtrington (the Rev. 0. S. Tudor-Evans) was advised that morning by telegram from the War Office that the Corporal had been killed; and most opportunely arrived at the bereaved home .to offsr sympathy and counsel just as they were readbig the above letter.
Buried Next Private 'Guest.
Sergeant Harold Clare., writing at the same

time, says:— "Dear Mrs. Barber,—lt is with regret that I report to you that your son has this morning given his life for his King and country which be loved so much. We were subject to 'heavy shell-fire this morning, when, unfortunately, poor Harry was fatally hit. He suffered no pain, but died instantly. He will be' buried by our chaplain by the side of poor Jack Guest.
"Will you please ace,ept our deepest sym- pathy in this your sad bereavement? We Lymm men feel. the loss of Harry and Jack mere than I can tell you—two gallant and

div.head: 111 !VI TERRITORIALS' ROLL OF HONOUR.
div.p: 111 !VI TERRITORIALS' ROLL OF HONOUR.
THIRD MAN , KILLED.
Amongst the Lymm members of the sth Cheshire,: at the Front, took place on Friday Morning the death of - Corporal Henry Barber, who was shot and died instantly whilst in the reserve trench.

The other local lads appear all to be well— though there is still Much sickness in the battalion. • On June 11th a letter from Private P. Clare ran: "We are still in the trenches yet. This is our tenth day in the fire-trench, and the Germans have been shelling us a-lot this Morn- ing. H. Barber got killed, poor lad; and three more wounded, hut not Lymm lads. We are having a .bit of bad luck this time in, and •1 think we are in for a few more days yet. A long stay; but we might have some good news waiting for us when we go out." "We have had a-little wet weather this lasi day or two. We have been over our boot-tops in water and mud. As the water cannot get away in the trenches, we have to fill buckets and carry it out. But it is. a lot better this morning [the 11th]; it is getting nice and dry again. Don't get downhearted; you know it's a long way to Lymm, but we might be there before long with a bit of luck. . . ."

Another- Territorial declares: "This is Our tenth day in the trenches; and as far as we know we shall be in for another ten. They are givinuus a doing this time." Private Ernest Hadden, early in the week, writes to his mother at Pepper-street:— "I am in the very best of health. . . . We finished our nice little, rest, and marched back to the firing-line the same night, going in the trenches the following, (Tuesday) night. The weather is still of the very best-7-sunshine dur- ing the day, nice and cool at night-time. This is my first stay in the firing-trench, and I am quite enjoying it ,up to now. Things are rather quiet at present." Private Stanley Gibbs, who has also been wounded, continues satisfactorily to progress at Toxteth Park Hospital, Liverpool,--where he expects shortly to leave.

Private Cecil Acton, who had been wounded, paid a short visit to his home at Crowley last week, and is now with Lance-Corporals Blease and Linley and Private Arthur Iladden in another part of the country.

Private Acton's arm has healed /very well, but he cannot yet use it comfortably. Yesterday 'morning Mrs. Hurry Percival, of "Newfield," received from her son, Corporal Richard Percival, a field service card saying he had been admitted into hospital sick and hoped to be discharged soon. A letter would follow at first opportunity.
Mr. and. Mrs.-V. Kirkpatrick, of the Bridge- water Arms, have been officially notified that their son, Private T. Kirkpatrick, is in 'hoS- pital suffering from fever.

The rumour that Private William 'Jackson, of "Newtields," has been wounded is untrue. A letter received by the Rector (the Rev. G. 8.. Thurston) runs: "This is our seventh day in the trenches. The weather has been very hot, but whilst I write it is raining, and much cooler. This is a very important line of trenches we are bolding. Yesterday the Germans took it into their heads to shell us; I am glad to say not a man was hit. We had some marvellous escapes, though. The only damage they did was to the trench. This we repaired when darkness came. "All our Lymm boys are—after the week's rest we enjoyed—feeling.much better. . . They all wish me to. convey to you their very best wishes, and they are looking forward to the Church Parade." -

div.head: CORPORAL HENRY BARBER.
div.p: CORPORAL HENRY BARBER.

Killed Instantly By Heavy Shell-Fire. Corporal Henry Barber, of Rush Green, is the third Lymm Territorial who has been killed at the Front. By his mother the news was first received on Tuesday morning in a letter, dated "In the Trenches," June 11th, from Captain G. W. C. Hartley. This ran :- "Dear Mr. and Mrs. Barber,-7-It is with very great grief and pain that I write to tell you of the death at 7.15 this morning of your son, Corpl. H. Barber. "This trench, and the one next to us—both occupied by the sth Cheshires for a consider- able period—this morning were subjected to heavy artillery fire, and in both trenches there were several casualties—inyolving among them a man I can ill-afford to lose, viz., your son. Though not actually in that
I
I
