div.p: CORPORAL HENRY BARBER.
Killed.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 19, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 19, 1915.

brave soldiers our country can ill-afford to lose. I wish I could talk to you and tell you all about this. Lam so very much upset I cannot write much. But we must try to remember it is God's will, and He has called them to Him. I trust you will be brave, and try to bear the pain which undoubtedly this sad news is bound to cause you. I 'feel sure the good people of Lymm will ,comfort you. We all have the, satisfaction of knowing—and I am glad to convey it to you—that he always did his duty; and it was whilst bravely doing his duty that he gave his life. The name of the place where he lies buried—a• beautiful little cemetery—will be communicated to you later. If I can do anything for you I shall be pleased to do so." . .
Officer " Honours."

On Wednesday morning a note was received from Second-Lieutenant j. B. Morgan. It was dated June 12th, and ran : " Dear Mrs. Barber,—l am sorry to inform you of the loss you have sustained in your son's death. He was struck by a shell which exploded in the trench yesterday. He died instantly and wehout pain. May I Offer you my sincere sympathy, and honour you as the mother of one who has died for his eountrY?"

very narrow, and Mr. Marsh's ear came very close to his. He was only six inches off it when he knocked the man down. His car was six feet wide. Be certainly thought, however, that there was room to pass between., Otherwise he could have stopped at once. , ' He had been a chauffeur for nine or , ten years, and had never had an accident before; his licence was perfectly clean. After the acci- dent he took Mr. Gilberts to -Dr. Thorpe's straight away; Mr. Houghton was in the car. "Thought There Would Be -Room."

The Chairman (Vice-Chancellor D. Stiewart Smith): Why couldn't you have stopped till the other car got past you? Defendant: I thought there would be room— in fact, I only just caught him with the front mudguard! Mr. John Houghton, of Westleigh, Ly-mm, said .he was in the car at the time of the acci- dent, and agreed with his chauffeur's state- ment. He was not travelling at an excessive speed. He had employed the man for about five years, and he was very steady and a teetotaller. He did everything possible for the man who was knocked down. Had he thought his • chauffeur had been grossly careless .he would have said' so.

div.head: Seventy Yards Behind.
div.p: Seventy Yards Behind.

A ":I'errier " writes: "Harry is in our com- pany:but .not in our platoon. His platoon!are in the reserve trench, just about seventy yards behind us; and the shells that just miss us sometimes catch them."

On Friday morning Private Joseph Clare wrote; "Corporal 11. Barber got hit with a 'piece of shrapnel on the back a ¶iis head. . . Ah, it ,is very -hard to see pals getting killed. We had only just got over Jack Guest, and now comes another. It will be bad enough for you in Lymm, but seeing them puts us all ' off ' work for a day or two; it is an experience that I don't want to have again if I have the luck to get over this.. . ."

div.head: SHIP CANAL EMPLOYE
div.p: SHIP CANAL EMPLOYE

Born at Bush Green twenty-four years ago, Corporal Bather was the only son of Mr. and Mrs. John Barber. Leaving the .day school at the age of nearly fourteen, he entered respec- tively the employ of 'Mr. C. E. Ardern (news- agent), Mr. Ernest Creasy (butcher), and Mr. Samuel Gould (farmer). With the last he re- mained for six and a half years. lle-then joined Mr. Eli Thomason as a carter, and after a few months entered as a labourer the service of the .Manchester Ship Canal Company---hike his father.

• He attended the Congregational. Church and Sunday School, and. also-for a long time acted .as instructor to tile Lads' Club—as Captain Hartley mentioned. In addition he acted as captain of the Saturday Football Club.. With everybody he was extremel,Y popular. To the Territorial movemhit he had belonged for neatly six years; and on the outbreak of war was "in his last. camp." He then trained in different parts of the country until February —when he crossed to France with his Lymm comrades.
It will be remembered—for "The Examiner" fully reported the episode at the time—that a month or two ago the Corporal had a narrow escape in the trenches, his pocket-book saving his life.
Only on Monday morning there arrived from him a field-card saying he was quite well. That was his lasi-, communication.
Besides father and mother, Corporal Barber —who was unmarried—leaves four sisters to mourn their loss.

div.head: PRIVATE JACK GUEST.
div.p: PRIVATE JACK GUEST.
More Tributes—From Battlefield And
Pulpit.
The Lymm Territorials are still much affected by the death of I%ivate sack Guest, and frequently refer to him in letters home. Captain's Loss. •
From Captain Hartley was received on Sun- day morning the following letter—dated June Bth:

"Dear Mr.. and Mrs. Guest,—l feel I want just to send yousa few lines of sympathy in the great loss you hav&sustained in the unfortunate death of your son, who had the ill-luck to bei shot early yesterday morning.

"He was undoubtedly one ,of the best .and nicest men under my command.- and altogether •fine and reliable soldier; and his loss to me and the company is very great. What his loss must be to you I can easily imagine; for I am sure he was a good and dutiful son-,--as I realised before the war broke out. for I knew him well at the Lads' Club. of which he was such a highly-respected member. Again ex- nn-;sing my very deenest sympathy with you, and apologising for these hurried few lines written under sin+ neculiar cirenmstances. Yonrs very trilY, G. W. C. Hartley (Captain)."

"He was killed at about half-nast two yester- (ley morning." writes Private P. Clare on the gth. .. . " is very sad, and has unset all of w: very much. He was unconscious all the while, and never spoke a word." Sketched for the Rector.

The Rector (the Rev. G. B. Thurston) has received from. Sergeant IT. Clare a long letter, which describes in detail how Private Guest met his death. A sketch is enclosed showing the positions of the German trenches, and the zig-zagged British trenches with look-out holes; between the two are thick barbed-wire entaugre- merits.

The course of the bullet is shown to have started far down the British line and to have passed over several divisions in the trenches. The writer adds ;. "The bullet was not shot from the Garman lines opposite, but from an- other trench on our left—our trench being sub- ject to enfilading fire. . •. . Quite a number of men have been wounded or killed in this manner. I thought at Arst,he would live. . . We have suffered.a very big loss." Corporal Jack H. Moston Writes: "I do feel sorry about Jack Guest, for he was a good lad and a good soldier. He always did his duty without a grumble." At Wesleyan Anniversary.

The Sunday school anniversary of the Rush Green Wesleyan Church was held on Sunday, when the. :afternoon preacher was Lance- Corporal S. Linley (of the sth Cheshires). Of their old scholar, 'Jack Guest, ,Mr. Linley spoke very feelingly; and initcle touching reference to his death at the Front.
Private Guest was a brother-in-law of Mr. John Elliott—son of Mr. and Mrs. B. Elliott— whose remarkably fine Army record we gave last week.
IF SOLDIERS WENT ON STRIKE!
" Tcrrier " Rebukes The Down-Tools Brigade.

• A young lady received Word•dated June llth, which says; "it is our eleventh day to-day in the fire-trench, and as far as we know we are not going out till next Tuesday night. The Germans have given us some shell this time; in the eleven days we have lost about 42 men killed and wounded, .so you can see what it is . 'I don't think we shall come in the trenches again for a long time after this— and maybe not again if we get out all right this time So there must be some good news Wait- ing for us. . . . I. hope so, a chap does not feel up to much after four months of a life like this. "I 'think that if every single young man would do his bit it would see this lot to a finish. . just fancy young men going. out on strike at a time like this! It is out here they ought to be. What would we get if we went on strike for a halfpenny a week—never mind a penny an hour like those chaps? Why, we ,should. just get Shot at dawn, and nothing else. And I wish they would make those men come here; they would be glad to work for less than they get now. If they think we have got the Germans beaten they are wrong—for the brutes (as T should call them) will stop at nothing. "Those men would change their minds if they Were here, and saw their pals shot down by their side. I can tell, you it makes us feel like a strike—e strike at the Germans with the co-ld -steel. That's the sort of strike that is wanted these days, and the sooner they realise it the better. - But never Mind; we are doing 0111' bit. What about the men that have been out here all winter? What is left of them?"

Volunteers' Church Parade.—After marching through the village, the Lyznin detachment of the Cheshire Volunteers on Sunday paraded at the Parish, Church. The Rector occupied the pulpit, and the lessons were read by Captain G. Williamson and Mr. AliTnes (a member of the corps). The captain, together with Sergts. Farrar and Moston, was in charge.—To-day there is to be a battalion parade at Cheadle. The [Tram platoon: will attend.

div.head: Striking I nference.
div.p: Striking I nference.

Mr. V. S. IVUod said this was a charge of driving to the danger of the public, and he respectfully submitted that before convicting they should be satisfied that the driver was guilty of gross negligence. It had been shown that he sounded his horn. On the question of speed: Mr. Marsh stated that he slowed down just before he got to the bridge, and it was at that spot that Mr. Houghton's car passed him. He then crossed • the bridge slowly, and next heard the thud. Well, if Mr. Houghton's car was going fast, what Mr. Marsh said was that while he was going slowly, Mr. Houghton's car only travelled from where it passed him to the point where the man was knocked down— only a few feet. Thus he could not have been going fast. Miss Marsh had corroborated. The chauffeur said quite candidly that he thought he had more room; this was a bona- fide that it was not done purposely. • Mr. Houghton had done everything he could—a great deal—for the man; and the chauffeur's licence was a perfectly clean one. ." There Was Negligent Driving."
The magistrates retired for some time. After their return, _ _ .

The Chairman said: We think this is a case where there was negligent driving—not that it was a very bad case; but still there was negli- gence. We fine the defendant five shillings and sixteen shillings special costs.

div.head: LICENSEE IN COURT. Sold " Fluid During Hours Prohibited
div.p: LICENSEE IN COURT. Sold " Fluid During Hours Prohibited
In War-Time.
"DESERVED HEAVIER FINE."

By order of the Colonel at Chester; the Superintendent of the Lymm division conducted —at the Petty Sessions on Wednesday—the prosecution of John Nicholls, licensee of the Bull's Head Inn, Lymm—who was summoned for having on May 29t1r, "kept his premises open unlawfully between the hours of six and eight a.m.; against the order of the competent military authority. At the same time Fred Owen, of the Bridge, Lymm, was summoned for aiding and abetting him. .
Mr., Leicester Caldecutt, solicitor, of Knuts- ford, conducted the prosecution on behalf of the police; and Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, of Warrington, appeared on behalf of both defendants.

div.head: "FOR ALL PURPOSES."
div.p: "FOR ALL PURPOSES."

Mr. Caldecutt -stated that the proceedings were taken under Regulation 10 of the Defence of the Realm Act. The order for that district had been made by General McKinna, and a copy had been duly served upon Nicholls. The order was that the premises should only be open between 10.30 a.m. and 10 p.m. on week- days; outside which hours they were to be closed for all purposes. Therefore it -did not matter whatever the sale might have been. Early Morning Vigil.

The facts were that by reason of a complaint received by the Sergeant, he caused this par- ticular house to be put under observation— P.C. Atherton concealing himself at the back, so as to have a view of the yard. At about ten to seven, P.C. Atherton saw Owen—who lived next door—come to the wall and proceed to throw at the windows at the back of the house. Nicholls then came out to Owen, who handed him a bottle and a coin. Nicholls flicked the coin up, and it was .a, silver one. The bottle contained a dark 'fluid. Shortly afterwards Sergeant Davies joined P.C. Atherton. At 7.25 Owen again came out of his house, and threw gravel towards the back windows of Nicholls' house; and the bottle was passed to him. He went into his house, came out again and handed the bottle back again—a coin having been passed.
" It's No Use."

At a quarter to ten the two police together went and saw Nicholls, and told him that they had had his house under observation and what they had seen. He replied: "I have nothing to say about it. There are two of you; it's no use my saying anything about it. I am sorry." They also told Owen, and he only said: "I don't think. What drink I have had this morning I got last night." . "It does occur to me," concluded Mr. Caldecutt, " a most flagrant breach of this order, for which it is difficult to imagine that any excuse can be offered. This is a very bad ease indeed; and whatever it was that wa4 in the bottle, the offence is of course that the house was opened at a time it should have been closed. Otherwise it is difficult to imagine Why the transaction should have been carried out in so secret a manner." .

div.head: EVIDENCE NOT CONTESTED.
div.p: EVIDENCE NOT CONTESTED.

When the first witness was about to be called, Mr. Browne rose and said he had heard the very fair opening, and was not going to do any- thing but admit the whole of the regulations, nor to deny/the facts stated. Therefore he put in a technical plea of guilty. Next Door and Whit Week.
P.C. Leonard Atherton having corroborated the evidence,

Mr. Browne went on to say that principally the order was made for the benefit of soldiers and persons employed on the manufacture of munitions; and in this case neither were con- cerned. It was a case of the man living next door, and it was a case of Whit week. Mr. Owen was employed at a Manchester ware- house, and at that* time was on holiday. On the morning in question there was no arrangement whatever, but he was not very well. It might be said that he "wanted a bit of the hair , of the dog that bit him the night before." Un- fortunately he attracted the attention of Mr. .Nicholls—who was under the impression that he was allowed to supply non-intoxicating liquor, and supplied something detailed by the police.

Now there was no possible legal excuse, ha granted; but .Mr. Nicholls came to that house with a great number of years' good character, eta had kept it for three years. Unfortunately he was tempted, and did supply Mr. Owen with something in this bottle—under the `im- pression that he was doing him a kindness„ It was purely the case of a man On his holidays without any serious intention. It ivfy the first of this nature in this tPetty Sessional] division; and would and must be a warning to all.

div.head: THECHAIRMAN'S WARNING.
div.p: THECHAIRMAN'S WARNING.
The magistrates retired for several minutes. On their return,

The Chairman (Vice-Chancellor D. Stewart Smith) said: These are two very serious cases. Regulations have been promulgated by authority to meet the war conditions in which we find ourselves; and it is essential for national safety that those regulations should be obeyed. Now we take into consideration the fact that this is the, first case in the Lymm district, and it must not. be supposed that because these penalties are light' we intend to make any future penalties light. It is a case which per- haps deserves heavier fines than we intend to impose; but we think that it will call attention to .these cases in the district. The licensee will be fined £5 wih £3 3s. special, costs—with .the alternative of six months' imprisonment—and Owen must pay £2 and it Is. special costs— with the alternative of one month's imprison- ment.
Mr. Browne afterwards explained, on behalf of Chesters' Brewery company, that it was absolutely contrary- to their wishes that any.- thing like that should take place.
CORPORAL GEORGE APPLETON.
Wounded

of the unlucky men. I gat a slight wound on the back of the left 'shoulder with this rotten shrapnel, and another slightly above the left knee. I had to go to the dressing station to have it dressed, but I am back again with the regiment, and it was not serious; so don't worry. " "Many a time I thought we were going to be blown to atoms, because the Germans were fairly giving us pOmpey,' and the shrapnel is a terrible thing. There were three other chaps by my side who got wounded, but none of them seriously; so we may be thankful it was not worse. Anyhow we are still pegging away at it. When we were relieved at night and went in the dug-outs for an hour's sleep (if pos- sible) the Huns would start their shelling again and drop them right on top of us; so you can imagine what it was like. . ." With Manchester Solicitor. .

Born at Statham twenty-one years ago, Cor- poral G. Appleton was educated at the Lymm schools until attaining the age of fourteen. He has since entered the service of Mr. G. L. Wel- ford, solicitor, of Manchester. • On September Ist he enlisted in Kitchener's Army, and after over six months' training in various parts of the South, was drafted out to the Front a short time ago with the Rifle Brigade Since his departure he has . sent home several interesting letters—all ix ( the. cheeriest vein.

div.head: MOTOR ACCIDENT.
div.p: THE MOTOR ACCIDENT.
Chauffeur Summoned For Negligent Driving.

Further particulars of a motor 'accident already reported in "The Examiner," came to light at the Vetty Sessions on Wednesday—when James Lawless, chauffeur, of Pepper-:street, Lymm, was summoned for negligently driving a motor car on the highway on May 19th, to the danger of the public. He pleaded not guilty. The chauffeur was represented by Mr. V. S. Wood, solicitor, of Manchester; and Superin- tendent Sutherland conducted the case for the police. Injured Man's Story.

Edwin Gilberts, labourer, of 16, Newfields, said that at about 5.40 on the evening of May 19th he was walking from Thelwall towards Lymm. As he was nearing Brook Bridge he saw a motor car coming towards him. It was that of Mr. Marsh. He got well into the side of the road—about a couple of feet "off the sod." (There was a hedge, then "the sod," and then the macadamised road.) He heard nothing at all behind him, and Mr. Marsh's car passed him quite safely. At that time he had crossed the bridge, but was still near to it.. Suddenly something hit him right in the back, and knocked him over unconscious ;previously he had heard nothing. When he came round he found that his head was cut—it had to have five stitches. A young lady named Miss Marsh was by him, and Mr. Houghton's driver [Lawless] came next. He (witness) was lying "on the sod." He asked him wl\at had done it, and Lawless said he had and was very sorry. He replied: "What! A motor hit me? I never expected a motor to come .behind me." It was then about a quarter to six. Ile knew the road quite well: it should be wider, for 'there was not room .for the public and two cars—and it had no footpath. Mr. Marsh's car came in front of him; he did not remember whether he sounded the horn—he never heard it. The car had passed just about a second before the accident. '

div.head: Unheeded Horn.
div.p: Unheeded Horn.

Mr. Edward Marsh, farmer, of Bradley Hall, Appleton, said that when he was approaching the bridge he saw a car coming the other way. Being nearer) the bridge he assumed that he was entitled to take it first, and sounded his horn. He could see, however, that the other car did not take any notice; and in order to avoid, meeting he had to slow down. He was practi- cally on the other side of the bridge .when the other car came along, as just as he got to the other side he heard a thud. Mrs. Marsh turned round and said: "They've knocked that -man down!" • .

When he saw the car coming in the opposite direction he had thought it was coming fast, taking the road and everything into considera- tion. It was a dangerous place. ;He was coming down the hill on the Lymm side. Gilberts was knocked down on the Lymm side just by the cottage gate; it was the length of two cottages from the bridge to the point where he was knocked down. The two cars met prac- tically in the opening on the Lymm side of the bridge. He (witness) was driving slowly— about fifteen miles an hour, and had got over. the bridge when he heard the thud. Lady Cyclist's Evidence.

Miss Margaret Marsh, of Booth's Hill, Lymm, said she was cycling from Warrington to Lymm at the time of the accident. On arriving at the brook she saw Mr. Marsh's car coming in the opposite direction, and heard the horn blow. She heard a screecher go which sounded to be by the Pickering Arms. When getting near the brook she heard Mr. Marsh's car be- hind her, and got off her bicycle. She was on the other side of the bridge. She stood still at the corner, and saw Mr. Gilberts knocked down by Mr. Houghton's car—it must have been by the mudguard of the front wheel. His head struck the stones of the cottage gateway, and he lay knocked into the gateway. He had cut his head on the stones in the fall. There ,was nobody about in the road until a gentle- man came running round the corner. she thought Mr. Marsh's car had had the prior right of crossing the bridge, and that Mr. Houghton's ear was going fast. The screecher belonged to Mr. Houghton's car. Only Twelve Miles An Hour.

Defendant said that when nearing the bridge he blew his 'horn. The car was then going at about twelve miles an hour, as the speedometer indicated. He was then fifty yards from the bridge. ; He first saw Mr. Marsh's car when Coming round the coiner. They actually met on 'the Lymm side of the bridge. He saw Mr. Gilberts walking about two feet off the side of the road in the direction his car was going, and verged round between the other car and the man. div.head: WAR GARDEN FETE.
div.p: WAR GARDEN FETE.
Successful Penketh Function

div.head: Opened By The Mayer.
div.p: Opened By The Mayer.
GALLANTS ON THE GREENS

No matter where one goes in these appalling times, it seems virtually impossible to escape reminders of the conflagration- of passion that is devouring Europe and affecting in some degree the whole world. It was delightful in the charming arid spacious grounds of Hall Nook, Penketh, on Saturday afternoon and evening. The glorious sunshine, the flower- scented breeze, the hand music that -floated faintly or with swelling volume, according to the will of the wind, and mingled with the hum of bees, the glorious beauty of the scene and the indefinable sense of peace and aloofness from the world that crept on one and set one a-dreaming, seemed incompatible with the man- made horrors which the limping khaki-clad figures on the bawling and croquet lawns brought to the mind, saddening the scene, dark- ening the sky and turning the plaintive music into an insistent appeal for explanation of the great mystery of things..

div.head: MANY ATTRACTIONS.
div.p: MANY ATTRACTIONS.

Hall Nook made an ideal setting for the garden fete held in aid of the Prince of Wales' National Relief Fund, and the generosity of Mr. J. B. Aitken in lending his beautiful resi- dence for the occasion Was very keenly appre- ciated. The fete was well attended, and num- erous were the comments on the taste and skill with. which the grounds had been laid out. .A .good number of convalescent soldiers' from the Whitecross Hospital, Warrington, were atmongst the guests : There was no lack of attractions. - For those athletically inclined, tennis facilities were provided; for lovers of something less strenuous, two forms of "out- door billiards" were available, viz., croquet and bowls. These games, for which a 'small charge was made for the ' good, of the cause, were all well. patronised. Then, in the course of an exploratory prowl, "The Examiner" man came suddenly on a weighing machine -tucked away in an obscure •nook. This. side-show—we call it . a side-show because if one keepi .vigil long enough one's patience is usually rewarded with interesting sights—was visited by people of all shaPes- and sizes, and the inexorable hand of the avoirdupois , clock told many a home- truth with unflinching ,courage. At the entrance to this intelligence department was a mystic sign: "Something for nothing, •. if ll What the " if" was we know, not; being Scotch and scenting a trap, but if the device was by any chance intended to catch canny Caledon- ians, it was an inevitably futile effort in view of .the-fact- that there was quite a lot to be had for nothing, such as touring the stables, in- specting the gold-fish pond, playing onlooker at the tennis and croquet and bowls- contests, and listening to the excellent music of the Penketh Tannery Prize Band. FAR FRON THE CANNONS' ROAR. ConvaleScent heroes from hospital, and the nurses who accompanied them, entered with zest into the games of croquet, though, to be Sum-. some of the gallant fellows seemed to find it slow and an inferior pastime to cricket. Play- fully fiendish was the delight with which they cannoned opponents' balls back over ground that had already been covered once. Here, at least, genuine satisfaction was obtainable. It. was pleasant to see these comrades-in-arms vieing with one another with a mixture of gravity and gaiety and joyfully taking mali- cious advantage of whatsqever misfortune the luck of the game visited 'on a rival hammer- man. With mallet and coloured ball, these men who had seen nightmare-sights on the field of battle, became, in their light-hearted irre- sponsibility, like BO many gambolling children. Mercifully, the human mind can forget. A sergeant of dare-devil demeanour played a game of bowl .on one leg. His left foot was innocent of any covering 'but a grey sock and was apPar- ently in a state that made contact with any- thing solid painful.
SOME CHAMBER_ MUSIC,6SONGS AND

div.head: INSTRUMENTAL SOLOS.
div.p: INSTRUMENTAL SOLOS.

A repletion of attractions was afforded in two concerts, of an hour's duration each, given in Mrs. Aitken's tasteful and spacious drawing- room, and both of theta, it is pleasing to say, were well attended and gave manifest pleasure. In the first the Rawdon Briggs String Quartet —a combination well known to frequenters of the Manchester concerts—exclusively took part, rendering the whole of the four movements of Haydn's D • Major with that high degree of finish and refinement which has deservedly- made the four instrumentalists concerned collectively famous. Such a work gave to Schubert's varia- tions on the aria "Death and the Maiden" a sense of both contrast and relief, and, being played in not too slow a tempo, interest in tlese never for a moment flagged. Though the Minuet and Fugue of Beethoven proved a trifle heavy for a. hot summer afternoon, it should be ire- membered that these movements. were preceded by two items played with a refreshing brightness and pulsating vivacity which amply compen- sated one - for any irksomeness ' felt -at the moment. These items were a Mendelssohnian Scherzo and, coupled with it, an Irish Reel, entitled "Molly on the Shore,"..by Grainger. The programme of the second concert in- cluded some interesting songs sung with marked ability by. Miss Thraves, Miss Alice Horner, and Miss Livesey, and some instrumental solos well played by Mr. and Mrs. Rawdon Briggs and Mr. Walter Hatton, Mrs. John Dodds acting in the capacity of accompanist skilfully and with good judgment. In the evening the band played for dancing.

div.head: OPENING CEREMONY.
div.p: THE OPENING CEREMONY.

The opening ceremony was performed by his Worship the Mayor of ,Warrington (Alderman Peter Peacock) at half-past two, after a small group, with the Mayor and Mayoress in the centre, had been photographed. Mr. W. Furness, in formally introducing the Mayor to the gathering, said it was not usual for Warrington Mayors to visit the suburbs of the town, and he thought they were very honoured and privileged in having the Mayor and Mayoress present that afternoon. He felt .quite 'safe in voicing the unanimous appreciation of the company of the action of Alderman and Mrs. Peacock in gracing that day's 'function With their presence: (Applause.)

div.head: ..‘A FARTHING IN THE POUND."
div.p: ..‘A FARTHING IN THE POUND."

The Mayor, said he had persistently refused to attend any outside function since the war commericed, owing to the ninny and arduous duties that had devolved upon the Mayoress and himself since then. flaying referred to Mr. and Mrs. ,Furness as "the Mayor and Mayoress of this district," and alluded to the generosity of Mr. Aitken, his Worship expressed the hope that the efforts of the committee who had organised that day's proceedings would be liberally sup- ported. div.head: GREAT SAN KEY.
div.p: GREAT SAN KEY.

Only Half a Lamp.—At the County Petty Sessions, held in Warrington on Wednesday, before. Messrs. W. Fairclough and J. Rymer Young. Joseph Keenan, a roadthan, of 35, 1100 d lane, Great Sankey, was fined ss. (or six days' imprisonment) for having cycled without a light in Liverpool-road. Sankey, at 10.45 on the night of June 10th.—P.S. Henderson said he saw the man cycling without a light and called on him to stop, but he did not do so. Witness, therefore, jumped on his bicycle and gave chase. When he caught the man up and brought him to a standstill he found that he had only' part of a lamp on his machine, and that that was fastened on upside down. (Laughter.) •• •

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

An Undesirable Visitor.—Robert Rotherham, of South-lane, Bold, was at the County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, find 10s., inclusive, for having been drunk and' disorderly in Warring- ton-road, Penketh, on May 31st.—The evidence was that he was shouting and swearing and creating a nuisance. This was,his first offence.

. ,Farm Labourer Does the " Highway " Fling. .--At the County Petty Sessions, held at War- rington on Wednesday morning, Lawrence Quinn, a farm, labourer, employed at Penketh Hall Farm, pleaded, in answer to a summons for drunkenness, that he was "drowsy and sleepy."—The evidence of P.S. Henderson' however, showed that, on May 31st, far from the man being "drowsy and sleepy," he was dancing and flinging himself about in the high- way, besides shouting and swearing. In fact. his antics caused a crowd to assemble. Witness asked the man to go home two or three times. and eventually had to see him there.—The de- fendant, who had been before the magistrates on three previous occasions—the last timv being on May 31st—was ordered to pay an in- clusive fine of 10s., or to go to prison for seven days.

Wesleyan Sunday School Anniversary.—At the Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday, the children,;° anniversary services were held. The Rev- Manning, of Blackburn, a former minister 01 the Warrington circuit, was the preacher for the day. The children claimed his particular attention in the morning, and in the evening his discourse to the congregation was entitled "Observation, or Eyes and no Eyes!" In the afternoon a cantata, entitled "The *Great Light" (Finley Lyon) was well rendered by the choir and Sunday school scholars, unger the able conductorship of Mr: George Carman (choirmaster). A series of sofos. quartets and' choruses were greatly appreciated by the congregation, who were present in goodly num- bers. Mr. J. G. Withinshaw occupied the chair. The collections for the day were set- aside for theepurposes of the Sunday school. and the sum of £l4l was asked for. Thi‘: amount, however, proved too high a figure, but the substantial sum of 228 ,13s. 6d. icBs realised. Mr. A. Clatworthy presided at the organ throughout the special services.

They felt very honoured that he had found time to be present that day and open the fete. The open- ing ceremony would be incomplete without nn acknowledgment of the great obligation they and the National Fund were under for the kindness of Mr. Aitken in allowing them the use, of his beautiful grounds. div.head: YESTERDAY'S OMINOUS MESSAGE FOR TYRANTS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S OMINOUS MESSAGE FOR TYRANTS.
By C. E. P

The Star of the great War Lord Napoleon set for ever one hundred years ago, yesterday —on June 18th, 1815. That star began to wane with the retreat from Moscow. After this retreat, in .spite•of Napoleon's wonderful recovery, the Allies in time wore his forces down. He was • badly beaten at Leipzig in October, 1813, and he finally surrendered at Paris on 31st March, 1814. By the decision of the Allied Powers, Napoleon was suffered to retain a fragment of his former empire, the Island of Elba, off the coast of Tuscany, and he remained in practical banishment for eleven months. But, taking advantage, of the quar- rels of the Allies and of the dissatisfaction of the French with their Bourbon King, on the Ist March, 1815, he landed on the French coast near Cannes. He won Franco. without a blow; the whole army revolted and flocked to his standard.
An Enemy of the World. Strife among the Allies, and of this there was plenty, was hushed in view of the com- mon danger, and Napoleon was declared an outlaw in the following terms:

In breaking the'convention. which had established him in the Island of Elba, Buonaparte has destroyed the sole legal title to which his political existence is 4 attached. By re-appearing in France with projects of trouble and overthrow be has not less de- prived himself of the protection of the laws, and made it evident in the face-of the uni- verse that there can no longer be either peace or truce with him. The Powers, there- fore, declare that Buonaparte has placed himself out of the pale of civil and social relations, and that as the general enemy and disturber of the world he is abandoned to public justice.

England hastened to place an army under the,command of Wellington on the frontier of the \Netherlands. Of the 80,000 men forming this army only about half were English. The remainder were raw recruits from Belgium and Hanover. Wellington's purpose was to unite .with the Prussians under • Marshal Blucher and enter France by Mons and Namur, while the Russians and the'Austrians were to 'attack France by the way of Belforf. But Napoleon gave no time. for these tactics to develop; his policy was always, to attack. The Prussians were driven back with terrible loss on the Wavre. Blucher's 'retreat left Wellington's flank uncovered, an he with- drew to Waterloo, followed by the 'French under the Emperor. The two forces were about equal in number, but the units in Wel- lington's army. were of a very different value, and the hastily collected levies from the Netherlands broke away early in the battle, leaving the' English forces to bear the whole brunt of the onslaught.

Wellington's Coup de Grace. • The particulars of the great battle are well known. ,The fortunes of the day hung in the balance till late in the afternoon. Welling- ton, in his dispatches; tells how the end came: The enemy repeatedly charged our infan- try with bis cavalry, but those attacks were uniformly unsuccessful, and they afforded opportunities to our cavalry to charge, in one of which Lord E. Somerset's brigade, consisting of the Life Guards, Royal Horse , Guards and First Dragoon Guards, highly distinguished tilemselves, as did that of Major-General Sir W. Ponsonby, having taken many prisoners and an eagle. Theso- attacks were repeated till about - seven in the evening, when the enemy made a desperate effort with the cavalry and in- fantry, supported by the fire of artillery, to , force our left centre near the farm of La • Haye Sainte, which, after a• severe contest, was defeated, -and having observed that the troops retired from this attack in great con- fusion, and that the march of General • Bulow's corps by Ensclierniont upon Plauchenorte and La Belle Alliance had begun to take effect, and as I could perceive the fire of his cannon, and as Marshal Prince Blucher had joined in person with a corps of his army to the left of our line by Ohaim, I determined to attack the enezny, and imme- diately advanced the whole line of infantry, supported by the cavalry and artillery. Sue- eeeded in every point; the enemy was forced from his position on the heights, and fled in the utmost confusion, leaving behind him, as far as I could judge, one hundred and fifty pieces of cannon with their ammuni- tion, which fell into our hands. I continued the pursuit till long after dark, • and • then discontinued it only on account of the fatigue of our troops, who had been engaged during twelve hours, and because I found myself on the same road with Marshal Blucher, who assured me of his intention to follow the enemy throughout the night; he has sent me word this morning that he has taken sixty pieces of cannon belonging to the Imperial Guard, and several car- riages, baggage, &c., belonging to Buonaparte in Gemappe•

div.head: CHESHIRE IN LONDON.
div.p: CHESHIRE IN LONDON.
Interest In The Wounded Men Of The County.

The first annual general meeting of the Cheshire Society in London was held at the Cannon-street Hotel, Major Louis A. Newton in the chair. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the, report of the Council, observed that owing to the war the Society had been obliged to limit its activities, and he feared that while the pre- sent state of affairs prevailed they would have to move cautiously. .

Mr. J. C. Gardner, hon. treasurer, presented the accounts, which were approved. ,‘- • Mr. A. M. Latham (Recorder of Birkenhead), seconded by Mr. George .Leigh (Knutsford), moved the re-election of His Grace the Duke of Westminster as president of the Society for Um year 1915-Ip, and said he felt sure every member was proud to see their President filling such a useful place in the service of the country. Votes of thanks were accorded to the'follow- ing officers, who were re-elected to their positions: Messrs. J. .C. Gardner (hon. treasurer), W. E. Boughey (hon. auditor), C. W. Hill (hon. secretary), and T. Keith Howick (assistant hon. secretary). The members Of the Council retiring at the elk' of last year were Messrs. J. Arthur Cowley, W. H. Edge, H. Hugh Hughes, E. Sims Hilditch, J. C. Gardner, R. ,Mortimer Montgomery, E. Amphlett-White- house and A. Steele Sheldon, all of whom were re-elected.
THOUGHTS FOR WOUNDED CHESHIREMEN.

Major Newton suggested, amid applause, that the Society should preparp . a scheme for the visiting of wounded Cheshiremen who might be lying in London hospitals. lie proposed that a. fund for supplying comforts to wounded Cheshiremen be opened with a subscription of three, guineas from the society, and that a ladies committee should be formed for the pur- pose of. administei,kng the fund and organising the visitation of the military hospitals in Lon- don by ladies connected with the Society who would undertake the work.

This proposal was seconded by Mr. J. S. Huline and carried unanimously, and it was decided that Mrs). Newton, Mrs. W. B. Davis, Mrs. J. S. Huhue and Mrs. Ross Williams should act as a provisional 'committee, with the assistance of the hon. secretary. The meeting closed with a vote of tlianks to the Chairman, proposed by Mrs. W. B. Davi seconded by Mr. F. Powell, and carried unanimously.

div.head: RKER.
div.p: RKER.
Napoleon fled to Paris and his second and final abdication was followed by the triumph- ant entry of the English and Prussian armies into the French capital.
NEWS OF THE VICTORY. The Official Bulletin as Published in . " The Times."
The following appeared in. " The Times, Tuesday, June 22, 1815:
Official Bulletin.
" Downing-street, June 22nd, 1815.

" The Duke of 'Wellington's Dispatch, dated Waterloo, the 19th June, states that on the preceding day Buonaparte attacked with his whole. force, the British line, supported by a corps of Prussians; which attack, after a long and sanguinary conflict, terminated in the complete overthrow of the Enemy's- Army, with the loss of ONE HUNDRED and FIFTY pieces of CANNON and TWO EAGLES. " During the night the Prussians under Marshal Blucher, who joined in the pursuit of the enemy, captured SIXTY GUNS and a large part of Buonaparte's BAGGAGE. The allied armies continued to pursue the enemy. Two French Generals were taken."

div.head: CENTURY-OLD LEADER.
div.p: A CENTURY-OLD LEADER.
• The following was the, leading article of " The Times " dealing with the • above bulletin:—

" Such is the g. reat and glorious result of those masterly movements by which the Hero of 'Britain met and frustrated the audacious attempt of the Rebel Chief. Glory to Wel- lington, to our gallant soldiers, and to our brave Allies! Buonaparte's reputation has been Viecked. and his last grand stake has been lost in this tremendous conflict. • TWO HUNDRED AND TEN PIECES OF CANNON captured in a; single battle put to the blush the boasting column of the Place de Vendome. Long and sanguinary, •indeed, we fear the conflict must have been;- but the boldness of the Rebel Frenchmen was the boldness of despair, and conscience sate heavy on those arms which were raised against their Sovereign, against their oaths, and against the peace and happiness of their cpuntry. We confidently anticipated a great and immediate defection from the Rebel cause. We are aware that a great part of the French nation looked to the opening of this campaign with a superstitious expectation of success to a man whom, though many of them hated and many of them feared, all had been taught to look on as the first captain of the age. He himself went forth boasting in his strength and still more in his talents. He had for many years ridiculed Carnet's plan of a north- ern campaign, and had openly avowed at Paris his intention to break through the -Allied Armies, instead of Moving round both their flanks. With aalittle reserve had he declared that he would oiSen the campaign on • the Meuse and Sambre. In short, by a refinement in finesse, he had exposed his 'true plan, imagining that nobody would believe that such was his real intention. We do not deny that his plan might have been one of considerable ability, but be did not take into the account that he was to be opposed by abilities superior to his own. That unpalatable truth his vanity would not allow him to believe, nor mould it easily find credit with his admirers; but the 18th of June, we trust, will satisfy -the most incredulous. TWO HUNDRED AND 'PE? PIECES OF CANNON! When, where,. or bow is this loss to be. repaired ? Besides, what has become o,f. his invincible Guard, of his admired and dreaded cuirassiers ? Again we do not deny that these were good- troops; but they were encountered by better. We shall be curious to learn with what degree of coolness, of personal courage and self-posses- sion, Buonaparte played his stake, on which he must have been well -aware that his pre- tensions to Empire hung. It is clear that he retreated; nor are we prepared to hear that he 'fled with cowardice; but we greatly sus- pect that he did not 'court an honourable death. We think his valour is of the calcu- lating kind, and we do not attribute his sur- viving the abdication at Fountainbleau en- tirely to magnanimity. '. To the Official bulletin we have as yet little to add. The dispatches, we understand, were brought by Major Percy, Aide-de-camp to the Duke of 'Wellington; and we. have heard, but we hope the statement is prem- ature, that among the British slain was that gallant • and estimable officer, Sir Thomas Picton. But whoever fell on this . glorious day cannot have fallen in vain. The fabric of rebellion is shaken to its .base. Already we hear numerous desertions have taken place from the Rebel standard; and soon, it is to be hoped, the 'perjured wretches NEY_ and DESNOUTTES, and EXCELMANS, and LALLEMAND, and LABEDOYERE, and their accomplices in baseness and treason, will be left 'alone as marks for the indignation' of Europe and just sacrifices to insulted French honour." . •

The members of the 'various schools in the Warrington Adult School Sub-Union held their Field Day at Shirley last Saturday, when about 150 members and friends assembled to enjoy the various games and sports arranged by the Recreation Committee. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 19, 1915. THE LION OF WATERLOO.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 19, 1915. THE LION OF WATERLOO.
(Written in 1894, after a visit to the scene of the famous battle, which took place on Sunday, the 18th June, 1915.)
Thou noble brute, with strong paw lightly poised, High up in air, upon yon deadly ball, The rumour of thee hath been grimly noised In many a continental capital.
In vain thou lookest from thy mighty mound For other foes thy kingly wrath to dare: They could not meet thee op thy English ground, *But wreaked their petty insults on thee there.
The peasant ploughs these peaceful fields, and lo! Bullets he finds where he expected grain; And round him suddenly red harvests grow Of warriors fighting the old fight again.
And. ere I climb to thy great feet, the sky Unlocks its doors in cataracts of rain; And where the legions of the dead men lie Rages and roars a sudden hurricane.
The lightnings leap, and the great thunders roll, • With horrid crash, across the shuddering land, As when white icebergs Meet around the pole, Or shiver into splinters on the strand.
Beneath thy feet the battle smokes again, " The hero of a hundred fights " is there; And, standing by the distant cottage, fain To trample on him, is the world's despair.
Round yonder barn, by a few stalwarts held, Fierce hosts of warriors surge like seas in storm; But still the little handful, still unquelled, Hold like a fortress the beleaguered farm.
Their ammunition fails, and vainly now They seek to keep the enemy at bay; Hell in their eyes, revenge on every brow, Into the house the foemen force their way,
Escape is hopeless, for the windows, barred, Prevent the egress of the dauntless few; Behind, the maddened legions press them hard; The dead in front into the well they threw.
I drank that day the water—never wine Seemed half so Magical a drink to me; Distilled from heroes' veins, it swelled in mine Till every pulse in them sang Liberty."
Again the solid squares in order stood, Like rocks confronting the relentless wave; Back from the contest, drenched in their own blood, Again recoiled the bravest'of the brave. C
Hour after hour the .foaming sea of steeds Broke baffled on the solid rock of men; As one drops out another still succeeds; • Again they charge but to recoil again.
And yonder, where the ancient chateau hides Amid the .umbrage of the sheltering trees, A valiant little garrison derides A ravening horde of desperate enemies.
The red wall round it seems a wall of men, Half hidden in the treacherous mists of morn; But ,Bonaparte's battalions seek in vain To make a breach within that rampart worn.
I saw it, broken into fragments, still Remaining to attest the time-worn tale; A monument to the undaunted will Which held it till the day began to fail,
And, with the dusk, the solid squares became A thousand sudden thunderbolts of war, Let loose, at last, in England's mighty name, The baffled tyrant's latest hope to. mar.
Along the very road I proudly trod, In one grim rabble, the great army runs: They fought right well—the issue was with God, And with our honest English hearts and guns.
. . Nor shall the 'need of genarotis praise be grudged To our allies, who, burning for the fight, For hours in vain, through thick morasses trudged, And, hence, could only reach us with the night.
But round you church, upon whose roof I saw The cracks and crannies of the fusilade, As village gossips still relate with awe, A noble stand the toilworn warriors made,
And ernshed the foe to powder, moving on. To where the larger battle ebbed and flowed, Arriving footsore, as the day was gone, And joining in the chase up yonder road,
While the foiled arbiter of Europe's fate— The grandest warrior in the world save one— Fled from the bloody field disconsolate... His proud -sword shattered, and his great dream done.
And, as the moon —stole o'er these haunted -plains, Dead eyes stared blankly at its silver face; And, soon, a solitary horseman reins His trembling steed amid the bloody place,
And, in the silver gleam, I surely see The great world-victor. Has he come to keep A carnival amid this butchery? Ye little know him—he has come to weep!
For, if defeat be food for honest tears, Tears well may grace an honest victory too. At best it brings much heartbreak—all these years Have not effaced the graves of Waterloo!
And, therefore, at thy feet, oh, lion bold! Love of my country surging in my veins, pondering on all war means, cry "Mold! Count up its losses, estimate its gains;
"And, as ye see this smiling land, and think Of all the gallant troops of dead men there, Ask if these fields need human blood to drink, Then pray for peace, and may God grant the prayer!"
ARTHUR BENNETT.
* The French Army, on their march to Antwerp, in 1832, broke a piece from the tail of the great bronze image. •

:The world will think of Lewis Carroll as one who opened out a new and delightful vein which added at once mirth and refine- ment to life. May we not say that there has flowed into the literature of our time LL rill bright and sparkling, health-giving, and purifying wherever its waters extend?

That happy rill has flowed through the literature of Many nations. Translated into most European languages, it has carried joy to children and to all who have childlike hearts. All through America and the Colonies, even in Arabia, they know Alice and the Cheshire Cat.
Nothing can make Hill Cliffe and Daresbury more beautiful to us, but these remembrances may make it just a little dearer.

div.head: DARESBURY AND ITS ASSOCIATIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY AND ITS ASSOCIATIONS.
Sunday School Union Lecture.
By ARTHUR MOUNFIELD.

Leaping ancient things and ancient names, let us spend a little time with Some people who have been associated with the neighbour- hood in more recent times, by the fact that they have worshipped or were married or buried here. We mention ,first the Boyer family of Stockton Lodge.. The Lodge stands by the -roadside on the north side of "London Bridge," and is familiar enough to both natives and travel- lers. The older portion . can be easily , distin- guished from the newer part, and is more than two centuries old. Here in a different day lived John de Beauvoir, a member of a French Hugenot family. The persecution of the French Protestants drove many to take refuge in England, and they brought to our land industries and knowledge, for which we have reason to be grateful. John de Beauvoir was a native of Marseilles, born there in 1714, and after a sojourn in the Channel Islands came to England. It was hardly to be ex- pected that the English people would make the: needful effort to pronounce Beauvoir, and they promptly simplified it to Bover.

John 80-ver entered the Navy and attained the rank of Post Captain, serving England in several campaigns against his former coun- trymen. He was with Admiral Byng %Olen that unfortunate commander was sent to .in- tercept the French fleet, and was in service on the warship Buckingham in the expedition which brought the Admiral to a traitor's death This chapter in the Captain's career concerns us hero because it brought him into friendship with Admiral Hoare, the builder of the house known as " Belle, Field," whom we must soon mention.

It was upon being appointed Natal Super- intendent of the Cheshire district that Cap- tain Bover came to live at Stockton Lodge, but previous to his sea battles he had married a Cheshire lady of good family, Mary Malbon, of Bradeley Hall. They were married in Daresbury,ChUrch in 1752, and lived at Stock- ton Lodge surrounded by their thirteen children.

Two sons followed, him in the Navy, and his three ,daught4s brought Jame to the family name by their beauty. 'Ann, -Sophy, and Maria Boyer were all beautiful, but the most winsome was Maria. The Court artist Hoppner painted her portrait, and lovers in legions flocked to Stockton Lodge.. But Maria did not find the right one, and died unmarried at the Lodge in 1810.

div.head: ADMIRAL HOARE.
div.p: ADMIRAL HOARE.

We have already mentioned Admiral Hoare, the friend Of Captaiit Boyer. It was he who built " Belle Field," beautiful for Situation upon the south -side of lull Cliffe, and none can fail to admire his admirable choice of a site for his home. The Admiral had ideas of his own on the subject of what a house should be like. He had only known one kind of dwelling, and one manner of life. And so his house, when it was built, was erected upon the model of g ship, and ship life • and ship language prevailed. The house was long and its. Windows like port holes. His sleep- ing room was fitted with a hammock, and his servants were compelled to rest in similar appliapees. . Time was indicated by ii. ship's bell, and Cheshire domestics were compelled to learn the mysteries of two-bells, four-bells and the dog-watch. Their opinions upon these things have not found a place in the pages of history, but doubtless they had opinions, as they certainly would have upon the subject of hammocks as things- to sleep in. Worse still they had to learn the mean- ing of a ship's signals, for when they worked in the fields the Admiral flew the order to " cease work and come to supper " in the form of coloured flags hoisted on a flag pole.

div.head: QUARTER DECK.
div.p: THE QUARTER DECK.

This flag pole stood in the centre of the circular garden. which still remains, Here was the " quarter-deck," from which the Admiral took his time by sextant from the sun, observed the wind, and made entries each day in his log-book. The dry-land sea- man exacted from his servants all the respect which an admiral merited. They must ap- proach him with doffed hat and talk nautical language, or be despised. Said one who knew him very well, " He was a terrestro-nautico animal, but with all his foibles not a warmer-hearted, kinder or more hospitable creature ever lived." The ways of land creatures were evidently not worth learning, and he talked salt and water to the end of his days. The novelist Smollet drew a picture—very much overdonewe should say —of the Admiral under the name of 'Hawser Trunnion. Those who wish to see this carica- ture of the Admiral may find it in the early pages of " Perigrine Pickle."

div.head: LEWIS CARROLL AND HIS "WONDERLAND."
div.p: LEWIS CARROLL AND HIS "WONDERLAND."

Yet another very interesting association of Daresbury is the fact that it' was the birth- place' and early home of Lewis Carroll, the author of "Alice in Wonderland." Charles, Lutwinge Dodgson, for that was his- .true name, was the eldest son of Charles Dodgson, who was vicar of Daresbury in 1832, the year of his birth. . His birthplace was the old parsonage, situate more than a" mile from the Church, and he began his career on January 27th. For eleven years he 'lived in this quiet spot. So quiet, indeed, was it that the pass- ing of a farmer's cart was quite an event. The children of the manse—ten others fol- lowed Charles—were left to find their own diversions, and it fell to him to discover amusements. Always imaginative, he in- vented the strangest of pastimes. He made pets of the most odd and unlikely animals, and 'surprised his parents by counting certain snails and toads among his closest friends. He gave them presents and toys, and weapons which they could use if attacked. Earth- worms and other burrowing creatures were 'especially dear to him, and he conjured up in imagination, their doings in their underground houses.

It was .well for future generations of children that life was quiet at Daresbury, for the boy invented a wonderland which will be the delight of children to tlie end of time. Hill Cliffe was a favourite resort, and its wild life especially attracted him. The homes of the true and original March Hare, Brer Rabbit and the Cheshire Cat are on the wooded slopes of Hill Cliffe. Years after- wards, when the .story was written out, and the title chosen, he told his ,friends that ." Alice in Wonderland" was the dream and invention of . his youth, and that he had simply uncovered it from the midst of his youthful memories.. Nothing that be afterwards wrote had any- thing of the. freshness or genius of " Alice." He wrote " Alice's Looking Glass," which ik of similar type. Of this a small girl made the comment that the Alice of the looking- glass " did try to be like the other Alice," and this is,. perhaps,, the best comment that literary criticism could supply. Lewis Carroll went to Oxford as a young man, and remained there as a tutor in mathematics until his death.. He published several books on his own subject, and con- cerning these a. good story•is told of Queen Victoria. The. late Queen admired " Alice " very much and gave instructions that any- thing else which the author wrote should be brought to her notice. His next book was duly secured, and we may picture the dear old lady settling down to make the acquaintance

div.head: At Cottages And Farms.
div.p: At Cottages And Farms.
WEATHER AND -ROADS.
(Queries and correspondence should be addressed to "The Hub," c/o The Editor. Replies can- not. be sent by post and all queries will be ,answered in our columns.)

•There is a number of people, in varying grades of life, who are praying for rain at the present time. Farmers desire it, especially in some parts of the country; market gardeners all over are depending on rain for their crops; and even cyclists are hoping for a short spell of wet weather. The roads are getting worse and worse; only a good soaking rain will put them into anything like decent going order. To indicate the extent of the drought in certain districts the statement .of a gardener to the effect that. he had to "put in his bean-sticks with a crowbar" will be sufficient. From my own point of view, it is not only on account of road condition that I want rain, but the country will be so much more beautiful if we can have a good downpour. "There are none so queer as folk" is a trite saying. Last December we were complaining of too lunch wet weather; now we are sorry it is so dry.

div.head: CYCLING CAPES
div.p: CYCLING CAPES

I have always been adverse to the use of such things, and rat contention that the majority of them are of little use is borne out by the following, which I read in. a cycling contem- porary:" The more I see of cycle tapes the less I like diem, and vice versa. It is years since. I possessed one of these (sometimes) necessary evils, for I prefer to get wet rather than pre- tend to keep dry. A few days ago, however, when I was some 60 miles away Wan my billet, and the rain was coining down by tho yard, I plunged into a cycle shop and parted with seven of my hard earned shillings in ex- change for a mackintosh cape. I dived.iiito it, and went on my way—not rejoiciit. Soon I found that the faults were as usual.' • To give the cape its due, it does provide some pro- tection,,aDd perhaps my trouble is that I expect too much. Anyhow, the usual lake formed in the ' lap ' of the cape, and when I threw it overboard the moisture usually fell On my legs. The accommodation in the cape was strictly limited, and I was afraid all the time that something would go.' The opening down the front let in the moisture gently but steadily, and worst of all the cape made no pretence of protecting the lower part of my .coat. I sup- pose capes have their uses, but they have their shortcomings too."

div.head: SIDECARS FOR CYCLES.
div.p: SIDECARS FOR CYCLES.

At one time a trailer attached to any ordin- ary cycle was a more Or less common sight. To-day one very rarely sees such a combination. It is the same in this case 'as with the motor- cycle, the trailer has been superseded by the sidecar. .Their use appears to be rapidly on the increase. •During the past few weeks I have noticed\ a considerable number of cycles fitted with small; light sidecars for the accommoda- tion of a child. It is really an excellent outfit for a family party. On one occasion I passed on the road a father, mother and daughter; each riding such a combination machine with a child passenger. It is a move in the right direction. The more that can be done to get that section of the community which, cannot afford a ill:lore expensive means of , transport, into the country and the fresh- air, the better.

div.head: VALUE OF CYCLING.
div.p: THE VALUE OF CYCLING.

The value of cycling as an Id to health has never been more clearly demonstrated than in the case ,of Sir Frank Bowden, Bait, whose name appears in the list of birthday honours. Sir Frank returned from ‘China in 1886 with a fortune and a debilitating constitution. He tried every remedy, including all the European spas without effect, until he was advised to try cycling. The result was an im- mediate and complete recovery, and from that Sit Frank took an intereSt in cycling, whieh has gradually developed, and to-day, he and his only son, Mr. Harold Bowden, are the pro- prietors •of the Raleigh Cycle Co.—the largest cycle manufacturing ccimpany in the world, whose output of cydles last year was over 60,000 machines. The 'whole story of the bene- fit which Sir Frank has achieved in nearly 30 years. of cycling, is told in his book, "Cycling for Health," a book which ought to be in the hands of every middle-aged man who finds him- self beginning to feel that he i, as the saying goes, "not so young as he used to be."

div.head: HANDLE-BAR CLUTCH CONTROL.
div.p: HANDLE-BAR CLUTCH CONTROL.

The following quotation taken from a motor cycling contemporary sums up the opinions of many riders, my own included: "It is rather surprising to find anybody praising foot-con- trolled clutches in these days, and I am sure the majority favour hand control. I admit that I found hand control:required some mastering in the days of sensitive two-lever carburetters, pre- sumably because the hand control of those days did not possess very good leverage, and when one hand was exerting all its muscular energy at the left hand of the bar it was not easy for the right hand to perform delicate manipula- tions at the opposite end. But nowadays, when most clutch controls afford decent leverage and the, throttle lever can be banged open or shut fairly coarsely, the difficulty hardly arises. Given a clutqh control with a proper leverage, and a carburetter that is not sensitive, I am for the .hand control every time. I find that my usual roads jerk my foot up and down so vio- lently that delicate pedal work with a foot clutch is all but impossible." FITTING THE SPARE WHEEL.

Novices hear stories of 4rivers being able to fit a spare *heel in very little over a minute, and they wonder how it is done. If the job is tackled properly, it is a simple matter to speed up the fitting, but there are certain little points which are often either forgotten or unknown. One Such point is that the security bolts of the deflated tyre should be released before an en- deavour is made to !Cut on the wheel. If this is done the head of the tyre is loosened and the hooks of the spare wheel can be easily slipped into position. When once properly attached the security bolts must be screwed up as tightly as possible. The adjustable clamps of the spare wheel must be firmly screwed up—a wrench is a suitable tool to employ—and then the spring catches should •be released. The spare wheel may not have been used for some time, there- fore see that it is properly inflated.

RED CROSS WORK.
Presentation Of Certificates At Rathion
Court.

As we briefly reported in our last issue, the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Peter Peacock) on Vriday of last week visited the Raddon Court Red Cross Hospital, the last named for the purpose of presenting Red Cross certificates lately gained for first-aid and nursing work by Warrington candidates, pre- paratory to the forming of a new Voluntary Aid Detachment.
WHY WARRINGTON IS LINKED UP TO CHESHIRE.

Miss Sylvia Broadbent (the commandant of the local Voluntary Aid Detachment) who pre- sided, said that she thought the candidates might care to know why it was that Warring- ton was incorporated in the Daresbury Division of Cheshire. Warrington was, and quite rightly too, proud of being a Lancashire town, and possibly thought that Lancashire was higher in the scale of importance than Cheshire. Cheshire, however, had .been more forward in Red Cross work than South Lancashire. At .the outbreak of war, the'Red Cross workers of the Daresbury Division, which had had its active committee for five years, wished to train as many women as possible, and also men to serve in hospitals. They, therefore, organised lectures in Latchford and other townships of the division, and so many came from Warring- ton to attend the lectures, that she took steps to ascertain if Warrington could not be incor- porated with some division of Lancashire. A fter a deal of correspondence it was found that Lancashire was not in a position to under- take the organisation of Warrington, and she was asked to include it in the Daresbury Division of Cheshire, for Voluntary Aid Detachment purposes, until such time as a change might be found expedient. A Tribute to Miss Waring.

She appointed Miss Waring a; township- leader for Warrington, and until her departure from the neighbourhood, that lady did much excellent work, organising nursing lectures, a .rummage sale • and a lecture on Florence Nightingale, in aid of the funds of the Raddon Court Auxiliary Red Cross Hospital. Since Miss Waring's resignation she (the speaker) had not appointed another township leader, but the practical work of the B.R.C.S. in War- rington was being carried out by Miss Ewart, the class secretary, assisted by Miss Izod, the additional-class secretary. Miss Ewart had, she knew, little spare time, yet she had arranged several courses of lectures and organised examinations, as well as taking the courses her- Self, in order to qualify for nursing, which she was now doing at the Emergency Hospital.

div.head: Thanks Where Thanks Are Due.
div.p: Thanks Where Thanks Are Due.

She wished to thank Miss Ewart most heartily for her devoted work. Words could hardly express the gratitude the Detachment felt for the services of the lecturers and examiners, the Misses Phillips and Davy, and Drs. Sutherland and Hutton, who had all given of their best, at a time when all must feel overtaxed with work. In asking the Mayoress to present the prizes, Miss Broadbent said she wished heartily to congratulate all those who had passed, and if there were -any who had failed, she hoped that they would not be discouraged, but would enter again at' the first opportunity,, and so qualify to help in the work of the hospitals and the tending of the wounded, which, if undertaken in the right spirit, was the noblest work that women could do. (Applause.) The Mayoress then presented the certificates to the successful candidates, a list of whom appeared in our last issue.

div.head: NO NOBLER WORK.-
div.p: NO NOBLER WORK.-

In the course 7f a short speech, The Mayor said he was very pleased to see that the ladies had so enthusiastically taken up so fine a work. Nobody could perform a nobler work. They had responded finely, and if the men did only half so well it would be a very good thing. (Applause.) Mrs. Dakin proposed, Mrs. Wheeler seconded, and those present carried, a hearty vote of thanks to tile Mayoress, while Miss Ewart pro- posed, and the Mayor seconded a similar com- pliment to the lecturers and examiners, which was also accorded.

div.p: WOMAN'S WORLD.

Germany. Attempts to compete with the Ger- mans in mechanical and cheap toys always ended in defeat for the French, on account of the cost of production. Although Germany could sell her tin toys for almost nothing, the moulds for making them are very expensive indeed, often costing as much as fire hundred pounds each. The smallest toys also require an enormous space in which to pack and store them in readiness for their respective seasons. Toy engines require theogfeatest attention and care in their construction, and teams of skilled workmen are employed from one year's end to another in merely testing them, before selling. Simple and Economical Fashions.

Fashion § were never more varied than this summer, yet the newest 'have an air of extreme simplicity, due probably to their mid-Victorian origin. "Full-gathered skirts are further adorned with frills and flounces, yet there is no exaggeration, no discordant lines. Paris shows three distinct types of bodices, and these are worn also, in London; they are the moyen age, the fichu of the Marie Antoinette type, and the pointed bodice. The latter is the latest novelty, and suits slim figures best. It shows the old-fashioned pointed front coming below the waist, sometimes it has a basque. As a rule the waist-line is high, although the one that is very long is preferred by some modish women. The tunic is still in high favour, anti by ,its means a change of dress may be economically provided. For instance the same transparent tunic may be worn over two or even three different skirts. If in blaek it may be worn over white, or vice versa. A blue skirt provides another change, for blue and black this year form a favourite combination. Lace too may be used to advantage, and many other variations suggest themselves to women who possess a talent for turning everything to account.

White Wear More Expensive. As a result of the war, together with the recent early appearance of hot wealher, there is something like a dearth of cotton and linen fabrics for washable frocks. The closing of a large number of Qontinenial houses has con- tributed to the shortage, with the inevitable outcoMe of a rise in prices. Not only is this the case with regard to the cost of material, but the laundries announce that all washing will be charged on a higher scale, and like everything else, white summer wear "will cost you more." So also with light fabric gloves, which in normal times come largely from Germany, Austria and Belgium, and it is only
4. 4. •:..:• 4. 4. in the abetter qualities, made in this country, that there is no scarcity. In coloured wear, navy blue, deep grey, and dark restful tones lead the way. The Picturesque; Hat.

White hats are to be as popular as white dresses, and these will be made in a variety of materials as well as in straws of a hundred different kinds. The picture hat in its most alluring guise is slowly but surely making headway. Shapes are particularly becoming this .year,. and even when the brims are very wide they ,invariably take an artistic line, hut more especially is this the c4se, where they curve at the side to show the coiffure. Aero- phane and tulle are more largely employed for these hats than any ' other fabrics, they are therefore particularly light, even when the brims are slightly stiffened with fine straw. Although only a narrow edging, this enables the wearer to bend the brim at will to suit her face and features. Transparent Crowns and brims are often made of gathered tulle, and for the sole trimming a • handsome ostrich feather is laid flat on the brim, and caught lightly here and there with hand-made chiffon and velvet roses. Ostrich feathers are seen on the greater number of the newest hats and plumes, long and lovely, are admirably grouped in divers ways, but as a rule, a flat effect is produced, the high mount having for the nonce disappeared. The Importance of Belts and Sashes.

Belts and sashes are .neater, but even more important than last year., And this is not stir.' prising, for they appropriately complete an elaborate tailored suit, or lend distinction to an inexpensive cotton frock. The (ild proverb that there is nothing like leather, seems ,to be guiding dressmakers as well as tailors just now in their choice of belts, • sashes and edgings. Incongruous as it may seem, crepe frills when bound with soft black leather look very well indeed. The newest patent leather used foF belts and sashes is particularly bril- liant and glistens like jet. Buckles are of the same material as belts, and are sometimes very ornate, being inset with a dull white kid. When stiff belts are used, little patch pockets are placed at the sides, but these are black. With blue serge and khaki cloth suits. black patent leather is at its best, although in a very soft make it is used at the -waist as a swathing for ninon and cotton and crepe afternoon frocks. Belts as well as sashes. vary in width. Black satin is extensively used in this connection also, and is always in good taste.

By MARJORIE.

The First Woman Superintendent of a Circuit. In America • many women hold pastoral charges among the Unitarians and Congrega- tionalists, and some years ago, a lady was appointed as minister to a Unitarian chapel in London. Women preachers have always been fairly numerous among the Methodists, but the office of superintendent of a circuit, has so far only been filled by men. The first woman to undertake the onerous duties, and the charge of six churches, is Mrs. George Kendall, whose husband is acting as chaplain.to the Expedition- ary Force and helping in the Havre Hospital. Mrs. Kendall has been a local preacher for three years, but in addition to ministerial duties, she has now charge of all financial and business arrangements of the circuit. Besides which, money is being raised for a new church, and all the details of a bazaar are under her superintendence. The Bead Industry.

Italy has very extensive manufactures of glass beads, particularly at Venice, the city whose magnificent and unique examples of Italian architecture are now in peril of attack from bomb and shell. The glass manufactory of Murano, was once a great source of revenue to the republic; the glass workers received special privileges, and great care was taken to preserve the secrets of the craft. Before the war Austria furnished India with large quan- tities of beads, and so far there is but one manufactory of beads in England, a very modest affair at Worsley. India, however, is now devoting a great deal of attention to this art, and China makes beads in great quantities. Beads are distinctively Indian ornaments, and ancient Indian craftsmen gave them a mystic meaning. A few years ago amateurs collected beads of all kinds, but those of India were especially prized.

div.head: HOME NOTES.
div.p: HOME NOTES.
Profitable Recipes and Useful Suggestions.
Pickled Cucumbers.

To pickle cucumbers so that they will not shrivel, select sound, fresh cucumbers, wash them clean; put them in bottles and cover with the following preparation, made in the propor- tion of one tablespoonful salt, one teacupful vinegar, one teaspoonful mustard. Mildew. •

To remove mildew from a linen tablecloth, take soap and rub it well; then scrape some fine chalk and rub that also in the linen. Lay the cloth on the grass. As it dries wet it a little and the mildew will comes out. Or, two tablespoonfuls of soft soap and the juice of a lemon. Lay it on tho spots with a brush, on both sides of the linen. Let it lie a day or two till the stains disappear. • R ustiess Studs.

Be very careful, say ls Maud, in "Farm and Home," when buying dress studs that they are of the " rustless " kind. Nothing is more irritating than to find, after a dress or blouse has been laundered, that the studs used have left ironmould marks. Practically every draper can supply you with the rustless kind, and the difference in the cost between these and others is not worth noting when you take into consideration how much more useful they are. Larded Liver.

To lard a piece of meat is to insert strips of firm pork fat, Eibout 2in. long and tin. thick, at regular intervals. A larding needle is used for the purpose, but the work may be done with a sharp skewer. A calf's liver, after the usual cleansing, is larded whole, and make a nice dish and a very economical one. Place the larded liver on some chopped onions and slices of pork, in a dripping pan; season with salt and pepper, and add herbs if desired. Pour over it some soup stock or gravy, and bake in a moderate oven for about one hour. When done, remove the liver to a hot platter, thicken the gravy with flour, and pour over the liver. Savoury Cabbage.

Ingredients: Two young cabbages. 1 pint. of good stock, loz. of butter, salt, pepper, and grated nutmeg, 2oz. of rice, some. browned breadcrumbs,' 2 tablespoonfuls . of grated cheese. Method: Wash and prepare the cab- bages, put them into boiling salted water, and,

after boiling foi ten minutes, drain them thoroughly, and cut them into pieces. Wash the rice, put it into a sauceplin with the stock, and simmer it for, ten minutes. Now add the cabbage and seasoning, and simmer until the cabbage and rice are tender and the stock is absorbed. Then put the mixture into a greased fireproof dish, sprinkle over the top with the crumbs and the grated cheese, and put into a quick 'oven to brown. Serve very hot in the fireproof dish. Steaming is one of the most satisfactory ways of dealing with vegetables, but some of the coarser varieties of cabbage, which are strong in flavour, must first be plunged into boiling water for a minute or two and then rinsed in cold water before they are stoarned. in this way much of the strong flavour is got rid of.

The Judge and the Bonnet. Gov. Fort, of New Jersey, tells this story: An old quaker woman was a witness in a case which was being tried before Judge Garrison over in Jersey, and she wore a big poke bon- net which muffled her ears and prevented her hearing the lawyer's questions. Finally the lawyer appealed to the judge, 'and he ordered her to remove the bonnet.
"I'll do no such thing," she said tartly. "I am accustomed to having my will res- pected," said the judge. "Well, I don't care if you are a judge, that bonnet stays right where it is !"
"Perhaps, madam," the judge put in, ironically, "you would like to take my place as judge, too, eh?" "Not a bit of it," she shot out, "there are enough old women on the bench in Jersey as it is."
