div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information ,hi Popular
Language.

The Filthy Fly. We know as a matter of fact that flies play a most important role in the distribution of the typhoid germs. When a fly has once visited the dining-room ,or larder and sampled the milk and other food articles, they are all con- taminated with germs, some of which may be capable of transmitting disease. The filthy habits of the domestic fly beggar description and ought to be sufficiently well known now to put each and all on their guard.—Dr. Olsen in "Good Health." Corns: Cause and Cure.

Corns, like bunions, are due to the continued pressure day after day of ill-fitting boots and shoes. They are ,most often present on the upper surface of the toes, but frequently on the sole of the foot, and also between the toes when they are -spoken of as soft corns. They are very easily cured as they often, if not always, disappear when .the cause is completely removed. A patient who has to remain in bed for a prolonged period will, in many cases, get up free of corns. They, however, soon reappear when the pressure from footwear begins. There are many simple preparations which will remove a corn. Those containing saliCylic acid are especially efficacious and an be obtained from any chemist, but unless the part is kept free from 'undue pressure the Corn quickly returns.

A corn is simply an overgrowth of the horny layer of the epidermis, or outer skin. Dipping down into the papillary layer of the skin below and protruding upward above the surface it forms a cone-shaped growth and is evidently an effort on the part of Nature to protect the underlying structures from rough usage by raising a shield above. Temporary relief can be obtained by soaking the feet in very hot water and paring the corn with a sharp in- strument as a razor or scalpel; Corns between the toes will often disappear by the use of wide boots and the wearing of a small pad of absorbent cotton behind the corn and between, the toes. When a toe is much deformed, as in the case of hammer toe, it is very difficult to remove all pressure from a corn situated on its highest part. The best treatment in a condition of this kind is ampu- tation of the toe.
It is well to remember that in old people gangrene sometimes follows the paring of a corn if done too closely.--1-Dr. Bell, in "Good Health."

div.head: WAR AND THE SCHOOLS. Something the Teachers Might Teach.
div.p: WAR AND THE SCHOOLS. Something the Teachers Might Teach.

The Principal, who, on rising, Was greeted with loud and sustained applause by the students, said that when they met together in that room a year ago, for the same purpose as had drawn them together that afternoon, none of them thought for a moment that their next meeting might be clouded over by the terrible war which had burst upon this and other countries. The war had penetrated into the whole life of the nation—into every, institution and into every household; indeed, it was mak- ing its mark and leaving its effect upon all, so much so, that it was impossible even on an occasion like that and in, such a peaceful college, to keep from their minds and thoughts what was going on across the water. More than that, the war had its effect and left its impression upon the work that was carried on within those walls. On such an occasion lie would like to endeavour to show to them the immense importance of the school to the nation in the present time of war, and from the school, of course, he would naturally pass to the teachers. He generally read one news- paper at home; his wife .read another. (Laugh- ter.) He commended the plan to them; it had great advantages, for husband and wife never wanted the same paper at the. same time—a fact which Made for domestic peace and happi- ness. (Renewed laughter.) The. other day he chanced to pick up his wife's paper, and in it he found an article dealing with the instruc- tions which had been issued by one of the great educational authorities of the country, to the teachers under its supervision, as to what use they should, make of the war in their schools. Tie was very much impressed with those instructions.
The Painful Doctrine of Hate.

In the first place there was nothing about them that was reminiscent of the horrible doctrine of hate—the painful doctrine which had been so .largely engendered in the minds of German children. The teacher was to ex- hibit a large map of the, world and the atten- tion of the children was to be called to those parts of the map representing the British Empire, aml it was to be shown to them how that great Empire, dotted about in all parts of the world, was united as one man for the defence of the old Motherland. Then the idea was to point out to the children that they were children of that great united Empire, and that they owed a duty to it, and that they should try to become worthy citizens of it. Further, the lesson would seek to show to them that the cause for which England was at war was the cause of justice, of right, and of freedom— that the British soldiers were fighting for the women and children, for the homes of their kinsmen and for the liberty of the nation. The lesson included a prayer, which ended: "Take care of us also who stay behind in this quiet land. Thou bast something for' us to do. Help us to do it. Give us grace to be good, unselfish and loving, that we. may cheer those about us who are anxious or unhappy. Look down in mercy upon those who are now fighting agains. us. And soon, if it please Thee, Inake.glad all the whole world with Thy blessing of peace: for the sake of Jesus Christ our Lord."

kind of teaching to the generations to come they would be doing a work which the country could not spare or value too highly. Turning from the school to the teacher, it was as well to remember that whilst the building did not matter very much the teacher mattered every- thing. Many of the male teachers were at the Front. (Hear, 'hear.) They were where one would- have them be. (Hear, hear.) Many of the men students in the training colleges were also at the Front. The places of the teachers and, students who were away fighting must be filled by women teachers, and, of course, that meant that they would require a far greater number of women teachers during the next few years than they had required in the past. And then came the pitiful part of the business, viz., that the numbers of those ,who were coming forward for the teaching profession were, he would not say further decreasing, but, at any rate, were not showing any appreciable in- crease, or anything like the amount of increase which would enable them to fill the places of those who were absent. He hoped that, at any rate, some of the girls who were suitable for teaching would not think so much of teaching as a profession for their lives, but, rather, at the present moment, as a national duty.

div.head: Call to the Women.
div.p: The Call to the Women.

He hoped that the women of the country at the pkent moment would, so to speak, say: "If the men must go abroad to fight, we will see—even if its only for a few years—that the children of the next generation are not without fit and proper teaching, though the men are not here to give it." (Hear, _hear.) "I can say little about the college itself," the Principal continued. "There is nothing more satisfactory than when you Call say little about a college. Our history during the past year has been fv history of quiet, uneventful work. The students have done all thy could and have spent busy lives to help on the cause we all have so much at heart. The work of the college has been carried on uneventfully and normally, and that is the greatest and best service we can render to our country. To be able to carry on our work quietly in a time of stress like the present shows that the organisa- tion of the college has been carefully thought out- aml steadily carried on.. (Applause.) And I wish to say, publicly and gratefully, that the fact that we have been able to go on as we have been going is due to my colleagues—the members of my staff—many of whom have worked with me for a very long time, and all of whom have worked through these troublous days so loyally and well, that I cannot hope adequately to thank them."

Sympathy With the Former High Sheriff. The Canon next referred to the fact that last year Mr. Alfred Watkin, of Lynim, formerly High Sheriff of Cheshire, was with them for the purpose of giving the prizes to the students. They expected to have had both Mr. and Mrs. Watkin with them that afternoou, but he was sorry to say that their son had been wounded while in action. The sympathy of the audi- ence would, he felt sure, be extended to the parents, and they all wished the gallant officer a speedy recovery. (Hear, hear.) Canon Stevenson concluded with a touching reference to the late Archdeacon Barber—whose kind and genial presence, he said, they all missed—and a few words of welcome to the Dean of Chester, of whom he said, "if any man knows every- thing about training colleges it must be he." THE IMPORTANCE OF THE TRAINING

div.head: COLLEGE.
div.p: COLLEGE.
Dean of Chester and "An Honourable and Responsible Calling."

The Dean of Chester, who, on rising to speak, was cordially greeted by the students and the relatives and friends present, said that although it was twenty years since he resigned the post of Archbishops' Inspector of Training Oalieges his interest in those institutions had not, waned in the slightest degree; indeed, during the eventful years that had elapsed since he as an inspector he had learnt, more and more, the importance of the training colleges to the wel- fare of the nation. Be would, therefore, like to remind tire students of the very honourable position they held. Their duty was to train themselves in character and skill to enable them in their turn to train the children who would be committed to their care, so that those who came after them might be well fitted to be a real strength to the natioh, for without due and thorough .education, not merely on intel- lectual lines, but-chiefly in moral and religious power and force, they could not carry out the great and signal part which fell to their lot. (Hear, hear.) The post of school teacher was an honourable and responsible one. They should feel its responsibility. They had to guard the children from evil, to turn them in the ways of righteousness and holiness in the sight of God. The phrase they often, unhap- pily, heard at the close of a long life was, "I don't think lever dkd any harm to any one." It was not really expressive of the discharge of Christian duty. It should be rather, "What good have I done—for the sake of Christ and our Eternal Father—to those about me?" (Ap- plause.) That was surely enforced upon them by the Gospel of the week. They were not taught that the rich man did harm. He was not unkind to his neighbours, but he was emi- nently selfish, and if they put the question to themselves, "Did that, rich man do any good to any one?" he did not think the answer would be in the affirmative, if they understood the life of the rich man and Lazarus. For the Service of God and the Good of

div.head: Mankind.
div.p: Mankind.

Therefore, in the sense of duty, he hoped the teachers would feel themselves upheld by the sense that they were discharging a duty for ,the service of God and the good of mankind. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The very appearance of the prizes on the table impressed upon the audience the fact that the students possessed intellectual powers above :the average. It might be that some possessed conspicuous ability, and if so they should con- sider whether there was not a warning to them to take care that their intellectual ability did not lead them to vanity and pride. The Infirmary match tickets are now circu- lated, and it is the duty of all.to help to make it one big success. The Warrington section of Northern Anglers hold their first match on June 27th, from the Cooper's Arms. It is rather early, but it is a kind of a canter for all who are lovers of the Weaver. MeMbers who are without their Weaver cards on the day of match will have to pay 6d. on. Will any member who has been overlooked With tickets for the open match please apply to the Centre Secretary? HOW THE MAYOR WON HIS CHAIN

That fickle and mysterious party who is popularly supposed to regulate the vicissitudes of the weather, earned good marks from thousands of juvenile holiday-keepers on Mon- day afternoon by the generous consignment of brilliant Sunshine- he sent to help to make the seventh children's athletic festival, held under the 'auspices at the Warrington and District Teachers' Association, a success. As ustail, the festival was held on the Warrington Football Ground. Nearly fifty events down for decision, divided into heats u varying numLers up to twenty. This spelt a big i usk for the honorary- secretary (Mr. W. IL; Minards) and his assistants. But the energotic staff of helpers were well: rewarded for their, efforts by the happiness that the youngsters derived tv.m the proceedings. Those who participated in the sports vied very keenly with one another,. some good sport was witnessed by thost who did not compete. At the conclusion of the sports, which lasted nearly five hours, the prizes were presented by the Mayor and Mayoress. The ceremony took place on the grand stand. The Mayor and Mayoress were supported by Councillor E. Osborne (president of the Warrington Football Club) and 'Mrs. Osborne, Mr. E. Hawkesworth (president of the Association), and Mr. W. H. Minards (hon. secretary). The President voiced the welcome of the whole assembly to the Mayor and Mayoress, and called upon the latter to present the prizes to the boys. This part of .the proceeding having been accomplished, the Secretary annotinced that the Parochial School and Balton School had tied for the boys' shield, and would each hold the trophy for six months of the ensuing year, the Parochial School to be solders for the first half-tear,
The Mayor then distributed the girls' prizes, and the Secretary gave out 'that he girls' shield had been won by the Beamont School.

NOT; COMPLETE WITHOUT THE MAYOR. The President invited the children to show their appreciation of the kindness of the Mayor and Mayoress by giving three cheers. Since Alderman Peacock came into office, he said, he had taken a very great interest in functions in which children were concerned in the borough, and they really felt that no meeting of that kind was complete without his presence. The cheers were heartily given. •

div.head: HOW HE GOT IT.
div.p: HOW HE GOT IT.

The Mayor, in acknowledgment,. said it was not often his privilege to be present at so happy a- gathering as that afternoon's, lie could only hope that, as they all grew older, they would be as keen in their various associations of life as they had, shown themselves in their sports that day.

His Worship proceeded to tell the story of how he had just heard a little girl remark that he (the Mayor) had won his gold chain in the war. He went up to the young lady and her friend and told them that he did not win it in the war, but that he got it for being a good boy. (Laughter.) In conclusipn, the Mayor expressed the pleasure it afforded the Mayoress and him- self to be present and to present the prizes, and thanked the children for their hearty reeeption.
Before dispersing, the children sang one verse of "God Save the King."

div.head: LIBERALS ON THE GREEN.
div.p: LIBERALS ON THE GREEN.
Victorious In First Friendly Match Of
The Season.

The members of the Warrington Liberal Bowling Club took part on 'Saturday .afternoon in the first of the season's friendly matches figuring in their fixture- card, their visitors being- a team of trundlers representing the Stag Hotel (Lower, Walton) club. The tourney was witnessed by a large number of bowling enthusiasts, and proved both interesting qnd enjoyable. Each club put twenty represenl.4.- tiVes- on to the green, and the games were refereed by Mr. T. Shaw, whilst the other officials were Messrs. F. Walker, E. A. Sanders, F. Hutton and A. Price, to whom, along with the referee, thanks are due. The games were 13 up, and they resulted in the Liberals winning both singles and doubles, the former by 246 to 172, and the latter by 123 to 64, the total points being: 'Liberals, 369; Stag Hotel, 236—the margin in favour of the Liberal bowlers being, therefore, the pretty substantial one of 133. •-•

div.head: WORKHOUSE PLAY.
div.p: WORKHOUSE PLAY.
One Box Of Dominoes For All Female
Mental Patients.

"Very little in the way of amusement seems to be provided for the patients. I was told that there are draughts and dominoes for the males, but, so far as I could ascertain, there is only one box of dominoes to amuse the whole of the female patients! no musical instrument or draughts or other games. I earnestly hope that a little more may be done to brighten the lives of these poor people."

The above is an 'extract from a report from the Local Government Board, read at Wednes- day's meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, of an inspection made by Mr. Bingley—One of the visiting Commissioners of the Board of Control—of the Warrington Workhouse.

The number Of inmates of unsound mind was given in the report' as 108. As on the. occasions of previous visits by his colleagues, the in- mates were scattered about the institution, the majority being in the old mental wards, but the others being in the hospital and infirm wards. In the ordinary course, they would all by . now , have been housed in the new mental block, which was ready for occupation, but this had been temporarily devoted to the use of , wounded soldiers, and was therefore not available for the. present. In the circum- stances, he had not thought it necessary to comment in detail on the somewhat shabby appearance of the wards and dormitories, under- standing thafl their occupation was merely temporary. The patients all looked clean and well cared for, and he received no complaints whatever.

div.head: BRICKS AND MORTAR.
div.p: BRICKS AND MORTAR.
The I.Varrington Working Men's Building Society.
DOING VELL DESPITE %X

The following annual report—the forty-fiftlt— was presented at the yearly meeting of the Warrington Working Men's Permanent 'Bene- fit Building Society, at the Golborne-street Schoolroom, on Monday evening:— During the year the sum of £1,694 Os. 51. has been received as subscriptions; £2,670 7s. 4d. for repayments; and £ll 14s. 6d. entrance fees, fines, •ic.; and banker's- interest, £59 f 2,. 1041., making the total receipts £4,135 ss. 1d:; the working expenses being £B5 is. lid.
The withdrawals amount to £1,316 us. lid
The sum of .53,275 has been advanced to mem- bers:

There are 239 subscribers, holding 329 shares; and 54 borroviers, holding 236 shares; making 293 members, holding 565 shares. • . The bonuses thiseyear amount to £748 2s. Gd. on the amount lent, of which sum 136 165.• is diVided as profit, and £6ll 6s. 6d. carried to the prospective interest account.

The total amount remaining owing upon mortgages is £13,141 10s., of which only £11,575, 17s. 9d. can be regarded as capital, the balance of £1,5688 12s. 3d. representing the pro- portionate amount of interest thereon, calcu- lated for the number of years the several mort- gages have still to run. The profits for the year, including £4 15s. id-. from last account, after deducting working ex- penses, amount to £507 14s. 10d., out of which the managers recommend a dividend of 4 per cent., which will take £482 3s. Id., leaving a balance'of £25 us. 9d., £25 of which they direct be placed to the credit of the contingent fund, and the balance us. 9d". carried forward to next year's account. The total amount owing to the Society on mortgages is £13144- 10s. The valuation of the property upon which the advances have been made is £25,800.

The -whole of the managers retire. Messrs. Harding, Hope, Baxter. W. li. Wallington, Wm. Charmxl and J. W. Parker are eligible, and offer themselves for re-election. Six additional managers will be taken from the register in rotation.

div.head: WORKING UNDER A SHADOW.
div.p: WORKING UNDER A SHADOW.

Mr. W. 11. Wallington, who was voted to Ow chair, said the Society • had been through a year of uncertainty. When they met last year no one had the least idea that the Society would have to work under such a shadow as that of the, past year. Ho was glad to say that as they would see by the secretary's_ re- port -and balance sheet, the transactions that had been carried out had been successful, and the Society was in a very sound financial Position, notwithstanding the troubles it had had to meet, and the uncertainties of the year. On the proposition of Mr. J. W. Parker, the report was accepted as read. The balance sheet was also adopted..

div.head: FOUR PER CENT. DIVIDEND.
div.p: FOUR PER CENT. DIVIDEND.

The-. Chairman said that one of the 'good points about that Society was that if anyone wanted his money he, was able to get it in a very short time, owing to the stable condition of the Society. He had great pleasure in declaring that a dividend • of four per cent. would. be paid to the shareholders on their in- vestments.

div.head: RE-ELECTI ONS.
div.p: RE-ELECTI ONS.

The six retiring managers were re-elected. The managers are therefore still as follows: Messrs. Jas. 'larding •(chairman), .1. Baxter, W. H.- Wallington, Harry Hope, W. Charnock, J. W. Parker, Harry Davenport, John Grealy. Arthur Ditchfield, Jas. Gibson, John Davies and Ernest Goulden.
Messrs. Robert Lee Und T. F. Wallington were re-elected surveyors, and Messrs. John Green Chappell and Geo. Armstrong, auditors..
MANAGERS' FEES
It was agreed that the managers' fees for the ensuing year be a shilling per head per meet- ing, as usual.
A VOTE OF THANKS.

Mr. Parker proposed a vote of thanks to the 'Chairman and to the Secretary. ..The Society, he said, were excellently placed in the matter of a chairman and a secretary. He did not know what they would do without them. (Hear, hear.)
The proposition was seconded by Mr. Hill and carried.
The Chairman and the Secretary (Mr. Peter Dalton) acknowledged the vote of thanks very briefly.

div.head: RUNCORN GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN GUARDIANS.
Children's Home Electric Light Plant.
The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was 'held at Dutton on Tuesdaf, Mr. Linaker, jun., presiding.
A VOTE OF SYMPATHY.

The Chairman moved that a vote of sym- pathy with Mr. Thos. Antivis, in the loss of his wife, be passed by the Board. They knew that Mrs. Antwia had been very ill, and that there was little hope, but while there was life, there was hope. She died on Monday, June 7th. Mr. Linaker! sen., seconded, and the members carried the resolution by rising in silence: .

div.head: PAYMENTS SANCTIONED.
div.p: PAYMENTS SANCTIONED.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the payment of £l2O to the Clerk as clerk to the Assessment Committee, an annual ,subscription of £6 6s. to the Liver- pool Eye and Ear Hospital, and of £l2 2s. 6d. to Dr. Larkin for temporary assistance obtained by him.

div.head: ELECTRIC LIGHT PLANT.
div.p: ELECTRIC LIGHT PLANT.

In the minutes of the Children's Home Com- mittee, there was a recommendation to the effect that the account sent in by the eontraefors who carried out the work of erecting the electric lighting plant should be considered by. a specially appointOd committee:.
Mr. Spruce said it was felt that the charges were excessive.
The Chairman: You can only be 'questioning the men's wages; is that what you think excessive?
Mr. Spruce: Yes. It's one and twopence an hour.

The Chairman: Well, that's nothing to grumble at. It's lower than 'trade union rate. I was surprised to, find it was not more. I can't see anything against the account. Mr. Woodward said the Board knew they were dealing with firsf:class workmen, who could get their wages anywhere, and he thought they ought to pay the bill without question and consider their course of action for the future. (Hear, hear.) The only thing they could possibly challenge was the rate per hour charged. It would be quite easy to find out the proper rate of pay, and they would probably find that everything was all right. The minutes were passed, with the exception of the recommendation referred to. It was agreed that the electric light plant accolint be passed.

div.head: INMATES AND VAGRANTS.
div.p: INMATES AND VAGRANTS.

The Clerk reported that there were 119 inmates in the house, as against 130 for the corresponding time last year. The vagrants for the eleventh week of the quarter num- bered 80, as against 123 for the corresponding week last year.

div.head: WAR BONUSES.
div.p: WAR BONUSES.

The FrOdsham Joint Water Committee re- ported that Mr. J. Illidge had been appointed chairman, and Mr. F. Barnett vice-chairman. At the meeting, Mr. P. Jones gave notice to move a resolution granting a war bonus to the engineers.
The Helsby Parochial Committee reported that a war bonlis of 2s. per week had been granted to the water engineers, on the casting vote of the Chairman. •

div.head: NOT PREPARED TO IMPROVE.
div.p: NOT PREPARED TO IMPROVE.

The Weston Parochial Committee reported the receipt of a letter from the Castner- Kellner Co., stating that they were not pre- pared to improve Sweetman's Cottages, but were prepared to pull them down. Messrs. Chadwick arid Tudor, with the clerk, were appointed a deputation to confer with the com- pany's representatives on the matter.

div.head: REQUIRED TO SHOW CAUSE.
div.p: REQUIRED TO SHOW CAUSE.

The committee further decided to make a recommendation to the Runcorn Urban Dis- trict Council that Mr. Woodier be required to show cause why the building recently erected by him in-Sandy-lane in contravention of the bylaws should not be pulled down, and the Surveyor was instructed to report on other similar buildings, if any, erected in Sandy-lane. The Rural District Council were also recom- mended o ask Mr. S. Palin to show cause why a building erected by him in Overkill should not be pulled down for the same reason.

div.head: SPECIAL RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. EXPENSES.
div.p: SPECIAL RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. EXPENSES.

The Local Government Board wrote, enclos- ing formal notice declaring certain sums paid to the Clerk as clerk to the Parochial Committees of the following parishes, to be special expenses of the Rural District Council :—Prodsham Lordship, £l5; Prodsham Township, Helsby and Stockton Heath, £25 each; Weston, £2O.

div.head: SEVEN SCARLET FEVER CASES.
div.p: SEVEN SCARLET FEVER CASES.
The Medical Officer reported seven cases a scarlet fever, two at Norley, three at Froilsham, and one each at Overton and Grappenhall.
HOW DO WE STAND?

Mr. Woodward, after the Surveyor's report had been read, wanted to know how the Coun- cil -stood in relation to their Surveyors. Were the Surveyors in the ,Council's debt, or the Council in the Surveyors' debt? Mr. Linaker. sen., explained as to the pay- ment of certain sums for work done.
Mr. Woodward said he thought it was time the Council had some •permanent arrangement in the matter.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 19, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 19, 1915.
Miscellaneous on Sale.
Photograph by Birtles
STOCKTON HEATH.

Visit of Lord Derby's Recruiting Band.— Lord Derby's recruiting band vigited Stockton Heath on Saturday and again on Monday even- ing, when it paraded the township prior to the holding of a public. meeting at West Avenue. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and the meeting was also addressed by Messrs. Bretherton and Wynne Jones, both of whom are associated with the West Lancashire Territorials, and by Captain Gordon Roberts and Mr. C. E. Linaker, jun., the recruiting officer for the district.

WALKING DAY NEXT FRIDAY. Next Friday is Walking Day. The Church school will start off from St. Thomas' at two o'clock, and the procession will wend its way to Wilderspool, along Ellesmere-road, Hill Cliffe-road, Whitefield-road, Cawdor-street, and into London-road. Tea will be served in the Church Booth and Church schools. After tea the youngsters will adjourn to the Park at Wilderspool, and the remainder of the day will be spent in games and sports. The Bluecoat School Band will be in attendance as usual.

div.head: BRIDE Al\7l) BRIDEGROOM.
div.p: THE BRIDE Al\7l) BRIDEGROOM.

A pretty wedding, in which many Warring- tonians will be interested, was solemnised at the Wesleyan Church, Frodsham, on Thursday, the bride being Miss Nellie Thornton, daughter of Mr. William E. Thornton, of Deynecourt, Frodsham, and grand-daughter of Mr. Henry Thornton, and the bridegroom Mr. Archer Hodgkinson, son of Mr. W. Hodgkinson, Apsley, Grappenhall, and of the well-known firrn of Messrs. W. Hodgkinson, Ltd., of Bridge-street, Warrington. The officiating minister was the Rev. W. Stevenson, who has charge of the Frodsham Chapel. The organist of the Frodsham Parish Church (Mr. Hibbert) played the Bridal March from "Lohengrin," and also Mendelssohn's Wedding March. The bride, who was given away by her father, was attended by two brides- maids and four train-bearers.

The bridesmaids were the Misses Ella Thorn- ton (sister of the bride) and Cissie Hodgkinson (sister of the bridegroom), whilst the bride's other attendants were the Misses Phyllis E. Thornton (sister of the bride), Winifred and Barbara Thornton (daughters of the uncle of the bride—Mr. J. U. Thornton) and Flossie Morton.
Mr. Reginald Lunt officiated as best man. The bride wore a charmingly-simple gown of ivory ninon de soie, with flounces of D'Alencon lace. From her shoulders hung a train of

ivory satin charmeuse, with orange blossom, myrtle, and white heather worked in true lovers' knot. An embroidered tulle veil was worn over a mob cap, with a coronal of orange blossom mixed with white heather and myrtle. She also carried a handsome sheaf of white lilies. _ _

The bridesmaids were attired in dresses of white ninon voile over pink silk. They carried bouquets of pink carnations. The mother of the bride wore a dress of mauve crepe-de-chene and ninon, over which was a tunic of fine black Chantilly lace and a waist of handsome ribbon embroidered in silver and gold • roses. The mother of the bridegroom wore a very prdtty dress of mole silk Poplin de soie, trimmed with satin and ivory lace.

After the wedding ceremony a reception was held at Deynecourt, the residence of the bride's father—a large number of invitations having been issued and accepted—and later in the day, the newly-wedded couple left Frodsham for Windermere, where the first part of th 4 honeymoon is to be spent, Mr. and Mrs. Archer Hodgkins= subsequently proceeding to Aber- deen.

The employes of Messrs. Itodgkinson, Ltd., as well as the local staff of the Refuge Assur- ance Company—with which the bridegroom is connected—were present at the wedding, and were subsequently suitably entertained at Mersey View, Overton. •

div.head: CRIPPLED CHILDREN FETED.
div.p: CRIPPLED CHILDREN FETED.
Happy Holiday In The Country Despite The War.
MOTOR JOY RIDE.

Thursday was the occasion of the annual out- ing of the Warrington crippled children, pro- moted by the local branch of the cripples' Guild. Many luxurious motor cars had been placed at the disposal of the promoters, and these were laden with happy, smiling children, as they moved off at about 1.30 in the afternoon on the journey to the pleasant rendezvous selected, their departure being ,witnessed by the Mayor and Majoress (Alderman and Mrs. Peter Peacock).

The route set forth in the itinerary was as follows: Sankey-street, Bridge-street, Wilders- pool-causeway, Stretton, Acton Bridge, Cudding- ton, and the Chester-road to the National Children's Homes, about a mile and a half from Frodsham. After a delightful ride through the beautiful countryside, now look- ing at its best, the destination was reached at about 4 o'clock. Soon after their arrival the children partook of an excellent tea, in the spacious schoolroom. For about three hours afterwards they enjoyed themselves at cricket, or in strolling about the grounds of the beauti- fully situated homes.

div.head: THANKS FOR KINDLY HELP.
div.p: THANKS FOR KINDLY HELP.

The workers having partaken of tea, the Rev. Hugh Williamson, on behalf of the Cripples' Guild, proposed a hearty vote of thanks to those who had lent the motors, to the drivers of the same, and to the promoters and organisers of the outing. Since their last outing, he said, they had had to change their marshal, for Mr. Bellian had left them, and was now, in a sense, serving his country. Mr. J. Paterson had stepped in and filled the breach. and thanks were 'due to him for performing his duty so well. Hearty thanks were also due to Mr. Schofield, the governer of the homes. , Mr. W. Twiss also spoke. The —motors returned to Warrington via Preston • Brook, having covered altogether about 33 miles through some of the most beauti--- ful. Cheshire scenery. The number of cripples who participated in the out;ng was 136, a decrease of five on last year's total. _ _

The committee desire to express their warmest thanks to the many ladies and gentle- men who so generously contributed cars or donations for the trip, to the Chief Constable for the courteous arrangements made for the safe use of the streets, and to the Alliance Box Co., Ltd.. who lent a large motor van which carried all the provisions for tea, and several bath chairs.

Donation, were sent by Mesdames S. Riehardson, Toft, Dodds, L. Bleckly. W. B. Roberts and Sainsbury,' and Messrs. .John J. Bleckly, Ziba Armitage, J. J. Crosfield, Holman Kingdom W. Hutchings, TT, P. div.head: BURTON WOOD BLAZE.
div.p: A BURTON WOOD BLAZE.
Cause Of £lOO Farm Fire Remains
Unknown.

A call was received at the Warrington Fire Station on Monday afternoon, to a fire which had broken out on a farm belonging to Mr. Bridges, at Burtormood. The brigade, with the motor fire engine,- and under the direction of Deputy-Superintendent Cook, were soon on the scene, and, they found that the roof of a barn, partly filled with straw, had been burning and had fallen in. - The flames were subdued after 2 hours' hard work, but not before damage to the extent of about a hundred pounds, had been done, about twelve tons of provender being destroyed, together with other things, Fortunately the brigade were able to prevent the flames spreading to the adjoining buildings. The cause of the outbreak is unknown. The Newton, Fire 'Brigade: had been sfnt for, but t4ei.r.-perrico§,were not requited,..

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
FINE PLAY AT ROYAL COURT NEXT MEEK.

A capital attraction has been secured for the coming week, when Mr. W. V. Garrod and Miss Bertha Kingston will pay a return visit, bringing with them, for the first time, a play that has won world-wide success. "The Prodi- gal Parson" has been toured for twenty years throughout the British Isles, and also secured success in Australia, the 'United States of America and South Africa. Its first visit to Warrington should excite some interest. The play possesses all the requisites that make for popularity—the story is of gripping interest; there is excitement, pathos and humour of the best Imality. There are opportunities for scenic display, and the company embraces some vocalists and dancers in addition to such well- tried favourites as Messrs. Owen Remonde, Edward Leroy and Charles Hailing; Mesdames 'Blanche Leroy, Hilda Trelawney and Maude Merrick. There will be a matinee on Monday, and .two performances nightly throughout the week.

div.head: Stirring War Play This Week.
div.p: Stirring War Play This Week.

This week the boards are occupied by an ex- cellent company in a stirirng war play—a well- written, melodramatic effort that lacks nothing in the Way of excitement or patriotic appeal, and which should be seen by all who like a play that bristles with incident and is leavened with an excellent vein of humour.

div.head: SPLENDID Katt GYMNASTS AT
div.p: SPLENDID Katt GYMNASTS AT

Something quite unique in the way of bar gymnastics is to be seen at the Hippodrome this week. The Carpatti Bros.,- Roumanian gymnasts, are an extremely accomplished couple, and one is also very funny and evokes many a hearty laugh. The piece de resistance If their excellent contribution is the twist- somersault from the first to tire third bar, over the middle bar. It is a wonderful bit of acrobatics, and is greatly applauded. There is a good deal in the revue "Something Doing" that is entertaining. The funny man fulfils his function very successfully, his weird get-up and quaint . antics and mannerism arousing con- siderable mirth. The piece is presented in four effective scenes, with no lack of variety in dresses. There is some music, and a good deal more rag-time. There is also a very charming dancer. A good turn is provided by the Two Tom-Boys, who claim to be "the only ladies presenting a comedy Humsti-Bumsti act."

div.head: Fine Bill Next Week.
div.p: Fine Bill Next Week.

Gus Harris, the people's chorus idol," will top the bill at the Hippodrome next week, and other attractive turns will. include De Busse, with his piano-accordian, and Rich Taylor, the renowned whistling ventriloquist.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S RIG DRAW AT STAR KINEMA.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S RIG DRAW AT STAR KINEMA.

"Mistress Nell," a splendid film founded on the love :story of Nell • Gwynne, the great- hearted actress and the philandering Charles the Second, will form the premiere, in a tip- top programme at the ever popular Star Kinema on the first three days of next week. "The Dancing Girl" will be the title of the big week- end attraction. The programmes at the "Star" maintain their high level, and may always be relied upon for a sterling evening's amusement.
WAR ITEMS.
ARMLESS SOLDIER'S LITTLE JOKE.
Example of the spirit of the wounded war- riors at the Lord Derby War Hospital Was shown after a concert.
Visitor: `,` How have you enjoyed it, 'Tommy '?" " Tommy " (both of whose arms have been amputated): "Splendid, ma'am! Didn't you hear me clapping?"
OVER 60 SOUTH LANCS. MEN IN HUNS'
HANDS.

Over sixty men of the Lancs. Regi- ment are known to be prisoners of war in the hands of the Germans, and these men, some of 'whom are woundsid, require help in the way of extra nourishment. Gifts of cigarettes, tobacco. or any of the following articles will be grate- fully received at the Parr Hall, whence despatches are made to prisoners twice weekly: Tea, sugar, Nestle's milk, cocoa, Lyles' golden syrup (11b.), Oxo (in tablet form), assorted cheese biscuits, fresh, hard-baked bread, rolled oats, soup-packets, &c.

The Harm of Hypocrisy. h - If, he said, they had privileges, they Wu% have duties. What a marvellous privilege was to join in the worship of the Church. I was not merely joining in the phrases of th,e service with a large or small congregation !I: an isolated, village, but it was taking Puri,ti the great worship of the Catholic Church, went on in some part of the world at es.`"it hour of the day. What -a wonderful thing was to be able to work for a great cause wil" a. feeling of absolute confidence, and not a° people feeling that the ground might give waY beneath their feet at any moment. Mr. ella'c; Booth, in his book, "The Religious Life 01 London," said that amongst all the different denominations of Churches he had' visited, tr most reverent :worshippers were those of ti_ut" High Church.. "May it be so here," _e preacher went on. "May ,the strangers Wu° come here be struck by your reverenee. Professor Drummond said that he was speasi big to a young man at an American stree corner when a venerable gentleman passed. The young man said: "That's the .an, Dv' lessor, who makes more infidels in this towil than anyone else." "Why." said the Professor. "that's Deacon man replied, "he's the biggest scoundrel ill, the town, and his hypocrisy drives men out 01 the Church every day." Infidel Propaganda. . Roman Catholic priest left the Catholic Church and translated ft certain German book, whiel,t, he labelled, "'the Riddle of the "Universe. That book would probably. have been praett cally unnoticed had it" not been for Robyn' Blatchford, who took it up and advertised it klif his popular newspapers And a great deal °t harm had arisen out of the translation of th' book.

They did II? know how much good they could do apparently insignificant ways. If they all al.t something for God, irrespective of whether was popular or said to be important, the p05_51,- bilities were greater than they could foresv,`.; Just as rays of sunshine and drops of 111,1; helped to produce a bountiful harvest froal earth, so the effect of the combined efforts ° Churchmen in the work of God would b° great and glorious harvest of souls.

THE EXAMINER, 1 URDAY, JUN. 1, 19, 1915.
PRIVATE HOLBROOK LITTLEWOOD. Wounded. .

he was visited on Thursday iky his wife, who fouUd him in the best of spirits and progress- ing favourably. He is the first local soldier to be brought to that hospital. Private Littlewood, who is twenty-one years of age, formerly worked for the Firth Mattress Co., at Howley. He has been in the Territorials about four years—indeed, his period of service would have expired in March—when he answered.the call. He is at present a member of D Company, and after training at Edinburgh and in Kent, he was-drated to the Front on January 9th. As a boy he attended the Holy Trinity Day School, and he worshipped at St. Ann's Church, Wiuwick-road. He also regu- larly attended the Wycliffe P.S.A. Sergeant Allcock, of the Territorials, who, as we reported in our last issue, has also been wounded, is a cousin of Private Littlewood. MISSING. 1)1{1X .VIE JAMES GOUGH. Private James Gough, 2nd Cheshire Regi- ment, son of Mr. Owen Gough, 299, Liverpool-- road, reported unofficially in "The Exam- er " last week as being missing, is now re- ported officially as missing after an engage- ment at a place not stated on May Bth. WARRINGTON CANADIAN Missing After The Fight In Belgium. William Albert Thoma§, of the 48th Canadian Highlanders, is reported as missing. ?Ye is the son of Mr. John Henry Thomas, an iron- worker, at the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., who lived in Longshaw-street until two years ago, when he emigrated to Canada. At that time William Albert was a shopman in Warrington and a Boy Scout. He is nine- teen years of age.

Sir,—ln reference to your article of MO' 22nd, in which you discussed the earlier closing of shops, I had hoped that some steps would have been taken to attain that most laudable and desirable end. It is surely quite possible that the earlier closing of shops and markets can be effected without any loss to tradesmen: nay, with shorter hours and consequently curtailed expenses, such a move should prove a boon! But early closing can only be Made effective and just by a law or laws for such being formu- lated by the Town Council. Voluntary action -7 by any section of tradesmen is not sufficient. I, therefore, suggest that the Mayor convene - a meeting of tradespeople in order to ascertain their views, which I trust will provide the Coun- cil with a mandate to legislate in the matter. • DRAPER.
